He looked at the loom in the corner, the empty water bucket, the narrow bed pushed against the wall. He didn't feel cramped. He didn't feel the itch to leave. He felt the gravity of the place settling over him, heavier and more comforting than the Stellium mail ever was. "I'm going to fix the fence tomorrow," Kaelan announced, unbuckling his sword belt and hanging the weapon on the wall. It looked like just a piece of iron now, dormant and heavy. "And I'm going to make tea," Kaela said, moving to the small kitchen shelf. "And then we are going to sleep for a week." "Deal." Kaelan walked over to her. He didn't ask. He wrapped his arms around her waist from behind, resting his chin on her shoulder, watching the water boil. The silence in the room wasn't empty. It was full of the fire's crackle, the wind outside, and the steady, synchronized beating of two hearts that had crossed the universe just to stand right here. "Welcome home, Moon," he whispered. "Welcome home, Sun," she replied, leaning back into him. They stood there as the twin suns set, the heroes of the age, invisible and content, ready to do absolutely nothing for a very long time.

title: Part 5: Chapter 5: The Cottage
content: The morning suns did not burst into the cottage; they crept in, filtered through the thick glass of the small eastern window and the grey slate of the low eaves. The cottage was small—a single, square room of whitewashed stone and heavy timber beams that smelled of dried sage and old woodsmoke. In the medieval sense, it was a "hall house," but stripped to its absolute minimum. To the left was the hearth, black with decades of soot, where a cast-iron pot hung on a swing-arm. To the right was the workspace: Elara’s heavy oak loom and Kaelan’s sharpening wheel, sitting so close they almost touched. In the far corner, behind a modest folding screen of stretched canvas, stood the washbasin and the cedar chest for linens. And pushed against the warmest wall, away from the draft of the door, was the bed. It was a narrow frame, rope-strung and topped with a mattress of straw and wool. It was designed for one person, or perhaps two small children. It currently held two full-grown adults. Kaela woke up because she couldn't move her left arm. It was pinned under the solid weight of Kaelan’s chest. He was fast asleep, sprawled on his side, his face buried in the curve of her neck. His arm was thrown over her waist, heavy and possessive, anchoring her to the mattress. His leg was hooked over hers, their limbs a tangled knot of linen and skin. In the old days—the bad days of the Wedge—this proximity would have made him flinch. He would have rolled onto the floor to escape the "crowding." Now, he slept like a stone in a river, completely at peace only when there was zero distance between them. Kaela didn't shove him off. She shifted slightly, nuzzling her face into his shoulder. She breathed in the scent of him—wood shavings, clean sweat, and the faint, permanent smell of ozone. "You're crushing my arm," she whispered, not really complaining. "Mmm," Kaelan grunted, tightening his grip reflexively in his sleep. "It's a structural support. Essential." "You're hogging the quilt." "I am the quilt," he mumbled, radiating a low, steady heat that kept the morning chill at bay better than any wool ever could. He opened one eye—gold and blue and sleepy. He grinned. "Morning, Moon." "Morning, Sun." They lay there for another hour, watching the dust motes dance in the light beams. The cottage was cramped. If Kaelan stretched his legs, he kicked the loom. If Kaela reached out, she knocked over the water bucket. But to them, the smallness wasn't a hardship. It was a luxury. It meant they never had to shout to be heard. It meant they were never out of reach. By mid-morning, the "boring" work had begun. Kaelan stood in the garden, shirtless, sweat gleaming on his back. He was fulfilling his promise. The old, rotting wooden fence that the deer had leaped over for years was gone, torn out and used for kindling. In its place, a wall was rising. Kaelan didn't use mortar. He was building a dry-stone wall, fitting jagged river rocks together with the precision of a master puzzle solver. He picked up a heavy granite boulder, weighing easily a hundred pounds. He didn't groan. He didn't use a spell. He just hefted it, turning it in his hands until he saw the line of the grain. He set it down. It wobbled slightly. Kaelan placed his hand on the stone. He didn't melt it; he just warmed it. He softened the microscopic edges of the rock with a pulse of thermal energy, then pressed down. Click. The stone settled into place, locked tight against its neighbor. "It's too high," a voice called from the porch. Kaela was sitting in the rocking chair, shelling peas into a wooden bowl. "The deer can't jump six feet, Kaelan. You're building a fortress, not a garden fence." Kaelan wiped his forehead with his forearm. He leaned against his wall, which was currently waist-high and thick enough to stop a siege engine. "Deer are ambitious," he argued, grabbing another rock. "And I don't want them eating your mint again." "You just like lifting heavy things." "I like things that stay where I put them," he corrected. He worked until noon. The wall grew, a grey, impenetrable barrier that circled the small plot of earth. It was overkill. It was magnificent. When the suns were high, Kaela came down the steps. She carried a wooden platter with a loaf of bread (warm, heavy, and slightly burnt on the bottom—just how he liked it), a wedge of sharp cheese, and a skin of water. "Break," she commanded. Kaelan dropped the rock he was holding. He sat on the grass, his back against his new wall. Kaela sat next to him. She didn't sit across from him. She sat shoulder-to-shoulder, her knee pressing against his. They shared the bread. Kaelan tore off chunks, handing the softer inside pieces to her and keeping the crusts for himself. "It's straight," Kaela observed, looking at the wall. "And solid." "It'll last a thousand years," Kaelan said, chewing contentedly. "Long after we're gone, the deer will still be confused." He took a drink of water and handed the skin to her. He watched her drink, his eyes tracing the familiar lines of her face. He remembered the Voidlands. He remembered the silence. He remembered the terrifying vastness of the Star-Eater’s ribcage. He looked at the tiny garden. He looked at the one-room cottage with its slate roof. "I love this place," he said suddenly. Kaela lowered the waterskin. She looked at him. "The garden?" "The smallness," Kaelan said. He gestured to the hut. "I love that I can hear you breathing from the other side of the room. I love that I trip over your boots." He reached out and took her hand, his calloused, stone-dusted fingers lacing through hers. "I never want space again, Kaela. I just want this." Kaela squeezed his hand. She leaned her head on his shoulder, the rough stone of the wall pressing against her back, the warm sun on her face. "Then we stay," she said. "We bake bread. We fix fences. We sleep in the small bed." "Sounds perfect," Kaelan whispered. He picked up a stone, but he didn't put it on the wall. He just held it, feeling the weight, grounding himself in the here and now. The deer would never get in. The cold would never get in. And for the first time in their lives, neither of them wanted to get out.

title: Part 1: Chapter 1: The Art of Doing Nothing
content: The morning suns were late, or perhaps Kaela was just early. She lay in the grey twilight of the cottage, listening to the world wake up. The wind was brushing against the slate roof—the roof Kaelan had laid tile by tile two years ago—making a soft, scratching sound that used to terrify her, but now just sounded like home. She didn't move. She couldn't move, even if she wanted to. Kaelan was a heavy sleeper. Not just in depth, but in actual mass. He was sprawled across the majority of the narrow mattress, his left arm thrown over her waist like a seatbelt, pinning her to the sheets. His face was buried in the curve of her neck, his breathing slow and rhythmic, sending puffs of warm air against her skin. Kaela stared at the wooden beams of the ceiling. She counted the dried bundles of sage and lavender hanging from the rafters. Seventeen bundles, she thought. We need more mint. She shifted her leg, trying to find a patch of cool sheet. Kaelan instantly grumbled in his sleep, his arm tightening reflexively, pulling her flush against his chest. "You're a furnace," she whispered, poking his forearm. "Structural... integrity," Kaelan mumbled, not opening his eyes. "Don't wiggle. You'll collapse the building." "The building is stone, Kaelan. It's fine. My bladder, however, is not." Kaelan sighed—a long, dramatic exhalation of a man being asked to perform a Herculean task. He rolled onto his back, releasing her from the clamp. "Fine," he groaned, rubbing his eyes with the heels of his hands. "But you're letting the cold in." Kaela sat up, shivering as the morning air hit her skin. She grabbed her shawl from the bedpost and wrapped it around her shoulders. "It's summer, Sun. It's not cold. You just run at the temperature of a smelting pot." She climbed over him—there was no space to walk around the bed—and padded across the cool floorboards to the washbasin behind the screen. When she came back, Kaelan was awake. He was propped up on his elbows, watching her with sleepy, gold-blue eyes. His hair was a black disaster, sticking up in every direction. "Tea?" he asked hopefully. "If you start the fire," she countered. "Deal." Kaelan didn't get up. He just pointed a finger at the hearth across the room. He didn't use a spell; he just projected a tiny, concentrated thought of heat. Pop. The kindling in the fireplace smoked, then burst into a cheerful orange flame. "Show off," Kaela smiled, filling the kettle from the water bucket. "Efficiency," Kaelan corrected, falling back onto the pillow. "Come back here while it boils. You're too far away." Kaela set the kettle on the swing-arm over the fire. Then, she walked back to the bed. She didn't hesitate. She climbed back in, curling up against his side, resting her head on his shoulder. He wrapped his arm around her immediately, the circuit of their touch closing with a contented hum. They lay there for ten minutes, watching the firelight dance on the whitewashed walls. They didn't talk about space. They didn't talk about wars. "Horg says Clinker is teething again," Kaelan murmured, his fingers idly tracing patterns on her arm. "He chewed through the gate latch yesterday." "We should bring him some apples," Kaela said. "The sour ones from the old tree. He likes the crunch." "And Joren wants me to look at the watchtower steps. Says they're creaking." "You built those steps a year ago. They're solid oak." "Joren just wants company," Kaelan said. "He wants to tell me the story about the River Troll again." "You should let him." "I will." The kettle began to whistle. "Work time," Kaelan groaned, but he was smiling. He kissed the top of her head. "I'll handle the fence today. You get the apples." "Deal." Sunstead in the mid-morning was a bustling ecosystem of red dust and gossip. Kaela walked down the main street, a basket hooked over her arm. She waved to the Tanner, who was stretching a hide in the sun. She nodded to the Miller’s children, who were chasing a hoop with a stick. She didn't wear a hood. She didn't hide her face. Two years ago, people used to stop and stare when the "Scions" walked by. They would bow, or whisper, or look terrified. Now, they just waved. "Morning, Kaela!" Mrs. Gable shouted from the open window of the bakery. The smell of yeast and cinnamon wafted out, thick enough to chew. "Morning, Mrs. Gable," Kaela called back, leaning on the windowsill. "Do you have the dark loaves?" "For you? Always." The baker bustled disappear and returned with two loaves of bread—dark, heavy rye with a crust like bark, exactly how Kaelan liked it. "And," Mrs. Gable added, sliding a small paper sack across the counter with a conspiratorial wink, "a little something extra. For the boy." Kaela peeked inside. It was a "broken" pie—a cherry tart that had collapsed in the oven. It looked like a mess. It smelled like heaven. "He'll love it," Kaela laughed. "He says the broken ones taste better because the juice caramelizes on the pan." "He says that so I don't feel bad about dropping them," Mrs. Gable huffed, wiping her floury hands on her apron. "He's a good lad. How's the wall coming?" "It's... substantial," Kaela admitted. "I think he's trying to fortify the garden against a siege, not a deer." "Let him build," Mrs. Gable advised. "Men like Kaelan need to move heavy things. Keeps them from thinking too much." She leaned closer, her voice dropping. "Is he... sleeping well?" The town knew about the nightmares. In the first few months after their return from the South, Kaelan had woken up screaming more than once, shaking the cottage with accidental bursts of heat. "He is," Kaela said softly. "No dreams for weeks. Just snoring." "Good," Mrs. Gable nodded firmly. "You tell him to come down for supper on Freeday. I'm making roast mutton. And tell him to bring that appetite of his." "I will. Thank you, Martha." Kaela put the bread and the tart in her basket. She walked toward the orchard at the edge of town, her heart light. She loved this. She loved that her biggest problem today was carrying enough apples to satisfy a giant, metal-eating badger. She loved that her brother was just "the lad" to the baker, not the Solar Engine or the God-Slayer. She picked a basketful of the hard, green apples from the wild trees near the river. As she walked back up the ridge path, she stopped. She looked at the cottage. From here, she could see Kaelan in the garden. He was shirtless, his back glistening with sweat in the midday suns. He was lifting a stone the size of a beer keg, setting it gently atop the wall. He stepped back, hands on his hips, admiring the line. He looked happy. Kaela felt a swell of affection so strong it almost knocked the wind out of her. Stay like this, she thought, projecting the wish into the universe. Just stay like this forever. The stone fit. Kaelan ran his hand over the rough granite. It sat perfectly flush against its neighbor, locked in by gravity and friction. "That," Kaelan declared to the empty garden, "is a good rock." He wiped his forehead with his arm. He looked at the wall. It was four feet high and two feet thick. It encircled the small plot of land where Kaela grew her herbs and vegetables. Ideally, a garden fence should be a light, wooden thing. This was a rampart. "Overkill?" he asked himself. He looked at the delicate green shoots of the mint plants peeking out of the soil. He remembered how upset Kaela had been three years ago when the deer ate them down to the roots. "Nope," he decided. "Necessary security." He picked up his water jug and took a long drink. The water was cool, drawn from the deep well. He heard footsteps on the path. He knew the rhythm before he saw her. Step-light-step. Kaela came through the gate. She was carrying a heavy basket of apples and bread. She looked flushed from the walk, her copper hair escaping her braid. "Delivery," she called out. Kaelan walked over to her. He took the heavy basket from her arm as if it weighed nothing. "You got the dark bread," he noted, peeking inside. "And... is that a pie disaster?" "Mrs. Gable sent it. She says you need to keep your strength up for all this... siege engineering." Kaela walked over to the wall. She pushed against it. It didn't budge. It felt as solid as the mountain itself. "It's high, Kaelan," she noted, looking at a spot where he had built it up to five feet to block the prevailing wind. "Deer can jump," Kaelan defended, breaking off a piece of the crusty bread. "Deer, yes. I think this would stop a battering ram." "Well, you never know," Kaelan grinned, sitting down in the grass with his back against his creation. "Rogue battering rams are a menace this time of year." Kaela sat next to him. She leaned her head on his shoulder. "It's beautiful," she said honestly. "It looks like it's always been here." "I like the stone," Kaelan admitted, looking at his hands. "It's quiet. It waits for you." He offered her a piece of the pie. They ate in silence, watching the clouds drift over the Razor Peaks in the distance. Those mountains used to terrify him. They used to be the barrier between him and his destiny. Now, they were just scenery. "Horg wants us for dinner on Freeday," Kaela said, wiping cherry filling from her thumb. "Mutton?" "Mutton." "I'm in." Kaelan finished the pie. He brushed the crumbs from his chest. He reached out and took Kaela’s hand. Her fingers were stained with apple dust; his were grey with stone dust. "I was thinking," Kaelan said. "Dangerous." "I was thinking we should plant an apple tree. Inside the wall. Right there in the corner." Kaela looked at the spot. "It'll take years to fruit." "We're only twenty," Kaelan said. "We have years." "Okay," Kaela squeezed his hand. "An apple tree. And maybe a bench. So I can watch you work without getting grass stains on my dress." "I can build a bench," Kaelan said confidently. "I'll make it out of stone." "Of course you will." They sat there as the afternoon suns began to dip, bathing the red dust of Sunstead in a warm, golden light. It was a perfect Tuesday. The wall was straight. The bread was good. The sister was safe. Kaelan closed his eyes, listening to the hum of the bees in the clover, unaware that beneath him, miles below the crust, a clock he had set a billion years ago was about to strike midnight. "Nap?" Kaelan suggested. "Nap," Kaela agreed.

title: Part 2: Chapter 2: The Alarm Clock
content: The potatoes were coming in nicely. Kaelan knelt in the rich, red soil of the garden, his hands caked in dirt. The stone wall he had finished yesterday stood solid and grey against the morning suns, a fortress protecting the mint. It was a quiet Tuesday. Horg was hammering a plowshare down in the valley—a rhythmic clang-clang that was the heartbeat of the town. Kaela was sitting on the new stone bench Kaelan had built into the corner of the wall. She was shelling peas, the pods popping with a crisp snap. Kaelan pulled a potato from the earth. It was lumpy and brown. It was perfect. He wiped his hands on his trousers and sat back on his heels. He looked at her. "You missed a spot," he said, pointing to a pea pod that had fallen into the grass. "I'm saving it for the ants," Kaela replied without looking up. "They have quotas too." Kaelan laughed. He stood up, dusting off his knees. He walked over to the bench. He didn't sit down. He stood behind her, wrapping his dirty arms around her shoulders, resting his chin on top of her head. Kaela leaned back into him instantly, dropping the peas to rest her hands over his forearms. "You're getting dirt on my dress," she murmured, but she squeezed his arm. "It's clean dirt," Kaelan said. "It's our dirt." He tightened the hug, rocking her slightly. The hum of the Circuit—that golden, warm connection between their minds—flared with contentment. "You know," Kaelan whispered into her hair, "I was doing the math this morning. By my calculations, with the current interest rate of 'Forever,' I think I'm going to be paying this hug debt until the suns burn out." "Longer," Kaela corrected softly. "You forgot the compound interest from the winter of '16." "Right. The winter." He pressed a kiss to her temple. "So, eternity then? Is that the term?" "Eternity seems fair," she agreed. "Good," Kaelan said, his voice dropping to a rumble in his chest. "Because I'm never paying it off. I'm just going to keep defaulting on the loan so I have to keep holding you." "I accept your terms, Sun." They stayed there for a moment, suspended in the amber light of the morning. It was perfect. Then, the world stopped. It wasn't a sound. The birds were still singing. Horg was still hammering. It was a vibration. It started deep—so deep it felt like it was coming from the other side of the planet. It traveled up through the bedrock, through the red dust, and into the soles of Kaelan’s boots. Thrummmmmmm. It felt like a massive, subterranean generator cycling up. Kaelan froze. He pulled back slightly, his hand going to the stone wall to steady himself. "Kaela," he said. His voice was low, but it cut through the morning air. "I feel it," she said. She stood up, the bowl of peas sliding forgotten to the grass. She looked at her tea mug sitting on the bench. The liquid inside was rippling in perfect concentric circles. "Is it an earthquake?" Kaela asked, grabbing his arm. "The tectonic plate?" "No," Kaelan said. He closed his eyes. He engaged the Engine, pushing his senses down into the earth, past the crust, past the mantle. He felt the iron. He felt the massive, liquid metal ocean at the center of the world churning. It wasn't shifting naturally. It was spinning. It was aligning. And it felt... familiar. "It's not a quake," Kaelan whispered, his face draining of color. "It's a startup sequence." Suddenly, the air in the garden changed. The hair on Kaelan’s arms stood up. The iron shovel leaning against the stone fence rattled. Then, it lifted. It floated three inches off the ground, suspended by an invisible magnetic grip. "Kaelan," Kaela said, pointing to the porch. The iron nails in the timber beams were groaning. The cast-iron pot by the door was sliding across the floorboards, pulled North. "Gravity?" Kaela asked. "Magnetism," Kaelan corrected. He stood up, wiping the dirt from his hands. "Massive, planetary-scale magnetism." He looked at his own hands. The blood in his veins—rich with iron—tugged slightly, pulling him. "Why?" Kaela asked. "Why now?" Kaelan looked at the sky. He looked at the suns he had forged. He remembered a conversation from a billion years ago, in a library made of light. “I put a little extra iron in the core. Just in case.” "In case of what?" Kaela asked, reading his mind through the Circuit. "I don't know," Kaelan admitted, terrified. "I don't remember setting the alarm. But I definitely just heard it go off." The hum grew louder. And then, for the first time in history, the compasses in Sunstead didn't point North. They pointed Down. Far beyond the warmth of the Twin Suns, in the space between galaxies where light dared not tread, a Presence stirred. It did not have a body. It did not have a throne. Malakor had built a tower of stone to mimic it; Seraphina had sought to birth a body to house it. They were small minds. They thought in terms of matter. The Master was not matter. It was the Null. It was the static at the end of the radio signal. It had been waiting. For eons, the Earth had been silent—a shielded experiment hidden in the arm of the Milky Way. The "Extra Iron" Solas had placed in the core acted as a dampener, a magnetic Faraday cage that hid the Scions' light from the deep dark. But now, the cage was vibrating. The core was spinning up. The shield was dropping to become a weapon. The Unseen focused its attention. It didn't see with eyes. It saw with gravity. It felt the pulse of the binary star system. It felt the awakening of the Iron Heart. "Found you," the Void whispered across the light-years. It didn't send an army. It didn't send a fleet. It sent a Signal. A single, discordant frequency—an "Anti-Song"—aimed directly at the vibrating core of the blue planet. Malakor had wanted to rule the world. Seraphina had wanted to eat the stars. The Unseen simply wanted to turn the page. And Earth was a typo it intended to erase. "My hammers are floating!" Horg bellowed, trying to grab a sledgehammer that was drifting lazily toward the ceiling. The smithy was in chaos. Every iron tool—tongs, nails, horseshoes—was suspended in the air, vibrating with the low hum that was shaking the whole town. Clinker, the massive iron-bristle beast in the pen out back, was howling—a sound like grinding gears—as the metal quills on his back stood straight up, magnetized. "It's the core!" Kaelan shouted, running into the shop. He grabbed a floating anvil by the horn and hauled it down, slamming it onto its stump. "Horg! Get everyone outside! Away from the metal!" "What did you do, lad?" Horg yelled, wrestling a cloud of nails. "Did you break the sky again?" "I think I broke the floor this time!" Kaelan admitted. Kaela stood in the doorway. She wasn't looking at the floating tools. She was looking at the horizon. The sky to the North—over the Voidlands—was changing. The Auroras were back. But they weren't the gentle green and violet curtains of the past. They were red. Deep, blood-red ribbons of magnetic fire tearing through the atmosphere. "Kaelan," Kaela projected, her mind sharp and urgent. "Look North." Kaelan dropped the anvil. He stepped out. He saw the red sky. He felt the pull in his blood. "The core isn't just spinning," Kaelan realized. "It's projecting. It's opening a door." "Where?" "Underground," Kaelan said. "Deep. The Magnetic North just moved. It's not at the pole anymore." He pointed to the center of the Voidlands, right where Malakor’s tower used to stand. "It's there. The crater. It's an intake valve." "An intake for what?" Horg asked, stumbling out of the shop, watching his hammers drift out the window. "For us," Kaela whispered. She looked at her brother. She saw the fear in his eyes—not fear of a monster, but fear of his own creation. "The core is calling us home, Kaelan. We have to go down there. We have to answer the phone before..." "...before the thing on the other end hangs up," Kaelan finished grimly. He looked at his peaceful town, now rattling with magnetic tremors. He looked at the slate roof he had just finished. "So much for the garden," Kaelan sighed. He reached for his sword. It floated into his hand before he could grab it. "We need the boat," Kaelan said. "But we aren't sailing on water this time." "Magma?" Kaela asked. "Magma," Kaelan confirmed. "We're going to the center of the Earth."

title: Part 3: Chapter 3: The Magnetic Highway
content: The Iron Keel sat in the middle of the dusty street outside the forge, looking completely out of its element. It was heavy, squat, and distinctly marine. "You want to do what?" Horg asked, flipping up his welding mask. The air in the shop was thick with the smell of ozone and burnt hair; half his tools were currently bobbing against the ceiling, pinned there by the magnetic screaming of the North. "I want to slide it," Kaelan said, patting the oak hull. "The pull is strong, Horg. It nearly ripped the shovel out of my hand in the garden. If we reinforce the keel with pure, conductive iron, I can lock it into the current." "Like a leaf on a stream," Kaela added, looking at the map spread out on a barrel. "Only the stream is invisible, moving at sixty miles an hour, and aiming straight for a volcano." Horg scratched his beard with a pair of floating tongs. He looked at the boat. He looked at the vibrating compass on his workbench, the needle pinned hard to the North. "It's mad," Horg decided, a grin splitting his soot-stained face. "I love it. But you have a problem, lad." "Just one?" "Stopping," Horg said, kicking a dirt clod. "If you hook this tub to the magnetic line, you're going to be a missile. Momentum is going to be your enemy. If you hit a turn in the Red Canyon at full tilt, you'll smear yourself across the canyon wall. You need brakes." "I can cut the connection," Kaelan argued. "I'm the switch. If I let go of the magnetic feed, we stop accelerating." "Aye, you stop accelerating," Horg corrected. "But a two-ton oak boat moving at the speed of a galloping horse doesn't just stop because you asked it nicely. You'll slide for miles. You need friction." Horg got to work. The retrofit was brutal and loud. The town watched from a safe distance as the blacksmith and the Scion turned a fishing boat into a tank. The Runners: Horg took the iron bands from the hull and welded thick, polished plates of soft iron over them. He shaped them like sled runners—wide and flat to distribute the weight over grass and gravel, but sharp enough to bite into ice when they reached the mountains. "Pure iron," Horg grunted, fusing a seam with a shower of sparks. "Conducts the field better. You'll feel the road through these, Kaelan." The Brakes: This was Horg’s masterpiece. He installed two massive, lever-operated iron "plows" on the stern, flanking the rudder. "Drag-brakes," Horg explained, demonstrating the mechanism. "You pull this lever, and these teeth dig into the dirt. It'll tear up the road, and it'll shake your teeth out, but it'll slow you down before you hit a tree." The Steering: The river rudder was useless in the air. Horg replaced it with a heavy-duty "Tail-Skid"—a reinforced iron fin that could be ground into the earth to force the boat to drift-turn. "It's not precise," Kaela noted, testing the weight of the tiller. "It's brute force." "It's a boat on dirt, lass," Horg chuckled. "Precision went out the window an hour ago. You steer with weight. You steer with grit." The Canopy: Finally, they addressed the danger of rolling over. Horg bolted a cage of steel bars over the open cockpit, welding sheets of scrap metal to form a protective shell. It looked less like a cabin and more like a bunker. By sunset, the Iron Keel was unrecognizable. It sat low and heavy on its new runners, the iron gleaming in the dying light. "She's heavy," Horg warned, slapping the armored flank. "If the magnetism cuts out, you're going to be a very expensive lawn ornament." "It won't cut out," Kaelan said, looking North. The red aurora was pulsing brighter than ever, a bleeding wound in the sky. "The earth is screaming." "Then go," Horg said, handing Kaelan a pair of heavy leather goggles. "And bring it back. I'm running out of scrap metal to patch her up." Kaelan put on the goggles. He climbed into the armored cockpit. "Kaela?" She climbed in beside him, strapping herself into the harness Horg had bolted to the bench. She checked the drag-brake levers. "Brakes are set," she confirmed. "Map is ready. Navigation is... theoretical." "Theoretical is my favorite kind of plan," Kaelan grinned. He placed his hands on the iron dashboard Horg had installed. He closed his eyes. He reached out with his mind, past the wood, past the air, feeling for the singing, violent river of magnetic force tearing through the world. He found it. "Connecting," Kaelan whispered. He pushed his will into the iron runners. CLANG. The boat lurched violently. The iron skids magnetized instantly, locking onto the field lines with a force that groaned through the frame. The boat lifted an inch off the ground, hovering on a cushion of magnetic repulsion. "Hold on!" Kaelan yelled. He released the magnetic brake. The Iron Keel didn't roll. It shot forward. It accelerated with a force that threw them back into their seats. They blasted down the main street of Sunstead, kicking up a rooster tail of red dust three stories high, leaving a stunned blacksmith and a cheering town in their wake. They were surfing the planet. The plains of the Emerald Valleys blurred into a smear of green and gold. Kaelan sat in the stern of the Iron Keel, his hands vibrating against the iron tiller. He wasn't steering so much as aiming. The magnetic pull was a relentless, screaming force that wanted to drag them straight North at terminal velocity. "Speed check?" Kaelan shouted over the roar of the wind. "Fast!" Kaela shouted back from the passenger seat. She was grinning, her hair whipped into a frenzy by the slipstream leaking through the viewports. "We're doing at least sixty! We just passed the Old Mill in three seconds!" "Tree line coming up!" Kaelan warned. "The foothills are thick this time of year. We can't take them at this speed." Ahead, the rolling grass gave way to the dense, dark pines of the lower Razor Peaks. There was no road here—only deer trails and the memory of a path Kaelan had walked alone three years ago. "Brakes!" Kaela commanded. Kaelan grabbed the heavy iron levers Horg had installed on his left. He hauled back. SCREEEEEEECH. The drag-brakes—massive iron plows mounted on the stern—slammed into the earth. Dirt and rocks sprayed thirty feet into the air behind them. The boat shuddered violently, fighting the momentum. They slowed from a blur to a manageable, terrifying slide. "Slalom!" Kaelan yelled. They hit the trees. Kaelan fought the tiller. He drifted the heavy boat between two ancient oaks, the iron runners scraping bark. He banked off a mossy boulder, sending sparks flying into the ferns. It was chaos. It was exhilarating. They slid into a small clearing and coasted to a stop, the magnetic pull humming impatiently in the hull, waiting for Kaelan to release the brakes. The dust settled. Kaelan took a deep breath, his heart hammering against his ribs. He looked out the reinforced canopy. He froze. He knew this clearing. It wasn't just a patch of woods. To his left was a familiar, gnarled pine tree with a distinctive split in the trunk. And beneath it was a circle of blackened stones—the remains of a campfire. "I slept here," Kaelan whispered. Kaela looked at him. She followed his gaze to the fire pit. "On your way North?" "Yeah." Kaelan stared at the stones. A memory washed over him—not a vague recollection, but a visceral, sharp-edged echo of the past. He remembered sitting right there, three years ago. He had been cold. He had been eating a piece of dried meat that tasted like sawdust. But he remembered what he had felt. He hadn't felt lonely yet. The loneliness hadn't set in until the bear attack. That night, sitting by that fire, he had felt... relieved. Iron does not cuddle, the Wedge had whispered in his mind. He remembered looking at the empty space where his sister should have been and thinking: Finally. No more noise. No more weakness. I am a warrior now. I don't need anyone. He had hugged himself, shivering in the thin blanket, and told himself that the shivering was just weakness leaving the body. He had been proud of his isolation. He had mistaken the numbness of the Wedge for the hardness of a shield. "Kaelan?" Kaela’s voice pulled him back. She wasn't looking at the fire pit. She was looking at him, her silver eyes filled with concern. She could feel the shadow of the memory through the Circuit—the cold, oily residue of Malakor’s programming. Kaelan looked at her. He looked at the small, iron-reinforced cockpit Horg had built. It was tight. The seats were bolted so close together that their shoulders were pressed firmly against each other. There was no space here. No "dignity" of distance. And it was perfect. "I was such an idiot," Kaelan murmured, shaking his head. "I sat right there and congratulated myself for being alone. I thought I was free." "You were sick," Kaela said fiercely. She reached out and took his hand, squeezing it hard enough to hurt. "You had a parasite in your head telling you that love was heavy." "I know," Kaelan said. He released the tiller. He didn't care about the magnetic pull. He turned in his seat, fighting the constraints of the safety harness, and pulled her into him. He wrapped his arms around her, burying his face in her neck. He breathed in the scent of her—sage, sweat, and life. He hugged her with the desperation of a man who knows exactly how cold the alternative is. "I'm glad Horg built this small," Kaelan whispered into her hair. "I never want to be that far away from you again. Not even across a campfire." Kaela melted against him, her head resting on his chest. "You won't be. We're a set, Sun. Forever." "Forever," Kaelan agreed. He thought about that word. Forever. They were Scions. They were older than the trees outside. They had forged the stars before they were born into these bodies. These human forms—Kaelan and Kaela—were mortal. They would age. They would eventually wear out, just like the boots he had worn on his first journey. But the Twins... Solas and Lunara... they were eternal. When these vessels failed, they would find others. Or they would return to the light. But right now, feeling the thump of her human heart against his human ribs, Kaelan decided that he liked this version the best. He liked the grit. He liked the way she smelled like rain. He liked that he had to work to keep her warm. "Ready to go?" Kaela asked, pulling back slightly to look at him. "The mountain is waiting." Kaelan kissed her forehead. He let her go, but only far enough to grab the controls. "Ready," he said. He released the brakes. "Hang on, Moon. We're going up." The Iron Keel surged forward, leaving the ghosts of the past in the dust, rocketing toward the Razor Peaks and the burning heart of the world. The suns dipped below the jagged rim of the High Chasm, painting the sky in bruises of violet and indigo. "Camp," Kaelan said, his voice tight. He pulled the heavy iron levers. The drag-plows bit into the shale, throwing up a cloud of grey dust. The Iron Keel shuddered and skidded to a halt just fifty yards from the edge of the cliff. "We're stopping?" Kaela asked, unbuckling her harness. "We made good time today. We could push for the ridge." "No," Kaelan said. He climbed out of the cockpit, his boots crunching on the loose rock. "I need to stop here." He walked to the edge of the precipice. The wind whistled through the gap, a low, mournful flute note that he remembered from his nightmares. Three years ago, he had stood here shivering, starving, and convinced that he was unworthy of love. He had seen a vision of his sister telling him to let go. He looked down. He expected the abyss. He expected the freezing mud ledge where he had landed, broken and weeping. But the mud was gone. Or perhaps, it had never really been mud—only seen through the filter of his own misery. Twenty feet down, fed by the spring thaw from the peaks above, was a pool of crystal-clear water. It sat on the wide stone ledge like a turquoise gem, calm and inviting. "It's water," Kaelan whispered. "It's a spring," Kaela said, appearing at his side. She looked down, fearless. "And we are dusty." Kaelan looked at her. He looked at the water. "I fell there," he admitted quietly. "I thought I was falling forever. But I just landed in a puddle." "Then let's wash off the memory," Kaela said. She didn't wait. She unclasped her cloak and laid it on the rocks. She pulled her tunic over her head. She kicked off her boots. In the twilight, her skin seemed to glow with its own soft luminescence. She wasn't ashamed. She wasn't hiding. She stood on the edge of the cliff, naked and unbothered by the cold wind. "Coming?" she asked, looking back at him. Kaelan took a breath. He stripped off his heavy travel gear—the leather vest, the linen shirt, the trousers stiff with red dust. He left them in a pile next to hers. "Yeah," he said. They climbed down the narrow goat path Kaelan had once clawed his way up. They reached the ledge. The air here was still, protected from the wind. They stepped into the water. It was brisk, shocking the heat from their skin, but it wasn't the biting freeze of the Voidlands. It was clean mountain water. Kaelan submerged himself. He let the water wash over his head, scrubbing the road dust from his hair. When he surfaced, he shook his head like a dog, spraying droplets everywhere. Kaela laughed, splashing him. He splashed her back. They played. In the place where he had once wanted to die, they played like children. Afterward, they sat on the warm stone ledge, letting the residual heat of the rock dry them. Kaelan opened the food pack. He handed Kaela a chunk of sharp cheddar and a thick slice of Mrs. Gable’s dark rye bread. They ate in silence, their shoulders touching, watching the stars come out over the chasm. "I hated this place," Kaelan said around a mouthful of bread. "I thought it was the end of the world." "It was the end of a world," Kaela corrected gently. "It was the end of the world where you thought you had to be alone." She leaned her head on his shoulder. "I like this place now. It has a nice view." "It does," Kaelan agreed. He finished his bread. He looked at his clothes drying on the rocks above. They wouldn't be ready until morning. "We'll sleep in the boat," he decided. "But... thanks for coming down here with me." "Always," Kaela said. She stood up, stretching in the moonlight. She offered him a hand. "Come on, Sun. Let's go home." Kaelan took her hand. He climbed back up the cliff, leaving the ghost of the broken boy down on the ledge, drowned in the clear water of the truth. They climbed into the cabin of the Iron Keel, curled up under the furs, and slept soundly on the edge of the abyss, untroubled by the dark. The suns rose over the High Chasm, turning the grey shale into gold. Inside the armored cockpit of the Iron Keel, the air was still and warm, trapped by the heavy iron canopy and the fur blanket. Kaelan woke up because his nose tickled. Kaela’s hair had escaped her braid during the night and was currently draped across his face. He didn't brush it away. He inhaled. It smelled of the mountain spring water they had bathed in last night—clean, cold, and mineral-sharp. He shifted slightly. Kaela was asleep on his chest, her arm thrown over his neck, her legs tangled with his under the furs. The contact was total. Skin to skin. Heart to heart. In the years since the Star-Eater, this had become his baseline. If he wasn't touching her, he felt like he was holding his breath. When he held her, he could breathe. "Morning," he rumbled, the vibration traveling through his chest into her cheek. Kaela stirred. She didn't open her eyes. She just tightened her grip, nuzzling into his neck. "Five more minutes," she mumbled. "The suns are up, Moon. And our clothes are on the rocks." "The rocks are cold." "I'll warm them." "You're already warm." Kaelan laughed softly. He kissed the top of her head. "We have a schedule. The magnetic pull is getting stronger. If we don't move, the boat might leave without us." They untangled themselves reluctantly. The morning air outside the blanket was biting, a reminder that they were heading North. They climbed out of the boat, shivering in the dawn light. Kaelan scrambled down the cliff path to the ledge where they had bathed. Their clothes were dry, stiffened by the wind and the residual heat of the stone. He tossed Kaela her tunic. She caught it, pulling it on quickly. They dressed standing on the edge of the precipice where Kaelan had once thought his life ended. Now, it was just a breakfast stop. Kaelan pulled on his trousers and boots. He shook out his linen shirt. "Do you remember," Kaela asked, fastening her belt, "when you told me iron doesn't cuddle?" Kaelan winced, buttoning his vest. "I try not to." "I do," she said. She walked over to him. She reached out and fixed his collar, her fingers brushing his neck. "I remember thinking you hated me." "I hated myself," Kaelan corrected. He covered her hands with his own. "I thought I had to be a wall. Walls don't have sisters." "I like the door better," she said, looking up at him. "Me too." They climbed back up to the boat. They ate a quick meal of dried fruit and hardtack, washing it down with water from the spring. Then, they got to work. "Goggles," Kaelan ordered. They pulled the heavy leather goggles down. Kaelan grabbed the iron levers. He closed his eyes. He felt the hum of the earth. It was screaming now—a frantic, magnetic siren song pulling them North. Click. The runners locked in. The boat lurched. "Hanging on?" "Drive," Kaela said. Kaelan released the brakes. The Iron Keel launched forward. They cleared the rest of the High Chasm in minutes, blurring past the jagged rocks. By noon, the terrain changed. The grey rocks gave way to the flat, obsidian sheets of the Outer Voidlands. The temperature plummeted. The wind howled against the iron canopy. They were surfing on black ice now. "Kaelan," Kaela said, pointing ahead. "Heat signature. Old." Kaelan looked through the viewport. Miles ahead, in the middle of the featureless black plain, was a blemish. It looked like a scar. The ice was pitted, melted, and refrozen in a chaotic, jagged pattern. Kaelan slowed the boat. He didn't stop, but he eased back on the magnetic feed, letting them drift closer. He knew this place. Three years ago, there had been a tent here. There had been green trees, a hot spring, and a woman in a red dress offering him a cup of wine. Seraphina’s Oasis. "This is it," Kaelan said, his voice hard. "This is where she tried to buy me." Kaela looked at the scar. Through the Circuit, she could feel the echo of the memory Kaelan was projecting. She felt the phantom smell of jasmine and rot. She felt the temptation he had felt—the desperate desire to just sleep, to stop fighting, to let someone else carry the weight. "She wanted to put you in a box," Kaela whispered. "She wanted to deliver you to the tower like a package." "She almost did," Kaelan admitted. "The wine... it smelled good. I was so tired, Kaela. I was so cold." He looked at the empty ice. "She offered me warmth. She offered me pleasure. She told me I deserved to rest." "Why didn't you take it?" Kaela asked, though she knew the answer. She wanted to hear him say it. Kaelan turned to her. He looked at her copper hair, messy from the wind. He looked at her silver eyes. "Because it wasn't you," he said. "She was beautiful," Kaelan acknowledged. "She was perfect. But she was empty. I realized... if I drank that wine, I wouldn't wake up. And if I didn't wake up, who would find you?" He reached out and took her gloved hand. "I poured it out," he said. "I chose the cold. Because the cold meant I was still walking toward you." Kaela squeezed his hand. She looked at the scar on the ice—the place where her brother had chosen pain over peace because he loved her more than he loved himself. "I'm glad you poured it out," she said softly. "Me too." Kaelan looked at the scar one last time. It held no power over him now. It was just a burn mark on the floor of the world. "Ready to leave it behind?" he asked. "Burn it," Kaela said. Kaelan grinned. He didn't use fire. He used speed. He shoved the magnetic levers forward. The Iron Keel surged. The runners shrieked against the ice. They blasted right over the center of the scar, shattering the refrozen ice, leaving a fresh trail of iron shavings and victory in their wake. They raced North, leaving the ghosts of the temptation in the dust, heading toward the true fire that waited in the deep. The magnetic river slowed as the terrain leveled out. They were at the very lip of the Voidlands proper—a desolate plateau where the red dust of the south met the black obsidian of the north. "Brakes," Kaelan said softly. He pulled the levers. The Iron Keel drifted to a stop near a cluster of jagged basalt pillars. The silence that rushed in to replace the roar of the wind was heavy. It wasn't a peaceful silence. It was a hollow one. Kaelan climbed out of the cockpit. His boots crunched on the black gravel. He looked North, toward the Crater of Silence, visible as a dark notch on the horizon. He felt it immediately. The Echo. It wasn't magic—Malakor was gone, his spells unraveled. It was the memory of the land itself. The rocks here remembered the weight of the Tower. The air remembered the taste of despair. For a second, Kaelan wasn't twenty. He was eighteen, bleeding, starving, and dragging a heavy iron sword through the snow, convinced that he would never be warm again. The ghost of that loneliness washed over him, a cold shiver that started in his marrow. "Kaelan?" He didn't turn around. He reached back with his hand. Kaela took it instantly. She stepped up beside him. She wasn't looking at the horizon; she was looking at him. She saw the shadow cross his face. She felt the dip in his internal temperature through the Circuit. "It's just a memory," she whispered. "It can't bite." "It has teeth," Kaelan murmured. "I can feel them. This place... it hates life, Kaela. It wants us to be quiet." "Then we should be loud," she said. Kaelan looked at her. The ghost of the lonely eighteen-year-old boy faded, replaced by the reality of the man holding his sister's hand. He smiled. It started small, then broke across his face like sunrise. "Come here," he demanded. He pulled her in. He didn't wait for permission. He wrapped his arms around her waist and lifted her off the ground, burying his face in the soft wool of her tunic. He squeezed her. He squeezed her until he felt the breath leave her lungs, until he felt the solid, undeniable resistance of her ribs against his. "Payment," he mumbled into her shoulder. "Accepted," she laughed, wrapping her legs around his waist, clinging to him like a koala. She kissed his cheek, a loud, smacking sound that echoed defiantly in the quiet air. "You're warm," Kaelan said, letting her slide down until her feet touched the ground, but not letting go. "You're the antidote." "To the Void?" "To everything." He looked past her. Nestled at the base of the basalt pillars was a small, steaming pool. It was fed by a thermal vent—the same geological unrest that was shaking the world was also heating the groundwater. It was the last water before the Crater. The last clean thing. "Lunch?" Kaela asked, following his gaze. "Bath," Kaelan corrected. "Then lunch. I'm not going down into the Magma looking like a dust devil." They walked to the pool. The water was crystal clear, bubbling gently over smooth black stones. They stripped off their travel clothes—the heavy leather vests, the linen shirts stiff with red dust. They left them in a pile on the warm rocks. There was no hesitation. They stepped into the water together. It was hot—volcanic hot—but to them, it was perfect. Kaelan sank to his neck, letting the heat penetrate his muscles, loosening the tension of the drive. Kaela splashed him. It wasn't a gentle splash. It was a two-handed wave of water that hit him square in the face. Kaelan sputtered, wiping his eyes. He grinned. "Oh, it's war." He lunged. They wrestled in the water, laughing, splashing, making enough noise to wake the dead. The heavy, oppressive silence of the Voidlands shattered. Kaelan caught her, pinning her against the smooth rock wall of the pool. He wasn't hurting her; he was holding her. Water sluiced down their skin. Kaela was laughing, breathless, her eyes shining silver. "You're wet," she pointed out, stating the obvious. "You're beautiful," he said, staring at her. The laughter died down, replaced by a warm, heavy contentment. He leaned his forehead against hers. "I love you," he whispered. "Sun and Moon." "Sun and Moon," she replied. They washed the dust away. They washed the ghosts away. Afterward, they sat on the edge of the pool, drying in the sun and the residual heat of the volcanic rock. They shared the last of the fresh bread and a wedge of hard cheese. Kaelan ate ravenously, one arm draped over Kaela’s shoulders, pulling her into his side so he could chew and cuddle at the same time. "It's deep," Kaelan said, looking toward the Crater. "The drop. I can feel the magnetic field folding in." "We'll handle it," Kaela said, finishing her cheese. "Horg built the boat to take a beating." "I'm not worried about the boat," Kaelan said. He kissed her temple. "I'm just glad I'm not falling alone this time." "Never again," she promised. They dressed in the warm afternoon light. Kaelan buckled his sword belt. Kaela braided her wet hair. They climbed back into the Iron Keel. Kaelan grabbed the tiller. The playfulness vanished, replaced by the steely focus of the Pilot. "Ready?" "Ready." Kaelan released the brakes. The magnetic runners hummed, locking onto the field lines. "Next stop," Kaelan said, grinning. "The center of the earth." The boat surged forward, leaving the pool and the ghosts behind, racing toward the lip of the crater and the long, dark drop into the fire. The afternoon in the Voidlands did not bring warmth; it just brought a harsher, flatter light. The Iron Keel was flying. The magnetic pull from the core was so strong here that the iron runners were humming a constant, high-pitched note, hovering two inches off the black ice. Kaelan sat at the tiller, his eyes locked on the horizon. He knew this path. Two years ago, this crossing had taken him four days. Four days of walking into a headwind that felt like knives. Four days of sleeping in cracks in the ice, listening to the hissing of Gloomwraiths circling his camp, waiting for him to freeze. Now, they were covering the same distance in four hours. "Slow down," Kaela said softly. Kaelan blinked. He hadn't realized his grip on the levers had tightened. He pulled back slightly, engaging the drag-brakes. The boat shuddered, slowing from a blur to a manageable cruise. "Why?" Kaelan asked. "We can make the crater by sunset if I push it." "Because you're tense," Kaela said. She reached across the small gap between their seats and placed her hand on his knee. "You're projecting static. You're remembering." Kaelan looked out the viewport. To his left, a jagged ridge of basalt rose from the ice like a spinal column. "That ridge," he whispered. "That's where they herded me." He pointed to a specific outcropping of rock. "I stood there. Three Gloomwraiths blocked the path back. They didn't attack. They just... pointed. They wanted me to go to the Tower. They wanted me to be the battery." He remembered the feeling of absolute helplessness. He remembered knowing he was walking into a trap and doing it anyway because he had nowhere else to go. "They aren't there, Kaelan," Kaela said. Kaelan looked. The ridge was empty. The shadows were just shadows—tricks of the light on black rock. There were no burning eyes. No hissing whispers. "I know," Kaelan said. "But the cold... it feels the same." "It isn't," Kaela corrected. She unbuckled her safety harness. She turned in her seat, wiggling until she could slide over the center console. The cockpit was tight—Horg had built it for function, not comfort—but she made it work. She squeezed into Kaelan’s seat, forcing him to shift back. She sat on his lap, her back against his chest, her legs draped over the side of the chair. "Better?" she asked, pulling his arms around her waist. Kaelan buried his face in her shoulder. The smell of the volcanic spring and the clean scent of her hair filled his nose, chasing away the phantom smell of ozone and decay. He felt the heat of her body pressing against his. He felt the steady, calm rhythm of her heart. "Much better," he murmured. "Drive," she commanded gently, resting her head on his shoulder. "Show the ghosts we aren't afraid." Kaelan grabbed the tiller again, his arms bracketing her. He released the brakes. The Iron Keel surged forward. They drove through the heart of the Voidlands. They passed the frozen lake where Kaelan had fallen through the ice and nearly drowned. They passed the scree slope where he had twisted his ankle and walked on it for miles. Every landmark was a scar. But now, they were blurring past them at sixty miles an hour, wrapped in iron and warmth. The suns began to set, turning the sky into a bruised purple canopy. Ahead, the horizon broke. The flat ice ended abruptly at a jagged, circular rim that stretched for miles. The Crater of Silence. Kaelan slowed the boat. They drifted toward the edge, the magnetic runners crunching over the loose obsidian gravel. He pulled the full stop. The boat settled. They sat there for a moment, looking out. The Crater was massive. In the fading light, it looked like a mouth waiting to swallow them. But it wasn't silent anymore. From the center, miles away, a deep, rhythmic thrumming vibrated through the ground. Thrummmmm. And rising from the central vent was a glow—not the violet light of Malakor’s magic, but the deep, angry red of the planetary core. "The intake," Kaelan whispered. "It's wide open." "It's waiting for us," Kaela said. She didn't sound afraid. She sounded ready. "We camp here," Kaelan decided. "On the rim. I'm not going down that slide in the dark." "Agreed." They didn't set up a tent. The wind on the rim was ferocious, screaming over the edge of the crater. They stayed in the boat. Kaelan engaged the thermal seals on the canopy. They ate a supper of hardtack and dried fruit, sitting hip-to-hip in the pilot’s seat because neither of them wanted to move to the passenger side. Outside, the Voidlands turned pitch black. The red glow from the crater cast long, dancing shadows against the iron hull. "It feels different this time," Kaelan said into the dark of the cabin. "How?" "Last time, I came here to die," he admitted. "I thought if I burned the tower down, it didn't matter what happened to me." He tightened his arms around her. "This time, I have to live. I have to get us back to the garden. I have a fence to maintain." Kaela smiled against his chest. "And a hug debt to pay." "And a debt," he agreed. They curled up together on the narrow bench seat, wrapped in the fur blanket. It was a tight fit, but that was the point. Kaelan listened to the wind howling outside—the same wind that had tried to kill him two years ago. Now, it was just noise. He closed his eyes, anchored by the girl in his arms and the iron beneath his feet, and slept on the edge of the volcano, ready to drop into the fire when the suns came up. Night in the Voidlands did not fall; it suffocated. Outside the armored canopy of the Iron Keel, the wind shrieked. It wasn't the clean, sharp whistle of the High Chasm. It was a jagged, multi-tonal moan that sounded like voices. Kaelan... surrender... Kaelan flinched, his hand jerking toward the sword belt he had just unbuckled. "It's just the wind," Kaela said softly. She was kneeling on the floorboards, unlacing her boots. "It sounds like them," Kaelan whispered. He was staring out the viewport at the black obsidian shifting in the dark. "The Gloomwraiths. I can hear them hissing." "There are no Wraiths," Kaela promised. She reached out with the Circuit, scanning the darkness. "The only living things for a hundred miles are us and a few very confused rock-rabbits." "My head knows that," Kaelan said, rubbing his temples. "My gut thinks they're waiting for the fire to die." He stood up. The interior of the boat was lit by the faint, blood-red glow reflecting up from the crater vent miles away. It cast long, twisting shadows against the iron ribs of the hull. Kaela stood up and reached for the hem of her tunic. It was their routine—shedding the day, shedding the armor, sleeping skin-to-skin. "Don't," Kaelan said sharply. Kaela paused, her hands still on the fabric. She looked at him. "Not tonight," Kaelan said. His voice was tight, bordering on frantic. "Keep it on. Keep the boots on, too. Actually... maybe we should sleep in the mail." "Kaelan," Kaela said gently, lowering her hands. "We are safe. Horg built this boat to be a tank. Nothing is getting in." "I know," Kaelan paced the small length of the cockpit. "I just... I can't be open tonight, Kaela. I feel like if I take my clothes off, the cold is going to touch me again. And if it touches me, I'll freeze." He looked at her, shame burning in his eyes. He was the Solar Engine. He was the man who had surfed a boat across a continent. But here, on the edge of the pit where he had once come to die, he was a scared eighteen-year-old boy again. Kaela didn't argue. She didn't tell him to be reasonable. "Okay," she said. "Layers. Armor. Whatever you need." She sat down on the narrow bench seat. "Come here." Kaelan hesitated. The seat was narrow—too narrow for them to lie side-by-side without one of them hovering over the edge. And he felt too jittery to lie still. "I can't sleep next to you," he admitted. "I'll twitch. I'm too wired." "Then don't sleep next to me," Kaela said. She patted the bench. "Lie down on your back." Kaelan frowned, but he obeyed. He lay down on the cushioned bench, his booted feet resting on the dashboard. He was stiff as a board, his arms crossed over his chest like a corpse. Kaela climbed up. She didn't lie beside him. She lay on top of him. She settled stomach-to-stomach, her legs draping over his, her chest resting against his. She nestled her head into the crook of his neck, her hair spilling over his face like a curtain, blocking out the view of the red-lit canopy. "Kaela?" "You need weight," she whispered against his collarbone. "You need to know I'm here. If I'm on top of you, you can't forget." Kaelan took a breath. The weight of her was heavy, solid, and undeniably real. It pressed the panic down. He uncrossed his arms. He wrapped them around her back, locking his hands together. He pulled her down tighter, crushing her against him. "Is this okay?" he asked, his voice muffled by her hair. "It's perfect," she murmured. "It's warm." The wind howled outside, sounding like a thousand dying ghosts. But Kaelan couldn't hear them anymore. All he could hear was the steady thump-thump of Kaela’s heart beating directly against his own chest. He closed his eyes. The tension in his muscles began to uncoil. "Tomorrow," Kaelan whispered, "when we go down the tube..." "Yeah?" "You sit on my lap. In the chair. Just like in the forest." "I wouldn't sit anywhere else," Kaela agreed. "I have to steer, remember? And I can't reach the tiller if you're hogging the seat." "Right. Steering." "And," she added, shifting slightly to get comfortable on the hard buttons of his tunic, "you have a debt to pay. This counts as double time." Kaelan smiled in the dark. "Double time?" "Hazard pay," she corrected. "For the ghosts." "Fair enough." He squeezed her, holding onto his payment plan like a lifeline. He wasn't the lonely boy in the snow anymore. He was a mattress for the most important person in the universe. And as the red light pulsed outside, Kaelan slept without nightmares, anchored to the earth by the girl who refused to let him float away.

title: Part 4: Chapter 4: The Clockwork Ocean
content: The suns rose over the Voidlands, but they brought no warmth to the crater. The light merely highlighted the jagged, black teeth of the obsidian rim. Kaelan stood by the Iron Keel. He checked the drag-plows. He checked the iron runners. He checked his sword belt. He was stalling. "It's time," Kaela said softly. She was already standing by the cockpit, her hand resting on the iron canopy. Kaelan took a deep breath of the freezing air. He looked at the central vent miles away—the glowing red eye of the world. "Right," he said. "Time." He climbed into the cockpit. He sat in the pilot’s seat. It was a tight squeeze, heavily padded with leather and fur. He looked at the empty passenger seat next to him. He looked at the dashboard. "Kaela," he said. "I know," she answered. She didn't go to the passenger side. She climbed into the pilot’s seat with him. She sat on his lap, her back resting against his chest, her legs draped over his thighs. She wiggled until she was settled, her head tucked under his chin. Kaelan let out a breath he didn't know he was holding. The weight of her was exactly what he needed. It was an anchor. He reached around her waist to grab the tiller and the brake levers. His arms bracketed her, creating a cage of bone and muscle that kept her safe. "Comfortable?" he asked, his voice vibrating against her back. "Perfect," she said, resting her hands on his forearms. "You can reach the controls?" "I can reach everything." He looked out the viewport. The crater floor was a sheet of black glass. The magnetic pull was a screaming siren in his blood. "Goggles down," Kaelan ordered. They pulled the heavy lenses over their eyes. Kaelan closed his eyes for a second. He engaged the Circuit. He felt the iron runners fuse with the magnetic field of the planet. Click. The boat lurched, hovering. "Going down," Kaelan whispered. He slammed the levers forward. The Iron Keel shot off the rim. They hit the crater floor at eighty miles an hour. Sparks flew from the runners as they skidded across the obsidian. Kaelan fought the tiller, drifting the heavy boat around jagged spires of rock, aiming for the red glow in the center. "The intake!" Kaela shouted, pointing. "The field folds in!" They hit the lip of the vent. Gravity vanished. The boat tipped forward, diving into the throat of the volcano. It wasn't a freefall. The magnetic field caught them. The vent was a lava tube—a perfect, circular tunnel that spiraled down into the crust like the rifling of a gun barrel. The boat locked into the spiral. They began to corkscrew. Round and round. Faster and faster. The G-force pressed them together. Kaela was crushed back into Kaelan’s chest; Kaelan was pressed into the seat. The light outside the canopy shifted from sunlight to the deep, angry red of magma veins running through the rock walls. "Heat rising!" Kaela yelled over the roar of the descent. "Hull temp is critical!" "I got it!" Kaelan roared. He took one hand off the tiller and slammed it against the iron dashboard. He engaged the Engine. But he didn't pull heat in. The friction here was too much; if he absorbed it, he would cook them both from the inside out. He pushed out. He projected a sphere of high-pressure thermal rejection around the boat. He created a bubble of cold air—a magical heat shield that forced the superheated atmosphere of the tunnel to flow around them. The cockpit temperature stabilized. They fell for hours. Or maybe minutes. Time distorted in the dark. They passed layers of the world that no human had ever seen. They saw veins of pure gold thick as rivers. They saw caverns filled with diamonds the size of houses. "Deeper," Kaelan gasped, sweat pouring down his face as he held the shield. "We're passing the mantle." The tunnel widened. The spiral straightened out. The red light turned blinding white. "Brace!" Kaelan shouted, wrapping both arms around Kaela, burying his face in her neck to protect his eyes. The Iron Keel shot out of the ceiling of the Underworld. They were in freefall for three seconds. SPLASH. The boat hit the liquid surface with a force that rattled their teeth. It hissed, skidded, and bounced. Steam exploded around them. The boat settled, rocking violently. Kaelan kept his eyes squeezed shut, holding the thermal shield, waiting for the hull to melt. It didn't. "Kaelan," Kaela whispered. She sounded awestruck. "Open your eyes." Kaelan opened his eyes. He lifted his goggles. They were floating on a sea of liquid iron, glowing with a soft, white luminescence. The "sky" above them was a ceiling of rock miles high, swirling with clouds of magnetic vapor. And rising from the sea, turning slowly with the rotation of the earth, were the Gears. Massive, continent-sized cogs made of a dark, star-forged metal, ticking away the seconds of the planet's life. "The Clockwork Ocean," Kaelan breathed. "I built a clock." "And someone," Kaela said, pointing to a dark speck moving toward the central mechanism, "is trying to stop the hands." The view from the viewport was beautiful, in the way a forest fire is beautiful just before it consumes you. They were floating on a river of liquid rock—a blinding, viscous torrent of gold and orange that flowed through a tunnel ten miles wide. The walls were made of pressurized diamond and slag, glowing with the ambient temperature of the deep earth. "Temperature rising," Kaela whispered. Her voice was tight. Kaelan didn't look at the gauges. He didn't need to. He could feel it. The heat here wasn't like the desert sun. It was a physical weight. It pressed against the iron hull of the Iron Keel, seeking any weakness, any crack in the plating. It wanted to cook them. Inside the cockpit, the air was sweltering. The iron canopy was radiating heat like a skillet. The smell of scorching wood—the oak hull beneath the iron plating—was getting stronger. Kaelan sat in the pilot’s seat, his hands fused to the iron controls. He wasn't steering anymore; the magnetic current had them locked in. He was cooling. He had his eyes closed, sweat stinging his eyelids. He was projecting the Thermal Shield—a sphere of high-pressure rejection that forced the superheated air away from the boat. But he was tired. He had been holding the shield for six hours. His energy reserves, usually infinite, were straining against the sheer magnitude of the planet's core. "Kaelan," Kaela said softly. She shifted in his lap. She was soaking wet with sweat, her tunic clinging to her skin. Her back was pressed against his chest, her head tucked under his chin. "You're flickering," she warned. "The shield dropped a degree. The hull is groaning." "It's... heavy," Kaelan gasped. "The pressure. It's like trying to hold up the sky." "Don't hold it alone," she commanded. She reached out and placed her hands over his on the controls. She didn't have his fire. She didn't have his nuclear engine. But she had the Coolant. She engaged the Circuit. Sync, she projected. Kaelan felt a rush of cold, silver energy flood his mind. It was like a bucket of ice water dumped on a fever. Kaela took the chaotic, roaring noise of the mantle—the pressure, the heat, the geological screaming—and she filtered it. She organized it. She took the load off his mind so his body could work. "Better?" she asked. "Much," Kaelan breathed, his heart rate slowing. The shield stabilized, pushing the heat back a few more feet. The smell of burning wood faded slightly. "We need to stop," Kaela said, looking out the viewport. "We can't ride the main current all the way down. You'll burn out." "There's nowhere to stop, Moon. It's all fire." "There," she pointed. To the left of the main flow, a massive shelf of black, solid rock jutted out into the magma stream. It was a "Slag Island"—a piece of the crust that had sunk but hadn't melted yet. It looked desolate, hot, and dangerous. It looked perfect. "Eddy current," Kaelan noted, seeing the magnetic lines swirling around the rock. "I can drift us in." He wrestled the tiller. The Iron Keel fought the current, surfing sideways across the magma. Sparks of molten rock sprayed against the shield. They slammed onto the black rock, the iron runners screeching as they dug into the stone. The boat slid forty feet and came to a halt. Kaelan slumped forward, releasing the shield. The heat of the mantle rushed in instantly. It wasn't the instant-death heat of the magma, but it was easily 130 degrees Fahrenheit in the air. "Out," Kaelan croaked. "The cabin is an oven. The hull is still conducting." They scrambled out of the boat. The air on the rock shelf was stifling, smelling of sulfur and ancient dust, but it was cooler than the iron box. Kaelan collapsed onto the dark stone. He ripped his tunic off, his skin red and steaming. Kaela sat beside him. She pulled her dress over her head, leaving her in her undergarments. Modesty was a luxury for people who weren't boiling alive. "Water," she rasped. She summoned a sphere of water from the barrel in the boat—carefully, so it wouldn't flash-boil. She floated it over to them. They drank greedily. Then Kaela splashed the rest over Kaelan’s head. He hissed, steam rising from his skin. "We have to sleep," Kaelan said, wiping his eyes. "Just for a few hours. I need to recharge the battery." "I'll watch," Kaela said. "No. We sleep together. If the shield fails while we're sleeping..." "...we cook," she finished. "Okay. Together." They lay down on the hard rock, away from the magma's edge. They lay face-to-face. They didn't cuddle for warmth this time; they cuddled for regulation. Kaelan focused on pulling the ambient heat away from her. Kaela focused on keeping his mind calm, slowing his metabolic rate so he wouldn't overheat. It was a delicate thermal dance. "Kaelan," Kaela whispered into the suffocating dark. "Yeah?" "Do you feel that?" "The heat?" "No. Deeper." She pressed her hand against the rock floor. She closed her eyes, extending her senses down, past the mantle, toward the core. "Someone is down there," she whispered. "Waiting." Kaelan felt it then. It wasn't the rhythmic thump-thump of the Clockwork machinery he had built. It was a static. A void. It felt like a shadow moving against the glare of the sun. It felt cold, ancient, and hungry. "It's not Malakor," Kaelan said, a shiver of true fear running through him despite the heat. "It's not Seraphina." "It's the thing they worked for," Kaela realized. "The Dark Master." "He's trying to stop the clock," Kaelan murmured. "He's trying to hold the pendulum." "Then we have to hurry." "We will," Kaelan promised. He pulled her closer, his sweat-slicked skin slipping against hers. "But first... we cool down." He closed his eyes, focusing on the image of snow, of the slate roof in the rain, of the cold spring water at the Bridge. He projected that cold into the circle of their embrace. Kaela sighed, her body relaxing. They slept in the throat of the world, a tiny bubble of life floating on a sea of fire, while far below, something older than the stars turned its gaze upward, wondering why the intruders hadn't burned yet. There was no sunrise in the throat of the world. There was only the relentless, blinding glare of the magma river. Kaelan didn't know how long they had slept on the slag rock. An hour? A day? It didn't matter. The heat was a constant pressure, a physical weight that sat on his chest and refused to move. He sat up, groaning. His skin felt tight, dried out by the superheated air. "Ready?" he croaked. His throat felt like he had swallowed sand. Kaela sat up next to him. She looked pale, her hair plastered to her skull with sweat. She nodded, not wasting breath on words. They climbed back into the Iron Keel. The hull was hot to the touch—not burning, thanks to the Stellium and iron plating, but hot enough to be uncomfortable. The air inside the cockpit was stifling. Kaelan took the pilot’s seat. Kaela climbed into his lap instantly. It wasn't a choice anymore. It was a mechanical necessity. If they separated, the Circuit weakened. If the Circuit weakened, the thermal shield faltered. If the shield faltered, they died. "Shield up," Kaelan whispered. He slammed his hands onto the dashboard. He engaged the Engine. He pushed the bubble of cold air out, forcing the ambient temperature down from deadly to merely miserable. "Magnetic lock," Kaela whispered, her head resting against his chest, her eyes closed as she guided the boat’s sensors. The runners engaged. The boat lurched off the rock shelf and back into the main flow of the magma river. They accelerated. The journey became a blur. There were no landmarks here, only the endless, flowing river of liquid fire and the diamond-studded walls rushing past. Time dissolved. "Talk to me," Kaelan rasped after what felt like an eternity. The silence was getting loud again—filled with the roar of the fire and the static of the Dark Master waiting below. "About what?" Kaela mumbled. She was lethargic, the heat sapping her energy. "The garden," Kaelan said. "Tell me about the garden." "The mint," Kaela whispered, latching onto the memory like a lifeline. "It was coming back. The green shoots. They smell like... cold rain." "Cold rain," Kaelan repeated, visualizing it. He projected that image into the shield, hardening the barrier. "And the wall," he added. "The stone wall. It's cool to the touch in the morning. It has dew on it." "I like the wall," Kaela murmured. "It keeps the deer out. It keeps us in." "I want to go back," Kaelan admitted. "I want to sit on the bench and do absolutely nothing." "We will," she promised. "Just... keep driving." They went deeper. The tunnel widened. The ceiling vaulted upward, vanishing into a haze of magnetic auroras. They were entering the Outer Core. The river emptied into a vast, churning ocean of white-hot liquid metal. And rising from that ocean, dominating the horizon, were the Gears. They were colossal. Cogs the size of continents, forged from a black metal that drank the light of the magma. They turned with a slow, inexorable rhythm—click... thrum... click... thrum. They were the clockwork mechanism Solas had built eons ago to regulate the planet's magnetic field and rotation. But something was wrong. "Kaelan," Kaela said, sitting up straighter, her eyes snapping open. "Look at the pendulum." In the center of the gear assembly, a massive pendulum swung back and forth. But it was erratic. It was stuttering. And wrapped around the main drive shaft, looking like a tumor made of shadow, was a cloud of static darkness. "It's Him," Kaelan said. "The Unseen. He's jamming the gears." "He's trying to stop the rotation," Kaela realized. "If that clock stops, the magnetic shield drops. The atmosphere strips away. Earth dies." "Not today," Kaelan growled. He pushed the tiller forward. He poured more power into the runners. "We have to get to the Control Platform," he said, pointing to a flat, obsidian disc hovering near the main axle of the clock. "It's right next to the darkness," Kaela warned. "It's going to be cold." "Good," Kaelan said, sweat dripping from his nose. "I could use a little cold." The Iron Keel surged across the white-hot sea, a tiny speck of defiance racing toward the mechanism that kept the world turning. The Iron Keel drifted past the final barrier of the Outer Core. The liquid metal here wasn't orange or yellow. It was blinding, pure white. The heat was no longer a physical sensation; it was a frequency. It vibrated in their bones. Inside the cockpit, the iron canopy was beginning to glow dull red. The air smelled of scorching leather and singing hair. "Hull integrity at 40%," Kaela rasped. She was slumped against Kaelan’s chest, her skin flushed, her breathing shallow. She was pouring every ounce of her will into the Circuit, keeping Kaelan focused, but her biological body was failing. "Almost there," Kaelan whispered. His skin was gold. He was pushing the Thermal Shield so hard that the air around the boat was distorting, creating a mirage bubble. They floated toward the central island of solid iron—the Inner Core. Rising from it was the Cosmic Clock. It was a mechanism of impossible scale. Gears the size of continents clicked and whirred, driving the rotation of the planet. And hanging from the center was the Great Pendulum—a massive weight of star-metal swinging back and forth through the liquid iron sea. Tick... Tock... Tick... But the rhythm was wrong. It was stuttering. "There," Kaela pointed, her hand trembling. Standing on the main drive shaft, right next to the Pendulum, was a figure. It wasn't a shadow like Malakor. It wasn't a biological abomination like Seraphina. It was a Construct. A being made of void-metal and static, shaped like a man but hollow. It held a massive, jagged spear of anti-matter. "The Gear-Breaker," Kaelan named it. "A servant of The Unseen." The construct wasn't attacking the gears. It didn't have to. It was waiting for the Pendulum to swing past a specific point—a point where the gears were grinding, sparking, and slowing down. "It's catching," Kaelan realized. "Why is it catching?" He looked closer. His Scion eyes pierced the glare of the magma. Lodged in the teeth of the main drive gear was a massive, misshapen lump of metal. It wasn't star-metal. It wasn't void-metal. It was pure, crude iron. "The Extra Iron," Kaelan whispered. The realization hit him harder than the heat. "I put it there. I added mass to the core to shield the planet. But I didn't account for the drift. Over a billion years... it shifted. It migrated." "It's a doorstop," Kaela gasped. "You jammed your own door." The Gear-Breaker raised its spear.
