Your father—Colonel Viktor Krov—entered the US in 1984 using a stolen identity. He married your mother to cement his cover. He had a child—you—to look like a family man." Sarah flinched. "He... he had me to be a prop?" "He had you to be a shield," Ross corrected gently. "But that doesn't mean your mother didn't love you. She was a victim, too. We believe she discovered his identity three years ago. That’s likely why she died." "He said it was cancer," Sarah whispered. "We are reopening the autopsy," Ross said grimly. "If we find evidence of poisoning... the charges will escalate from Espionage to Capital Murder." Sarah stared at the table. The monster wasn't just mean; he was a killer. "What happens to his money?" Stella asked. "The tuition? The house?" "The assets are frozen," Ross said. "The government is seizing everything connected to the Halloway identity under the RICO Act and Espionage Act. The bank accounts, the house in Ohio, the cars. It’s all evidence." Sarah looked up. "So I have nothing? I can't pay for school?" "You have something better," Stella interjected. "You have a claim." She looked at Agent Ross. "She is a victim of a federal crime," Stella said. "Under the Victims of Crime Act, she is entitled to restitution. And until then..." Stella put her hand on Sarah’s shoulder. "We cover the gap. You are living in the Fortress. I am paying your tuition. We will file for financial aid as an 'Independent Student' now that your father is incarcerated. You aren't dropping out." Agent Ross nodded. "Your friend is right. The government will eventually release funds for you, but it will take time. In the meantime, Sarah... I suggest you change your name. 'Halloway' is about to be on every news channel in the world." Sarah looked at Leo. Leo was watching her, his face calm and steady. He tapped his Quantum Communicator. Name is just data, he typed. You are the hardware. the hardware is good. Sarah managed a weak smile. "Hardware is good." "Take your time," Stella said. "Pick a new name. Pick a new life. You get to choose this time." Sarah looked at the file Agent Ross was holding. It contained the lies of her father. Then she looked at the Fortress crew. The people who had saved her. "I don't know who I am yet," Sarah whispered. "But I know where I'm staying." You are staying here, Leo typed. In iron point. "Exactly," Stella said. "Let's go home. We have a guest room with your name on it. Whatever name that is."

title: Part 10: The Identity Protocol
content: The FBI agents had left with their prisoner. The door was closed. Sarah sat at the small table. She looked at her hands. She looked at the file Agent Ross had left—the one detailing the lies of Viktor Krov. "He named me," she whispered. "He picked 'Sarah'. He picked 'Emily'. He picked 'Halloway'." She looked up at Stella. "I don't want any of it. If I keep the name Sarah... every time someone says it, I'll hear his voice." Stella nodded. "Then we burn it. All of it." Judge Silas Miller, still in his street clothes, clicked his pen. He pulled a blank Petition for Change of Name form from his briefcase. "Okay," Miller said. "We are doing a full scrub. New First. New Middle. New Last." "Last name is Porter," Sarah said immediately, looking at Leo. "If the offer still stands." Offer confirmed, Leo typed on his Titan console. Crew is family. "Okay," Sarah said. "Sarah is gone. Who am I?" She looked at the engineering textbook in her lap. She looked at the M.U.L.E. bracket on the back of Leo’s chair—the thing she had helped build. She wanted a name that sounded structural. Something that couldn't be broken. "Maya," she said. "I always liked Maya. It sounds... solid." "Maya Steele Porter," Judge Miller tested it. "Has a nice ring to it." Sarah—no, Maya—nodded. "Do it." Miller filled out the form. - Petitioner: Sarah Emily Halloway. - New Name: Maya Steele Porter. - Reason: Safety / Witness Protection. He signed the order. "Done," Miller said. "Sarah Halloway is legally dead. Long live Maya Porter." They didn't go home. They went straight to the city. Stella walked into the high-end salon on Main Street. She didn't have an appointment, but she had the Platinum Card. "We need an emergency session," Stella told the stylist. "The full works. Cut. Color. Radical change." Maya sat in the chair. She looked at herself in the mirror. She had mousey brown hair, pulled back in a ponytail—the way her father liked it. Conservative. Quiet. "Change it," Maya said to the stylist. "I don't want to recognize her." "What color?" the stylist asked. Maya looked at Leo’s wheelchair—Jet Black with neon accents. She looked at the BTA trains. She looked at the modern world she was joining. "Black," Maya decided. "Blue-black. Like ink. And cut it short. An angled bob. Sharp." "That's a commitment," the stylist warned. "Going that dark... it's hard to go back." "I'm not going back," Maya said. For three hours, the Fortress waited. - Leo sat in the waiting area, working on his laptop. - Luna read a magazine. - Olivia brought coffee milk. - Stella paid the bill in advance (\$300 + Tip). The stylist applied the dye. The chemical smell filled the air—the smell of change. She snipped the long, brown ponytail off and let it fall to the floor. The chair spun around. Maya stood up. Her hair was a sleek, sharp helmet of Midnight Blue/Black. It framed her face, making her eyes look fiercer, older, and stronger. She didn't look like a scared girl from Ohio anymore. She looked like a cyberpunk engineer. She looked like she belonged in Roebling Hall. She looked in the mirror. She touched the sharp angle of the cut. "She's gone," Maya whispered. Leo rolled up to her. He raised his seat elevator to look her in the eye. He tapped his Quantum Communicator. Hello maya, the robotic voice said. Nice upgrade. Maya smiled. It was a real smile. "Hello Leo," she said. "I like the new specs."

title: Part 11: The Plastic Anchor
content: "Transaction?" Brenda asked. "New License," Stella said. "And a legal name change." Stella slid the paperwork across the counter: 1. The Court Order (Signed by Judge Miller). Sarah Halloway to Maya Steele Porter. 2. The Old ID (Ohio Driver’s License). 3. The Birth Certificate (US Citizen). 4. The Residency Proof (Affidavit from Stella + Deed). Brenda reviewed the Ohio license. "You drive?" "Since I was sixteen," Maya said softly. "He insisted on it. Part of the cover." "Well, Ohio reciprocates with Rhode Island," Brenda said, punching the hole in the old card. "No road test required. Just vision." Maya looked into the machine. She read the letters. "Okay, Maya," Brenda said. "Stand on the line. Look at the blue dot. Don't smile." Maya stood. She touched her new, sharp black hair. She looked at the camera. She didn't smile, but her eyes were fierce. She looked like someone who had taken the wheel of her own life. FLASH. The machine behind the counter whirred. A moment later, a warm piece of plastic dropped into the tray. Brenda handed it over. RHODE ISLAND DRIVER'S LICENSE NAME: PORTER, MAYA STEELE ADDRESS: 8 Ocean View LN, IRON POINT, RI 02840 DOB: 04/12/1988 HAIR: BLK EYES: HAZ CLASS: D (Operator) Maya held it. It wasn't just an ID; it was a license to move. "Thank you," Maya whispered. "Welcome to Rhode Island," Brenda said. "Watch out for the rotaries." The Exit They walked out to the parking lot. Leo rolled up to her. He looked at the card. License verified, he typed. You are a pilot. "I can drive," Maya realized, a slow smile spreading across her face. "I can drive us to the beach. I can drive us to the store." "You can drive the Sentinel," Stella promised, handing her the keys just to hold for a moment. "Once you get used to the snow tires." Maya clutched the keys and the license. She had a name. She had a home. And she had the keys to the tank. "Let's go home," Maya said. "I'm starving." "Clam chowder," Stella said. "Clear." "Clear," Maya agreed.

title: Part 12: The Ghost Tax
content: The insurance office was wood-paneled and smelled of coffee. Mr. Russo, the agent who handled the Porter Home and Auto bundles, sat behind his desk typing. "Okay, Stella," Russo said. "Adding a driver to the 2001 Holt Sentinel. Name?" "Maya Steele Porter," Stella said. She slid the brand-new, still-warm Rhode Island license across the desk. Russo typed the license number into his terminal. He hit Enter. He waited. He frowned. He hit Enter again. "Stella," Russo said, peering over his glasses. "The system is flagging this. It says 'No Record Found.' According to the DMV database, this license was issued... yesterday?" "It was," Stella confirmed. "And there's no previous history," Russo noted. "No credit check. No prior carrier. As far as the computer is concerned, this person was born yesterday." He looked at Maya. "You're eighteen," Russo said. "Have you driven before?" Maya hesitated. She looked at Stella. "I drove in Ohio," Maya whispered. "Since I was sixteen." "Okay," Russo said, reaching for a notepad. "If you give me your old license number and your old name, I can link the records. It’ll prove you have two years of clean driving. That will save you about \$800 a year on the premium. Otherwise, you’re rated as a 'New Operator'—same risk category as a sixteen-year-old." Maya froze. Linking the records meant typing "Sarah Halloway" into the system. It meant connecting the new, clean Maya Porter to the toxic, tracked Sarah Halloway. Mr. Russo looked at the computer screen. He looked at the "No Record Found" error. He looked at the \$800 surcharge. "Stella," Russo said, taking off his glasses. "I've been your grandfather's agent for thirty years. I'm trying to save you money here. If this young lady has a license from another state, we can link the records. We can pull her history. It saves you nearly a thousand dollars a year." He picked up his pen. "What was the previous license state? Ohio?" Maya froze. Stella placed her hand firmly on the desk. "Mr. Russo. Stop." She glanced at the small TV mounted in the corner of the office. It was tuned to the National News Network. The headline scrolling across the bottom read: SPY RING BUSTED IN RHODE ISLAND. COLONEL VIKTOR KROV REMANDED WITHOUT BAIL. DAUGHTER 'SARAH HALLOWAY' IN PROTECTIVE CUSTODY. Stella pointed to the screen. "You see that?" Stella asked. Russo looked. He read the name Sarah Halloway. He looked at the girl sitting in the chair—the one with the brand-new, jet-black bob cut and the terrified eyes. He looked back at Stella. The realization hit him like a truck. "Oh," Russo whispered. "Oh my god." "Her name is Maya Porter," Stella said, her voice low and intense. "Sarah Halloway is gone. And she needs to stay gone." She leaned in. "If you link those files, Mr. Russo... if you type 'Sarah Halloway' into your database to save me eight hundred bucks... you create a digital bridge. A bridge that her father's lawyers can find. A bridge that foreign intelligence can find." She tapped the new license on the desk. "We need an air gap. Total isolation. This policy cannot have a single byte of data connecting her to Ohio. She needs to be a ghost." Russo looked at Maya. He saw the fear. He saw the new life she was trying to build. He remembered Arthur Bennett, and how he always protected his own. Russo deleted the text in the "Prior History" field. "Understood," Russo said, his voice grave. "New driver. Zero history. We pay the surcharge." "We pay the surcharge," Stella confirmed. "It's the cost of safety." Russo typed quickly. He wasn't just an agent anymore; he was part of the cover-up. "I'm flagging the file as VIP / RESTRICTED ACCESS," Russo said. "It means only I can open it. No customer service reps. No data sharing." He printed the card. INSURED: STELLA MARIE PORTER AUTHORIZED DRIVERS: 1. STELLA PORTER 2. OLIVIA PORTER 3. MAYA PORTER VEHICLE: 2001 HOLT SENTINEL He handed it to Maya with both hands. "Drive safe, Ms. Porter," Russo said. "And welcome to the neighborhood." They walked out to the parking lot. The Holt Sentinel was parked in the front row, its snow tires gripping the asphalt. Stella stopped. She held up the keys. "You're insured," Stella said. "You're licensed. You're a ghost." She tossed the keys to Maya. "You drive." Maya caught the keys. She looked at the heavy, American steel of the Sentinel. It wasn't the rental car her father drove. It was the Tank. "Really?" Maya asked. "We need to test your winter driving skills," Stella smiled. "Leo, you're copilot. Navigate her to the grocery store. We need milk." Leo rolled to the passenger door. Maya helped him transfer in—she knew the drill now. She folded his manual chair and put it in the trunk. She climbed into the driver's seat. She adjusted the mirror. She saw Maya Porter looking back. Ignition, Leo typed from the shotgun seat. Maya turned the key. The V8 roared to life. She put it in gear and drove the Fortress out of the lot, leaving Sarah Halloway behind in the database of ghosts.

title: Part 13: The Maiden Voyage
content: Maya sat in the driver’s seat of the 2001 Holt Sentinel. The steering wheel was huge. The hood stretched out forever. It felt like piloting a boat. Stella sat in the back seat, buckling her seatbelt. "Mirrors adjusted?" "Yes," Maya said, gripping the wheel at 10 and 2. Leo sat in the passenger seat ("Shotgun"). He had his MagnaByte Scribe mounted on his lap. He looked at Maya. He didn't look scared. Navigator ready, he typed. "DESTINATION: UNKNOWN. YOU DRIVE. I GUIDE." "Where are we going?" Maya asked. The island tour, Leo typed. "FIRST STOP: FUEL." Maya drove out of the lot. The Sentinel’s V8 rumbled. It was heavy, but powerful. She pulled into the gas station down the street. "Regular," Stella instructed from the back. "Fill it up. We have a long drive." Maya got out. She pumped the gas. It was a simple act—something she had done a hundred times in Ohio for her father—but this time, she was using Stella’s card, filling Stella’s car, for a trip she was driving. It felt like freedom. Head north, Leo typed. Enter I-895 at exit 3. Maya merged onto the arterial road. She accelerated onto the on-ramp for I-895 East (signed North). The Sentinel roared up to 65 MPH. Maya merged into traffic. The car floated over the bumps. "Stay in the middle lane," Stella advised. "Until Leo tells you otherwise." They cruised past Exit 4 (Exeter) and Exit 5 (Liberty). Then came the signs. EXIT 6 - US-1. LEFT LANE ENDS. The funnel, Leo typed. Merge right. now. Maya checked her blind spot. A massive delivery truck was barreling down the left lane, trying to beat the squeeze. "He's cutting you off," Stella warned. Maya didn't flinch. She tapped the gas, surged ahead of the truck, and signaled right. She slid the massive Sentinel into the center lane just as the concrete jersey barrier forced the left lane to vanish. "Nice move," Stella said approvingly. "Assertive." Good calculations, Leo agreed. They crossed the Jamestown Bridge. Maya kept her hands steady as the wind buffeted the car. Then, the Newport Bridge loomed ahead. The toll plaza was approaching. "Center lane," Stella said. "Token lane." She handed Maya a gold RITBA Token from the center console. "Don't stop completely," Stella coached. "Just roll down the window and toss it in the basket. Aim for the net." Maya slowed to 5 MPH. She rolled down the window. She tossed the token. CLINK. GREEN LIGHT. The gate flew up. Maya accelerated up the massive span of the bridge, the bay sparkling 200 feet below. Take exit 12, Leo typed. " ADMIRAL KALBFUS RD / US NAVAL BASE." Maya took the sharp exit ramp. It curled to the right like a cloverleaf loop, swinging them around 270 degrees and dropping them down to street level. She stopped at the traffic light at the bottom. Directly across the intersection was the massive, hulking concrete structure of the Former Newport Jai Alai (now a slot parlor). It looked like a bunker. Right turn, Leo instructed. "Follow Admiral Kalbfus Road. We're taking the back way to Newport." His next instruction was to have Maya make a left onto Farewell Street. The streets of Newport were narrow, colonial, and crowded even in winter. Maya threaded the wide Sentinel through the traffic on America's Cup Avenue. Right on bellevue, Leo directed. They turned onto the legendary avenue. The mansions rose up on either side—massive stone palaces behind iron gates. They passed Stanton’s Reach. "That's the one the agent tried to sell Grandpa," Stella said from the back. "Seventy rooms and a drafty roof." Maya looked at it. It was beautiful, but cold. They followed Bellevue all the way to Ocean Drive. The road curved along the rocky coastline. The waves crashed against the cliffs. "I've never seen the ocean like this," Maya whispered. "In Ohio, it's just... corn." "This is your backyard now," Stella said. They looped back up the island, turning onto Broadway. They passed a large brick building on the hill. Newport Hospital. "That's where we started," Stella said, pointing. "Me, Luna, and Leo. Born right there on the third floor." Leo looked at the hospital. It was the origin point. Data source, he typed. They crossed into Middletown. They were on West Main Road—a busy, four-lane commercial strip with fast traffic. Destination on left, Leo typed. Bayview creamery. Maya saw the sign. But it was on the other side of the road. There was no traffic light. She had to make a Left Turn across two lanes of oncoming traffic. "Wait for the gap," Stella said. "Don't force it." Maya waited. Cars zoomed by. A truck. A van. Then, a break. Maya hit the gas. The Sentinel surged. She cut across the lanes smoothly and pulled into the parking lot of the BayView Creamery. She put the car in park. She turned off the engine. Her hands were shaking slightly, but she was smiling. "You did it," Stella said. "Highway. Bridge. City. Left turn. You passed." Leo looked at her. He raised his hand for a high-five. Excellent piloting, he typed. You can drive the tank. "I can," Maya said, unbuckling. "I really can." "Good," Stella said. "Now let's go inside. I'm buying you a Colossal Cooler to celebrate. You're officially a Rhode Island driver."

title: Part 1: High Command
content: The rain lashed heavily against the single-pane windows of their modest, cramped living room, but Mary barely heard the storm. The worn, braided rug stretching between the faded couch and the television stand had been completely transformed into an active, high-stakes battlefield. At seven years old, Mary sat cross-legged in the center of the rug, completely enveloped by the warm, safe presence of her two older brothers. The house was small, with low ceilings and creaky floorboards that stood in stark contrast to the sprawling, ostentatious McMansions going up in the wealthier suburbs, but to Mary, it was an absolute sanctuary. Ethan, the eldest, was hunched over the centerpiece of their campaign: a sprawling, asymmetrical fortress constructed entirely of brightly colored Snap-Bricks. His brow was furrowed in deep architectural concentration. He carefully pressed a long, reinforced gray plate into the upper parapet, testing its weight-bearing capacity with his thumb. "Okay, the structural integrity is solid on the west tower," Ethan announced, leaning back and wiping a smudge of dust from his forehead. He looked directly at Mary, his eyes bright with collaborative excitement. "It’s reinforced. It can definitely hold the Supreme Commander without collapsing." Mary beamed. She reached into the communal toybox beside her and pulled out her favorite Stella Doll. This particular Stella was wearing a glittering, highly articulated evening gown, but in the context of the rug, she wasn't going to a gala; she was the brilliant, undisputed tactical general of their entire army. Mary leaned forward and carefully positioned the glamorous doll on the newly reinforced Snap-Brick balcony, overlooking the chaotic living room floor. Ethan immediately wrapped his arm around Mary’s waist, pulling her into a warm, heavy side-hug as they both admired the placement. Mary leaned her head happily against his shoulder, entirely used to the constant, grounding affection her brothers provided. "Supreme Commander Stella is in position," Mary declared, her voice ringing with absolute authority. She pointed toward the hallway. "But the enemy forces are advancing past the coffee table. What is the status of the heavy cavalry?" Connor, sitting cross-legged on Mary's other side, sprang into action. As the tactician, he had spent the last twenty minutes meticulously organizing a defensive perimeter. "Heavy cavalry is locked and loaded, Commander," Connor reported with a sharp, entirely serious salute. He gestured to a fierce, perfectly aligned row of Morph-Mechanics. The plastic robots had all been shifted into their heavy vehicular and beast forms, creating an impenetrable wall of armor at the base of the Snap-Brick fortress. Behind them, crouching behind the legs of the coffee table, was a squad of Frontline Commandos. The rugged, military action figures were positioned flawlessly for a flanking maneuver. "The Frontline Commandos are holding the valley," Connor explained, scooting closer until his knee bumped against Mary's. He leaned over, resting his chin on Mary's other shoulder so the three siblings were practically huddled into a single, cohesive unit. "But we need Stella to give the order. Do we send the Velocity Die-Casts down the plastic orange track to break their lines, or do we hold the fort?" Mary narrowed her eyes, completely immersed in the tactical weight of the decision. She looked at the gleaming Velocity Die-Casts waiting at the top of the ramp Ethan had built over the arm of the couch. She looked at the Frontline Commandos, and then up at her Stella Doll standing proudly on the balcony. Neither of her brothers tried to rush her. They didn't snatch the toys, and they certainly didn't tell her that dolls couldn't lead military campaigns. In this house, on this rug, Mary's imagination was the absolute, uncontested law. "We hold the fort," Mary decided, her voice dropping into a dramatic, hushed whisper. "Stella says we wait until they get past the rug fringe. Then, we release the Morph-Mechanics." "Hold the line!" Ethan barked, fully committing to the narrative. He squeezed Mary tighter, a bright, booming laugh escaping his chest. "Nobody moves until the Commander says so!" Connor grinned, reaching across Mary to high-five his older brother. Mary giggled, burying her face into Ethan's sweater as Connor wrapped his arms around both of them from the side, turning the tactical huddle into a massive, tangled pile of hugs. They collapsed onto the carpet together, a mess of laughter and warm, physical affection, completely insulated from the gloomy rain outside. The campaign would eventually end, and they would ultimately use their Foam-Strike Blasters to safely and violently demolish the Snap-Brick towers in a hail of foam darts. But for right now, the fortress was impenetrable, the Supreme Commander was in charge, and Mary was exactly where she belonged—safe in the middle, fiercely protected and unconditionally loved.

title: Part 2: Untitled Chapter
content: By the time the sun fully set, the rain had softened into a steady, rhythmic tap against the bedroom window. But Mary and her two older brothers weren't in a bedroom anymore. They were miles away, deep in the uncharted, perilous wilderness. The sprawling, patchwork tent dominated the small room, constructed from a complex architectural web of fitted sheets, heavy winter quilts, and three dining room chairs Ethan had meticulously dragged down the hallway. To step outside the fabric flap was to risk the dangerous, dark forest, but inside, it was a perfectly insulated, glowing sanctuary. Mary lay perfectly content in the exact center of the mattress, sandwiched securely between her brothers. The physical affection between the three of them was a constant, unspoken baseline. Ethan lay on her right, his arm wrapped protectively over her stomach, while Connor was tucked against her left side, his chin resting comfortably on her shoulder. They were buried together under a mountain of blankets, creating a shared pocket of absolute warmth. The only light in the tent came from the cheap, plastic flashlight clutched in Ethan's hand. He pointed the beam straight up at the sheet above them, the pale yellow circle acting as their glowing, makeshift campfire. "And then," Ethan whispered, his voice dropping into a dramatic, gravelly octave as he wiggled his fingers in front of the flashlight lens. Long, monstrous shadows danced violently across the fabric ceiling. "The phantom bear stepped on a dry snap-twig. Crack." Connor immediately provided the sound effects, letting out a low, impressive growl from the back of his throat. He nudged his cold nose against Mary’s neck, making her giggle and squirm under the heavy blankets. "The bear was looking for the campers who stole his honey," Ethan continued, leaning his head closer to Mary's so the three of them were practically nose-to-nose in the dark. "He sniffed the outside of the tent. He was getting closer... and closer..." "But he didn't get inside," Mary interrupted, her voice ringing with the fierce, unshakeable authority she always wielded during their games. She reached up and pushed Ethan’s flashlight hand slightly to the right, banishing the shadow monster. "Because Supreme Commander Stella was guarding the flap, and she told the bear to go home." Ethan let out a bright, breathy laugh, completely and instantly yielding the narrative to his seven-year-old sister. "You're right. Stella told him to go away, and the phantom bear got scared and ran back into the woods." "Exactly," Mary nodded firmly, cuddling deeper into the heavy quilt. "We are totally secure." She knew the wooden dresser was sitting just a few inches past the fabric wall, and she knew the familiar amber glow of the hallway nightlight was waiting just beyond the bedroom door. They were perfectly safe inside their modest, quiet house. But as Ethan tightened his arm around her waist and Connor let out a dramatic, theatrical yawn beside her, Mary felt a profound, undeniable sense of safety that had absolutely nothing to do with the walls of the room. As long as she was anchored right here, right in the middle of her brothers, there wasn't a single monster in the woods—real or pretend—that could ever reach her.

title: Part 1: The Garage Barracks
content: The weight of the blankets in the converted garage was a heavy, grounding anchor. David woke to the familiar, rhythmic breathing of the three girls surrounding him. He was pinned securely in the center of the massive, custom-built bed. Meredith’s arm was thrown heavily over his chest from the left, acting as a human weighted blanket against his morning spasticity. To his right, Kate was curled on her side, perfectly bracketed by Morgan on the far edge. It was perfectly safe. It was entirely routine. But David still felt the hollow ache in his chest where Hannah was supposed to be. He blinked against the early morning light filtering through the blinds, doing the math in his head. Six hours. Hannah was still fast asleep in the dark of Pearl Harbor. He let out a low, sustained hum—a sound of quiet longing. Meredith shifted instantly, her eyes cracking open. She didn’t ask what was wrong; she just squeezed his shoulder and gave a single, understanding nod. Hannah had promised to call later that afternoon, and the entire family was counting down the hours until they heard from her. "Alright, troops," Morgan murmured, her voice raspy as she sat up and stretched her arms toward the ceiling. "Up and at 'em. It’s syllabus day." The morning routine commenced with clinical, loving efficiency. Modesty was a concept that simply did not exist within the walls of the garage. It had been burned away by years of necessity. Morgan and Meredith threw back the covers and seamlessly transitioned into caregiving mode, stripping off pajamas and moving directly into the adjoining accessible bathroom. It was a rapid, practiced blur of warm water, soap, and mechanical transfers. "Careful with the shit hose, Mer," Morgan deadpanned, holding up a fresh towel as Meredith expertly flushed Kate's MACE system. "You know she’s got a big day of functioning as a respectable adult today." Kate, sitting securely in her shower chair, let out a sudden, breathy series of silent giggles, her shoulders shaking at the toilet humor. David caught her eye and offered a double-blink of amusement. But beneath Kate's laughter, David could see the subtle, lingering shadow that hadn't been there a year ago. It was only recently that the protective fog around Kate's literal processing had begun to lift. She was just starting to piece together the terrifying reality that Connor’s "safe ride home" hadn't just been a reckless accident—it had been a trap. She was finally understanding what he would have done to her if the Holt sedan hadn't wrapped around that utility pole. Meredith caught the shift in Kate's eyes too. She didn't offer empty pity. She just kissed the top of Kate's wet, chestnut-red hair and efficiently attached the fresh urinary bag. "You look beautiful today, Kate. Doctor's appointment at ten to check the hardware, and then we're going to watch movies. You and David are eighteen. You call the shots today." Morgan leaned over the double vanity, pulling her heavy hair up into a massive, utilitarian claw clip. She paused, catching her reflection in the harsh bathroom light. A distinct, half-inch band of natural sun-kissed ash was creeping in at her scalp, stark against the dark brunette dye she’d meticulously maintained for the last year. She tilted her head, inspecting the roots, and then looked at Meredith’s reflection right beside her. Meredith’s natural waist-length ash hair was exactly the same shade as Morgan’s roots. "I think I'm done with the dye," Morgan announced suddenly, letting the heavy brunette mass fall back down her back. Meredith paused, holding a clean shirt for David. "You're ditching the brunette? Why?" A slow, wicked grin spread across Morgan's face, her "Fire" protocol already calculating the possibilities. "Because if we go back to being completely identical, we can play Twin Magic again. Think about the tactical advantage. Someone gives Kate a hard time, you step in and quietly warn them off. They walk away, turn a corner, and boom—I'm standing right there, looking exactly like you, ready to ruin their day. It’ll make us look like we can teleport." David let out a sharp, amused huff from his wheelchair, his lips twitching into a smile at the sheer chaos Morgan was planning to inflict on the world. "It's going to take a lot of chemical stripper to get that dark box dye out," Meredith noted pragmatically. "I know. I'll call Tracy," Morgan said, pulling a ribbed tank top over her head. "I'll make an appointment to ask about color removal for this afternoon, right after we get her hardware checked."

title: Part 2: The Commute
content: The drive from the quiet perimeter of Delaney Street to the concrete sprawl of downtown Norfolk took about thirty minutes. David watched the city wake up through the passenger window of the modified family van, the heavy, resistive-touch OmniTalk 3000 already clamped securely to his manual wheelchair's frame. He felt a tightening in his chest—a spike of sensory anticipation. Today was his very first day of college at the Community College of Hampton Roads. There were no high school IEP meetings here, no familiar aides, just thousands of strangers and his freshman SDV 100 orientation class. "We've got some extra time," his dad said, navigating the morning traffic with practiced ease since his own office was located right in the heart of downtown Norfolk. "Let's hit the Rocket Burger drive-thru. Get you some real food before you're stuck in that building all morning." David offered a sharp, agreeable grunt. Even after his bowl of cereal at home, a warm breakfast sandwich and a hashbrown sounded perfect to anchor his stomach before the sensory overload of a new campus set in. As they idled in the drive-thru lane, the scent of hot grease and coffee filling the van, David’s gaze drifted toward his lap. His hands tightened slightly against his legs. The excitement of his first day was warring with the heavy, persistent ache of missing Hannah. During high school, she had always been his safe harbor in chaotic school environments. Facing a massive college building without her sitting next to him felt incredibly isolating. His dad handed the cashier a few bills, grabbed the paper bag, and passed it over to the center console before glancing at David. The older man possessed the same hyper-observant radar as the twins. "I know it's hard, Player Two," his dad said softly, putting the van back into gear. "But she's going to be so proud of you today. And remember, you'll talk to her tonight. Hawaii is six hours behind us. By the time you get home and decompress, she'll be waking up for her day, and you can tell her all about yours." David tapped a quick, rhythmic acknowledgment against his thigh, his posture relaxing just a fraction. His dad was right. Their emotional bond remained entirely intact, easily surviving the 4,800 miles between Virginia and Pearl Harbor. The van navigated the final few blocks, eventually pulling to a stop at the curb right outside the front entrance of the CCHR Martin Building. "Alright, we're here," his dad said, putting the van in park and moving to unhook the wheelchair restraints in the back. He pulled his wallet from his pocket, extracted a crisp twenty-dollar bill, and tucked it securely into the side pocket of David's bag. "For lunch later. Treat yourself at the mall across the street." David gave his dad a firm nod, gripping the friction tape on the handrims of his chair. "Head straight up to the third-floor student lounge," his dad instructed, stepping back so the van's mechanical ramp could deploy. "You've got plenty of time before your eleven o'clock class. Find a quiet table, pull out your laptop, and turn it on. The second that screen boots up, you're going to see that picture of you and Hannah from her visit this summer. Let her ground you before the day starts, okay?" David smiled, a genuine, unshielded expression. He wheeled himself down the ramp and onto the downtown pavement, ready to face the overwhelming environment of the college campus, knowing exactly whose face was waiting for him behind the glass of his screen.

title: Part 3: The Walker Building Lounge
content: The automatic doors of the Walker Building slid open, welcoming David into the blissfully air-conditioned lobby. He gripped the handrims of his manual chair and navigated toward the elevator bank, the friction tape steadying his hold. He pressed the up button, waited for the familiar mechanical ding, and rolled inside, hitting the button for the third floor. When the doors parted again, David wheeled out and took an immediate right, heading down the quiet corridor toward the restrooms to handle his morning business. Once finished, he pivoted the chair and rolled back down the full length of the hallway. He passed the elevator bank he had just come from and continued to the very end of the corridor, turning right into the student lounge. It was completely empty. The quiet hum of the fluorescent lights was the only sound in the room, creating a perfect, low-sensory environment. David found a table near an electrical outlet and parked his chair. He pulled the warm, grease-spotted paper bag from his backpack and took his time eating his Rocket Burger breakfast sandwich and hashbrown. The food settled his stomach, grounding him in the morning routine. Once he finished and wiped his hands, he pulled his laptop from his bag, set it squarely on the table, and hit the power button. The screen flickered to life, loading his desktop. David felt an immediate, involuntary smile pull at the corners of his mouth. The wallpaper was a high-resolution scan of the photo Meredith had taken over the summer. Hannah was standing behind his wheelchair, her arms wrapped fiercely over his shoulders, her chin resting near his. They were both beaming. Staring at it, the overwhelming reality of the massive college campus outside the windows felt a little more manageable. He clicked the mouse and launched Quantum Suite WritePad. The stark white document window snapped open, maximizing across the entire screen and completely covering Hannah’s face. David stretched his fingers and began jotting down a few preparatory notes. He typed out the name of his first class: SDV 100 - Student Development. He knew it was quite literally an introduction to college—a course designed to teach freshmen how to study, how to use the library, and how to survive higher education. He wanted to be ready. A few minutes later, the sound of footsteps echoed in the hallway. A girl walked into the lounge, a heavy backpack slung casually over one shoulder. She paused, glancing around the empty tables before her eyes landed on David. She offered a bright, easy smile and walked directly over to his table. "Hey," she said, her voice friendly and conversational. "Do you mind if I join you? The tables downstairs are freezing, and it's practically a ghost town up here." David offered a sharp, rhythmic tap on the table—his affirmative cue—and gestured toward the empty chair across from him. It was nice to have some company. Sitting alone in a silent room was peaceful, but having someone to pass the time with before his first-ever college class felt like a quintessential freshman experience. "Thanks," she said, dropping her bag and pulling out the chair. "I'm Vesper." David rested his hands on his laptop keyboard. He opened a new, blank WritePad document, quickly typed a response, and swiveled the laptop a few inches toward her so she could read the screen. Hi Vesper. I'm David. It's my first day at CCHR. Vesper read the screen, her brow furrowing slightly in polite confusion. She looked back up at him. "Nice to meet you, David. How come you're typing? Did you lose your voice?" David didn't mind the question; people usually asked when they realized he wasn't going to speak. He pulled the laptop back slightly and typed again. I have cerebral palsy. I can't speak verbally. He turned the screen back to her. Vesper read it, her expression smoothing out into an easy, understanding nod. "Oh, gotcha," she said, leaning forward and resting her elbows on the table, completely unfazed. "Well, you type really fast, so that works perfectly. First day, huh? What class are you waiting for?" SDV 100, David typed. It's in the Martin Building at 11:00. Vesper’s eyes lit up with genuine surprise. "No way. I'm in the Martin Building at 11:00 too. I'm taking Applied Calculus right next door to the SDV rooms." David raised an eyebrow, his fingers flying across the keys. Calculus doesn't sound like an easy morning class. Vesper laughed, a light, airy sound. "It is if you like numbers. I'm just taking it for an easy A, honestly. Math has always kind of been my thing." She checked the clock on the wall. "Since we're heading to the exact same place at the exact same time, I can walk over with you later, if you want?" David nodded, offering a small smile. His literal, pragmatic brain processed the interaction exactly as it was presented: a fellow student waiting for class, making polite conversation, and offering to walk to the same building. It was a perfectly normal, pleasant start to his college career.

title: Part 4: The InfoLink Update
content: For the next hour, the conversation flowed easily. Vesper proved to be incredibly talkative, which suited David perfectly. He didn't have to strain to keep the interaction going; he simply listened, nodded, and occasionally typed brief responses into his open Quantum Suite WritePad document to answer her questions. She asked about his schedule, and he typed out his plan for the afternoon. I'm going to The Promenade at Granby after class. My dad gave me twenty dollars for a burger combo at the food court. Vesper’s face lit up. "Oh, I love the mall food court. I actually have a huge gap between my calculus class and my afternoon lab. Do you mind if I tag along? I'd love to grab lunch with you." David offered a sharp, agreeable grunt and typed, Sure. That sounds great. His literal processing cataloged the interaction cleanly: he was going to eat lunch, and she also needed to eat lunch. It made logical sense to go together. A familiar, high-pitched chime suddenly echoed from his laptop speakers. David minimized the WritePad window just enough to reveal the buddy list of InfoLink Messenger, keeping the main document stretched over the background photo of Hannah so he wouldn't accidentally close it. He saw Morgan’s screenname highlighted in bright green, signaling she was online. He opened a chat box and began typing rapidly. Dave: Hey. Made it to campus. Sitting in the lounge. Morg: Awesome! How is it? Overwhelming? Dave: It's quiet. I met a girl named Vesper. She has a math class next to my SDV class. We're going to get lunch at the mall after. Vesper leaned over slightly, looking at the chat window. "Who are you messaging?" David pointed to the screen and typed a quick explanation in WritePad. My cousin, Morgan. We live together. "Oh, that's sweet," Vesper smiled, leaning back in her chair. On the screen, Morgan’s reply popped up. Morg: That’s great! Make sure you get a good burger. Just remember Mer is picking you up at the mall entrance at 2:00 PM. I gotta run, leaving for the salon now. Wish me luck getting this dark box dye stripped out! Going back to blonde so Mer and I can play Twin Magic. David smiled at the screen, double-blinking in amusement at his cousin's tactical plans before typing a quick goodbye. He closed the InfoLink window just as the digital clock in the corner of his screen rolled over to 10:45 AM. He tapped the table to get Vesper’s attention, pointing to the time. "Oh, wow, you're right. We should head over," Vesper said, standing up and slinging her backpack over her shoulder. As David reached for the friction tape on his wheelchair's handrims, Vesper stepped behind him. "Here, let me. The brick sidewalk outside can be a pain. I don't mind." David paused, but then gave a short hum of appreciation, relaxing his grip. He was perfectly capable of pushing himself, but it was a warm morning, and saving his energy before his first class was a welcome luxury. He let her take the heavy rubber grips of the push handles. Vesper navigated the chair with surprising ease, pushing him out of the lounge, into the Walker Building elevator, and down to the ground floor. They rolled out into the humid Virginia air, crossing the single city block until the imposing brick facade of the Martin Building loomed ahead of them. Vesper pushed him through the automated doors and directly into the main elevator bank, hitting the button for the fourth floor. When the doors opened, the hallway was a chaotic, buzzing hive of freshmen trying to find their rooms. Vesper pushed him down the corridor until they reached the door for SDV 100. Right next door, the plaque for the 200-level Applied Calculus room gleamed under the fluorescent lights. "Alright, here we are," Vesper said, stepping around to the front of his chair with a bright smile. "Have a great first class, David. I'll meet you right out here when it's over, and we'll head across the street for those burgers." David nodded, offering a warm smile and a polite wave as she turned and walked into the math classroom. He gripped his wheels and rolled himself into SDV 100, feeling incredibly accomplished. His first college interaction was a complete success, and he hadn't even opened a textbook yet.

title: Part 5: The Color Correction
content: The chemical smell of the strip mall salon hit the twins the second they walked through the glass doors. It was a potent, sterile mix of aerosol hairspray, burning flat irons, and sharp ammonia. Morgan checked in at the reception desk, with Meredith standing shoulder-to-shoulder right beside her. Ten minutes later, Morgan was sitting in a black vinyl styling chair with a heavy nylon cape draped over her shoulders, while Meredith claimed the station right next to hers. Their stylist, an older woman named Tracy with heavily highlighted hair and a pragmatist's gaze, stood behind Morgan. Tracy ran her fingers through Morgan's waist-length, dark brunette hair, lifting the heavy sections and inspecting the half-inch band of natural, sun-kissed ash roots at the scalp. "So," Tracy said, catching Morgan’s eye in the massive wall mirror. "You want to go back to your natural blonde. How long have you been dyeing it dark?" "A little over a year," Morgan replied, leaning back into the chair. "I just touch up the roots every month. But I'm done. I want it perfectly matched to my sister's." Tracy looked over at Meredith. Meredith calmly reached back, pulled her signature plastic claw clip loose, and let her own waist-length, natural sun-kissed ash hair cascade down her back. "That's the target," Meredith said cleanly, her "Ice" protocol operating even in a salon setting. "Since we're identical, her underlying pigment is exactly the same as mine. I'm just here to serve as the physical color swatch." Tracy let out a heavy sigh, dropping Morgan's hair and resting her hands on her hips. "Honey, I'm going to be straight with you. You both have gorgeous, healthy hair, but permanent dark dye is stubborn. It stains the cuticle." "I know," Morgan nodded, having done her homework the night before. "I read that color doesn't lift color. You can't just slap blonde dye over the brunette and call it a day, right?" Tracy raised a genuinely impressed eyebrow. "Exactly. We have to strip it, and it is going to be a massive project. You're going to be in my chair for the next five hours. First, I have to apply a chemical color reducer to pull the artificial brunette molecules out. Fair warning: it smells exactly like rotten eggs. After we wash that out, your hair is going to look like a rusty penny. Then, I have to go in with bleach to lift you past that orange stage. Finally, we tone it back to match your sister's." "What about the damage?" Meredith asked, her eyes narrowing slightly in the mirror. "We'll take it slow," Tracy assured her. "But it's going to cost a pretty penny, and your scalp is going to tingle." Morgan stared at her reflection, imagining Vesper Vance. She pictured the inevitable moment someone tried to corner David or Kate, thinking they had outsmarted Meredith, only to realize the "Fire" protocol was standing right behind them, wearing the exact same face. The psychological warfare of Twin Magic was unparalleled. "Do it," Morgan said, her voice entirely devoid of hesitation. "Strip it. Whatever it takes to get it perfectly matched." Tracy chuckled, shaking her head as she turned toward the chemical mixing room in the back. "Alright, boss. Get comfortable. I'll go mix up the sulfur." While Tracy was mixing the color stripper, another stylist gestured for Meredith to move into her chair. Since she was already there, Meredith requested her standard maintenance—a thorough wash and a clean trim to dust the dead ends off her waist-length hair. Morgan watched her sister in the mirror. "You don't have to stay for the rotten egg part, Mer. It's going to reek." "I'm not going anywhere until I have to leave to pick David up at two," Meredith replied calmly, leaning her head back into the ceramic washbowl. "We're in this together. Plus, if Tracy gets the toner wrong, I need to be here to hold up a lock of my hair and object." Morgan smiled, settling deeper into the vinyl chair. The perimeter was secure, David was safe in his SDV 100 class, and the twins were preparing to rebuild their ultimate visual weapon.

title: Part 6: SDV 100
content: David rolled through the doorway of the Martin Building classroom, his tires gliding smoothly over the linoleum floor. He scanned the room, his analytical mind immediately taking inventory. The classroom was designed to hold thirty students, but it felt remarkably empty. There were only nine other students scattered across the rows, and as David navigated toward the front, he realized he was the only male in the room. He parked his manual chair at the designated wheelchair-accessible table near the front. He looked at the standard student desks arrayed behind him—rigid plastic chairs bolted directly to tiny, restrictive laminate tabletops. They looked incredibly uncomfortable. He felt a wave of relief that his physical mobility needs afforded him a wide, freestanding table where he could comfortably set up his laptop and angle his heavy OmniTalk 3000. At eleven o'clock, the female instructor, Professor Hayes, walked to the front of the room. She spent the first twenty minutes handing out syllabi, explaining the attendance policy, and outlining the purpose of Student Development 100 as the foundational survival guide for college. "Now," Professor Hayes said, clapping her hands together. "Since this is a small group, we are going to do an icebreaker. Let's go around the room with 'Three Truths and a Lie.' You'll give us four facts about yourself, and the rest of the class has to guess which one you made up." She pointed to the front row. "Let's start over here." The game moved systematically around the room, forcing the quiet students to introduce themselves. The first was a white Caucasian exchange student named Chloe. She leaned back, dropping her backpack onto the floor. A prominent Union Jack patch was pinned to the front pocket. "Right then," Chloe said, her voice carrying a thick, unmistakable Cockney accent. "One: I'm absolutely terrified of spiders. Two: I play ice hockey. Three: I put maple syrup in my morning tea. And four: I walk past the Queen's guards at Buckingham Palace on my way to my hometown school." The class, completely thrown by her heavy British accent and the flag on her bag, immediately assumed the Canadian stereotypes had to be fake. "It's the maple syrup," Jessica guessed confidently. "You definitely don't put syrup in tea." Chloe laughed, her Cockney lilt still perfectly intact. "No, the Buckingham Palace one is the lie. My parents are from East London and I picked up their accent at home, but I was born and raised in London, Ontario. Everyone always falls for the accent." The girl sitting next to her, Geneviève, was also a Canadian exchange student. She spoke with a beautifully clear cadence, effortlessly weaving perfect Canadian English with a flawless Québécois French accent. "One: I speak French at home. Two: I drove from Saint-Georges, Québec, to Virginia. Three: I love eating poutine. Four: I go snowboarding every single weekend." The class guessed correctly—her lie was snowboarding, as she actually hated the cold weather despite living in Canada. Next was Emily, a girl with a completely American-sounding name but deep, traditional Asian cultural heritage. "One: My grandparents own a traditional Japanese restaurant. Two: I know how to perform a full tea ceremony. Three: I have a black belt in judo. Four: I was born in Tokyo." Her lie was the birthplace; she had actually been born in California. The next three students were African American girls sitting in a loose cluster. Jasmine went first. "One: I work at a veterinary clinic. Two: I have five sisters. Three: I make my own jewelry. Four: I have a pet iguana." Her lie was the iguana, drawing a few laughs from the room. Kiara sat up straight for her turn. "One: I sing in my church choir. Two: I can do a standing backflip. Three: I love reading classic horror novels. Four: I've never broken a single bone." The class accurately guessed that the backflip was a lie. Maya leaned forward, resting her elbows on the uncomfortable bolted desk. "One: I run track. Two: I am double-jointed in my thumbs. Three: I bake wedding cakes with my mom. Four: I absolutely love scary movies." Her lie was the horror movies; she admitted she couldn't even watch commercials for them without getting nightmares. Next was Nia. She gripped the edge of her tiny desk, her knuckles slightly white. She was Jamaican, and her thick accent was laced with visible nerves. "One: This is my very first time in the United States. Two: I grew up five minutes from the beach. Three: I love spicy jerk chicken. Four: I am a competitive ice skater." Her lie was incredibly obvious, but her nervous delivery made the room smile warmly. David caught her eye and offered a slow, supportive double-blink. Nia seemed to relax just a fraction, realizing the classroom was a safe space. Before anyone could answer, Kiara chimed in with a grin. "Wait, you're not a bobsledder, are you? You know, feeling the rhythm, feeling the rhyme?" Nia let out a bright, genuine laugh, the tension completely leaving her shoulders. "No bobsledding for me, I promise! The ice skating is definitely the lie." The last two women in the back row were Caucasian Americans. Sarah spoke up. "One: I drive a manual transmission car. Two: I am highly allergic to strawberries. Three: I play the acoustic guitar. Four: I met the President of the United States." The class collectively murmured, and almost every student pointed to the fourth option. Sarah smirked, shaking her head. "Nope. I actually met him years ago when he was still the Governor of Arkansas. Shook his hand at a rally. The lie is the acoustic guitar. I have absolutely zero musical talent." Jessica went next. "One: I have a twin brother. Two: I work at a used bookstore. Three: I own a horse. Four: I speak fluent German." Her lie was the German fluency, admitting she barely passed high school Spanish. Then, the room went quiet. Every eye turned toward the accessible table at the front. David didn't panic. He was perfectly comfortable with who he was, and he knew exactly how to establish his boundaries. He stretched his fingers, pulling his laptop closer, and typed his four facts directly into the open Quantum Suite WritePad document. Rather than turning the screen, he highlighted the text and routed it through the OmniTalk 3000 clamped to his chair. The device required firm physical pressure on its resistive touch screen, but it was necessary for the room to hear him clearly. The heavy, robotic voice echoed through the quiet classroom. "One. I communicate fluently using my own system of non-verbal hums and taps. Two. I share a house with fiercely protective identical twin cousins. Three. I am currently taking lessons to get my driver's license. Four. I rely on this device to speak to new people." The class looked at him, mentally weighing the options. Geneviève tentatively raised her hand. "Is the lie number three? About the driver's license?" David smiled, a sharp, unshielded grin. He tapped his keyboard, letting the robotic voice confirm it. "Correct. My cerebral palsy affects my fine motor control, making driving impossible. Number three is the lie." A ripple of warm, respectful nods moved through the nine women in the room. Professor Hayes smiled, marking a check on her roster. David leaned back in his manual chair, feeling his muscles relax. SDV 100 was going to be an easy class.

title: Part 7: The Foundation
content: With the icebreaker finished and the tension in the room thoroughly dissolved, Professor Hayes moved to the dry-erase board at the front of the classroom. "Alright, let's talk about why you are all actually here," she began, uncapping a marker. "Student Development 100 is a mandatory class for a reason. Right now, you are all standing on the bridge between high school and the rest of your lives. And the biggest shock you are going to face this semester is the sudden, absolute freedom." David focused on his screen, his fingers resting lightly on his laptop keyboard. He had a fresh Quantum Suite WritePad document open, ready to take notes. "In high school, you had guardrails," Professor Hayes explained, pacing slowly across the front of the room. "You had teachers chasing you down for missing assignments. You had parents getting progress reports. You had a rigid, bell-to-bell schedule. Here at CCHR, all of that is gone. You are officially adults. If you skip class, no one is going to call your house. If you don't turn in a paper, I am not going to remind you. Your syllabus is your contract, and time management is entirely your responsibility." David typed the words Time Management and Self-Advocacy into his document. He felt a profound sense of validation washing over him. For his entire life, his schedule had been dictated by Individualized Education Programs, physical therapy appointments, and the deeply loving but unyielding protective perimeter of the Delaney Vanguard. Hearing a professor explicitly state that he was an adult responsible for his own success was exhilarating. It was the exact autonomy his father and cousins had promised him this morning. For the next half hour, Professor Hayes walked them through the survival mechanics of the Norfolk campus. She handed out detailed maps, circling the library in the Walker Building, the academic advising offices, and the campus tutoring center. "Self-advocacy is your greatest tool," she emphasized, making eye contact with the students. "If you are struggling in a class, do not wait until midterms. The tutoring center is free. My office hours are on the syllabus. You have to be the one to raise your hand and ask for help, because no one here is going to read your mind." David saved his WritePad document, intentionally leaving the window maximized across his screen. He didn't want to close it, knowing he would need to type out his lunch order when he got to the mall anyway. He simply closed the laptop lid, letting the machine slip into sleep mode, and slid it safely into his backpack. "Alright, that covers the ground rules," Professor Hayes announced as the digital clock on the wall clicked over to 11:50 AM. "Read the first two chapters of the textbook by Wednesday. Welcome to college, everyone. You're dismissed." The classroom instantly filled with the chaotic sound of chairs scraping against the linoleum and backpacks zipping shut. David gripped the friction tape on his wheelchair's handrims, navigating his way out from behind the accessible table. He offered a polite nod to Nia and Geneviève as he rolled toward the door, merging with the flow of students heading out into the fourth-floor corridor. The hallway was a sudden explosion of noise as dozens of classroom doors opened simultaneously. David wheeled himself out of SDV 100, letting his eyes adjust to the fluorescent lights of the hallway. Right next door, the heavy wooden door to the 200-level Applied Calculus room swung open. Vesper Vance stepped out into the hallway, her backpack slung casually over her shoulder. She scanned the crowd for a fraction of a second before her eyes locked onto David's wheelchair. The bright, easy smile from the student lounge instantly returned to her face. She walked smoothly through the flow of exiting students, slipping right into his personal space. "Hey," Vesper said, her voice easily cutting through the noise of the hallway. She looked down at him, her demeanor perfectly charming and thoroughly convincing. "Surviving so far?" David gave a sharp, affirmative grunt, offering a warm smile. "Good," she said, gesturing down the long corridor toward the main elevator bank. "My calculus professor spent fifty minutes talking about derivatives. My brain is officially fried. Are you ready to go get those burgers?"

title: Part 8: The Promenade at Granby
content: The transition from the academic quiet of the classroom to the humid Norfolk air was abrupt. Vesper easily took control of the heavy rubber push handles of David's manual wheelchair, steering him out the front doors of the Martin Building. They took a right on the sidewalk, took another right into the open brick plaza, and navigated the single city block over to Monticello Avenue. After waiting for the crosswalk light, Vesper pushed him across the wide street and through the main glass entrance of The Promenade at Granby. The blast of mall air conditioning was a welcome relief, but the noise was immediate. David had been to the upscale downtown mall plenty of times, and as they entered the main corridor, he let out a low, frustrated groan. The line for the central court elevators—Elevators M2, M3, and M4—was a massive, chaotic bottleneck of hungry office workers and college students. He wasn't going to wait in that sensory nightmare. David reached down, his hands gripping the friction tape on the push rims of his wheels. He took the reins of his chair back from Vesper and immediately pivoted to the right, heading away from the crowd and wheeling himself purposefully toward Norwood's. "Wait, where are you going?" Vesper asked, jogging a few steps to catch up with him. "The food court is on the third floor. Those elevators are right there." David didn't stop. He knew the layout of this mall perfectly, and he knew that Elevator M1 was tucked quietly into a far corner near the department store. Vesper let out a soft complaint about how far they were walking, but David took the lead, pushing himself down the quiet corridor until the brushed metal doors of Elevator M1 appeared on their left. He reached out and pressed the call button. While they waited, his mind shifted to his lunch options. A flame-broiled burger and fries from Crown Burger sounded exactly like what he needed. The ding echoed in the quiet corner, and the doors slid open. David wheeled himself into the empty elevator. It was a unique cab—tall, rectangular glass panels were set directly into the center of the brushed steel doors, allowing passengers to look out into the atrium. Vesper stepped in behind him. He pressed the button for the third floor, and the heavy doors slid shut, sealing them inside. As the hydraulic lift engaged and the elevator began its ascent, David looked out through the glass door panels, watching the atrium of the first floor drop away. "Okay, so here's the deal," Vesper said suddenly. The light, charming tone she had used in the lounge was completely gone. Her voice was sharp, flat, and aggressively loud in the enclosed space. "We will be eating from the value menu today." David blinked, his autistic brain struggling to process the sudden, jarring shift in volume and tone. She was practically screaming at him. His literal processing kicked in: she must be worried about how much money they had. He quickly reached into his pocket, pulled out his wallet, and extracted the crisp twenty-dollar bill his dad had given him that morning. He held it up, pointing to the cash and then tapping his own chest, trying to communicate non-verbally that he had his own money and could pay for himself. Vesper’s eyes narrowed into a glare. She completely failed to understand his communication, misinterpreting his literal gesture as a defiant challenge to her authority. She let out a sharp, angry scoff, her posture rigid and hostile. David quickly folded the twenty and shoved it back into his pocket, a spike of sensory anxiety hitting his chest. He was deeply unnerved. Why had she just screamed at him over lunch prices? As the hydraulic lift pushed past the second floor, the concrete lip of the third-floor landing slowly came into view through the glass panels of the elevator doors. And standing right there on the landing, perfectly framed in the glass before the elevator even leveled out, was Meredith. David didn't hesitate. The second the doors parted, he gripped his wheels, propelled himself forward out of the cab, and practically threw his arms around Meredith's waist. Meredith dropped her shopping bag instantly and wrapped her arms around his shoulders, pulling him into a fierce, heavy hug. The familiar Deep Pressure Therapy instantly regulated his spiking heart rate. Vesper stepped out of the elevator, her jaw dropping slightly in confusion. Her eyes immediately tracked over Meredith, taking in her thick glasses, her casual striped shirt, and her disproportionately large chest. David pulled back from the hug. He flipped his laptop open on his lap, bringing up the WritePad document, and typed quickly before routing it through the heavy OmniTalk 3000 clamped to his chair. "Meredith, this is Vesper. She is in the math class next door to SDV," the robotic voice announced, completely devoid of emotion. "Vesper, this is my cousin, Meredith. We are getting lunch. Meredith, would you like to join us?" Vesper’s face instantly twisted into a look of dark, heavy skepticism. Cousin. Vesper's eyes darted between David and this striking, waist-length-haired woman. The look she shot David made it abundantly clear she didn't buy the family connection for a single second, and that having this girl crash their lunch was a terrible idea. David, entirely focused on his OmniTalk screen, missed the judgmental glare completely. But Meredith didn't. She noticed every single micro-expression. As the device spoke, David locked eyes with Meredith. He offered a very specific, tense double-blink. Be my bodyguard. He didn't know Vesper well enough to know if she was a good person, but the screaming in the elevator had set off every alarm bell in his head. Meredith’s "Ice" protocol engaged instantly. She read David's tension, smoothly picked up her shopping bag, and offered Vesper a polite, chillingly perfect smile. "I'd love to." Vesper groaned quietly under her breath, a flash of deep irritation crossing her face, but she forced a tight smile and went along with it. They navigated to the Crown Burger counter. David pulled out his twenty-dollar bill, pointing to Meredith's tray and offering to treat her. Meredith accepted with a warm smile, but her eyes flicked over David's shoulder. She caught the perturbed look on Vesper’s face—a look of absolute jealousy, confirming her assumption that Vesper believed David was wasting his money on another woman. They found a table in the food court. David ate his burger, typing a quick question into WritePad. "Where is Morgan?" the OmniTalk 3000 asked. "She's still at the salon getting her hair dye removed," Meredith answered casually, taking a sip of her drink. She was very careful to only use her sister's name, deliberately hiding the fact that Morgan was her identical twin from the stranger sitting across the table. Vesper picked at her value-menu fries, clearly annoyed that David was focusing all of his attention and communication on his "cousin" rather than her. Meredith silently cataloged Vesper's irritation, letting the silence stretch until the older girl grew visibly uncomfortable. When the last fry was eaten, Meredith stood up, brushing off her jeans. She turned to Vesper with a tone that was flawlessly polite but left absolutely no room for debate. "Well, it was nice to meet you, Vesper. But it's time for David and me to go home." Vesper offered a stiff goodbye, clearly frustrated by the loss of control, and turned to walk back toward the academic buildings. The moment Vesper was out of earshot, Meredith's posture softened. She stepped behind David's chair, resting her hands gently on his shoulders. "I didn't like her," Meredith said quietly. "I was highly uncomfortable with how she reacted when you hugged me. And I didn't like the way she was looking at you." David let out a long, exhausted sigh. "Hey," Meredith said, leaning down to catch his eye with a warm smile. "Good news. You get to call Hannah tonight. Let's get you home so you can decompress. We just need to swing by the salon in Virginia Beach to pick up Morgan, and then we're back on Delaney Street. Sound good?" David tapped his handrims in sharp, grateful agreement. He let Meredith take the push handles, completely surrendering navigation to her. She steered him through the mall and out to the South Parking Deck. As they rolled out onto the concrete of the garage, the automated mall PA system chimed overhead. “Welcome to The Promenade at Granby. This is your Personal Reminder Service. Please remember that you parked on the South Deck, Level 3. That’s South, Level 3. Have a wonderful shopping experience.” Meredith navigated them to Level S4, where her sedan was parked. She opened the passenger door and expertly assisted David with the mechanical transfer from his wheelchair into the front seat. Once he was buckled in, she collapsed the manual chair and stowed it securely in the trunk. She climbed into the driver's seat, engaged the clutch, and smoothly shifted the manual transmission into first gear. They spiraled down to the ground floor, where Meredith paid the parking attendant. She pulled out of the garage, took a left onto City Hall Ave, and merged onto I-264 East, putting the concrete sprawl of downtown Norfolk in the rearview mirror as they headed back to the safety of the Vanguard.

title: Part 9: The Debrief
content: The interior of Meredith's practical sedan was cool and quiet, the low hum of the tires on the asphalt serving as a comforting white noise. They were cruising down I-264 East, leaving the concrete towers of downtown Norfolk behind them. David had his compact travel keyboard resting comfortably on his lap, tethered to the OmniTalk 3000 system. He didn't need to hit the audio trigger right away; he typed out his thoughts in a steady rhythm, letting the sentences queue up while Meredith kept her eyes on the road, her right hand resting lightly on the manual gear shift. "Okay, hit me," Meredith said, glancing at the rearview mirror. "What exactly happened between the lounge and the third floor?" David pressed the trigger. The heavy, robotic voice filled the cabin. "She seemed nice in the lounge," the device stated. "The thought of having lunch with someone was nice. But the central court elevators were packed. I knew Elevator M1 at Norwood's would be empty. She complained about the walk." Meredith let out a sharp chuckle, downshifting smoothly as traffic slowed slightly. "I had the exact same idea. I was on the third floor and didn't want to deal with the M2 crowd, so I went to the Norwood's corner to catch M1 down. Great minds." David typed his next sentence, his fingers moving a little faster as the frustration of the memory returned. "When we got inside the glass, she suddenly changed her attitude. She screamed at me that we were eating the value menu. I pulled out the twenty dollars Dad gave me to show I could pay. She got angrier." Meredith’s jaw tightened, the brief humor vanishing entirely. Her "Ice" protocol was deeply sensitive to people who raised their voices at her cousin. "She screamed at you? In a closed elevator?" "Yes," the robotic voice answered. "I do not wish to get to know Vesper any further. Can you or Morgan accompany me on Wednesday? So I am not alone." "Absolutely," Meredith said without a second of hesitation. They were approaching Exit 14A. Meredith pressed the clutch and downshifted, slowing the sedan to take the sweeping ramp for I-64 Eastbound toward Chesapeake. "We'll both come. We can bring Kate, too. Make it a full Vanguard escort." David's eyes lit up. A sharp, breathy giggle escaped him. He began typing furiously, a massive, unshielded grin spreading across his face. "If she bothers us, we can deploy the Poop Button." Meredith burst out laughing as she merged the sedan onto I-64. The "Poop Button" was their ultimate, undefeated psychological operation. Meredith and Morgan were not fighters, and they never threatened physical violence; instead, they engaged in advanced, utterly absurd biological warfare to protect their perimeter. "Oh, Vesper would absolutely shatter," Meredith laughed, accelerating over the Twin Bridges into Virginia Beach. "Can you imagine? I'd tell her it's an industrial, military-grade model. Then I'd look at Kate's urine bag and tell Vesper she's standing in the splash zone." David slapped his knee, shaking with silent laughter. The best part of the strategy was always Kate herself. Kate never lied, but she never helped the predator, either. She would just sit in her manual wheelchair, technically honest, while the twins escalated the horror. "She'd ask Kate if it can actually spray," Meredith continued, wiping a tear of mirth from her eye as she took Exit 286B, looping onto Indian River Road Eastbound. "And Kate would just say, 'It's related to bowel management,' and Vesper would run away thinking we hold certifications in advanced bowel warfare." They were both laughing their asses off as the tension of the afternoon completely evaporated. The threat of Vesper Vance felt microscopic compared to the unified front of the cousins. A few minutes later, Meredith pulled the sedan into the Kemps River shopping center, parking near the glass storefront of Tracy's hair salon. Meredith killed the engine and turned to David, her tone shifting back to practical caregiving. "Okay, so before we go in, I need to warn you. Morgan is about an hour and a half into a five-hour color correction. You know how she wanted to go back to being blonde so we can run Twin Magic again?" David offered a sharp, affirmative grunt. "Right. Well, Tracy had to use a chemical color stripper first. It smelled like straight rotten eggs," Meredith explained, wrinkling her nose. "Right now, Morgan is sitting in the chair with bleach on her head. Her hair is going to look like a rusty penny. It’s going to be bright, brassy orange." David double-blinked, a fresh wave of amusement hitting him. "Don't laugh at her," Meredith warned, though she was smiling. "She's suffering for the cause. Tracy still has to tone it back to my exact shade of ash. But by tonight, the Vanguard will be back to full, identical strength. Ready to go secure the perimeter?" David nodded enthusiastically. He was ready to get Morgan, get home, and count down the hours until he could log onto InfoLink Messenger to tell Hannah about the absolute disaster of his first college lunch.

title: Part 10: The Salon Debrief
content: The moment David and Meredith pushed through the glass doors of Tracy's salon, a wall of putrid, sulfurous air hit them. True to Meredith's warning, the chemical color stripper smelled exactly like rotten eggs. David wrinkled his nose, but he gripped the handrims of his manual wheelchair and pushed forward, determined to power through the stench for Morgan's sake. They found Morgan sitting in Tracy's chair in the back of the shop. The dark brunette dye was completely gone. In its place, Morgan's heavy, waist-length hair was a shocking, brassy shade of rusty orange. "Don't say a word," Morgan warned, glaring at Meredith through the reflection in the massive wall mirror. "Tracy is mixing the bleach right now." David let out a sharp, breathy giggle, wheeling himself directly into the spot next to her styling chair. Meredith pulled up a rolling stool and sat close to David, allowing him to lean his weight heavily against her shoulder. The firm, continuous physical contact provided the grounding Deep Pressure Therapy he needed to offset the sensory nightmare of the salon's chemical odors. "So, how was the first day?" Morgan asked, wincing slightly as Tracy returned and began painting cold bleach onto her orange strands. "Did the SDV class survive you?" David flipped his laptop open, resting it on his lap, and quickly typed out his response into WritePad before routing it through the OmniTalk 3000. "The class was great," the robotic voice echoed over the hum of the salon's blow dryers. "There are only ten students. I am the only guy in a room with nine women." Morgan laughed. "Oh, you'll be perfectly fine. You were raised in a house completely overrun by women anyway." David double-blinked in agreement. Living with his mother, Meredith, Morgan, Kate, and having Hannah essentially move in during her father's Diego Garcia deployment meant he was entirely comfortable in female-dominated spaces. "The mall, however, was a different story," Meredith chimed in, leaning her head against David's. "Tell her about your new friend." David's fingers flew across the keyboard. He gave Morgan a flawless, pragmatic breakdown of his encounter with Vesper Vance. He explained the polite conversation in the student lounge, the walk across the street, the decision to use Elevator M1 to avoid the crowds, and the sudden, jarring moment Vesper screamed at him about the value menu. Morgan’s eyes narrowed in the mirror, her "Fire" protocol instantly flaring to life. She didn't hesitate for a single second. "We are coming with you on Wednesday," Morgan declared, her tone deadly serious despite the foil packets jutting out of her hair. "We’ll bring Kate. If this Vesper girl even looks at you wrong, we are deploying the Poop Button." Meredith burst into laughter, and David slapped his knee, his shoulders shaking with silent mirth. "What?" Morgan demanded, looking between them. "We literally just had the exact same conversation in the car," Meredith wheezed, wiping her eyes. "I told him we'd threaten her with the splash zone." David offered a bright smile. It was a terrifyingly comforting reminder that the twins operated on the exact same protective wavelength. Tracy, working the bleach through Morgan's hair with practiced precision, chuckled from behind the styling chair. Having been the Delaney family's cosmetologist for years, she was intimately familiar with their specific brand of psychological warfare. She knew perfectly well that Kate's MACE was a legitimate medical device for bowel management, not an industrial poop launcher, but she completely supported the twins' mythology. "You know, David," Tracy said, catching his eye in the mirror. "I see a lot of people sit in this chair, and I hear a lot of stories. A girl who acts sweet when it's just the two of you, but snaps the second she thinks she's losing control over a lunch order? That is a massive red flag. You're making the right choice keeping her at arm's length. She sounds like bad news." David tapped a rhythmic acknowledgment on his laptop case. Hearing it from Tracy was all the validation he needed. If the woman who handled the Vanguard's hair thought someone was a threat, her judgment was as good as gold. With the debrief complete, David settled deeper into Meredith's side, opening up his class portal to tackle his very first college assignment. Professor Hayes had assigned a "168-Hour Time Management Audit." He needed to map out exactly how he planned to spend every hour of the upcoming week—blocking out time for sleep, SDV 100, transportation, and homework. As he diligently typed out his schedule, blocking off the evening hours specifically for his daily Link chats with Hannah, he felt a profound sense of peace. He sincerely hoped Vesper would just take the hint and leave him alone. He didn't want to subject a stranger to the horrifying, fictional capabilities of Kate's medical equipment. But as he looked at Morgan's fierce reflection in the mirror, he knew the Vanguard was ready. Vesper seemed exactly like the kind of person who would push the boundary, just to find out if the twins were bluffing.

title: Part 11: The Library Intercept
content: The five-hour marathon finally came to an end. Tracy turned off the blow dryer and spun Morgan’s vinyl chair around to face the mirror. Morgan stared at her reflection. The dark brunette was entirely gone, but the result wasn't the exact sun-kissed ash she was aiming for. Instead, her long hair was a bright, warm honey-caramel.
