The shelves were stocked with colorful softcovers and massive, intimidating hardcovers. Jessica stopped at a tag labeled HPE 204. There was a stack of thick, glossy textbooks. The cover featured a generic, abstract image of a double helix DNA strand merging with a silhouette of diverse people. Title: Human Sexuality: Biological and Psychosocial Perspectives. Edition: 4th. Condition: New. Jessica picked one up. It was heavy. "Price check," she noted, flipping it over to check the barcode sticker. "\$115.00 New." She looked at Freddie and Paige. "We need three," Freddie said immediately. His voice was gaining strength, fueled by the logic of the situation. "Three?" Paige asked. "That is... three hundred and forty-five dollars. Can't we share?" Freddie shook his head. "Negative. We need to annotate independently. I need to highlight the definitions. You might need to highlight the social dynamics. If we share, the data gets corrupted. We need individual databases." Jessica nodded. "He is right. If we are going to treat this like a manual, we each need our own copy to study." She reached out and grabbed two more copies from the stack. The weight of three textbooks in her arms was substantial. "That is a lot of money, Jess," Paige worried. Jessica smiled, adjusting her grip on the books. "Don't worry about the budget. That is what the 'Avery Grant' is for." "Aunt Marge," Freddie clarified. "Aunt Marge," Jessica confirmed. "She told me specifically: 'Buy the kids whatever they need to get smart.' I think this qualifies." They walked to the checkout counter. The cashier, a student worker wearing a maroon polo, scanned the three identical books. Beep. Beep. Beep. "Taking the class together?" the cashier asked, making small talk. "Study group," Jessica said smoothly, pulling out her debit card. She swiped the card through the reader. Authorizing... Approved. The receipt printed with a rhythmic zzzt-zzzt-zzzt. Jessica handed a bag to Freddie and a bag to Paige. "Possession is nine-tenths of the law," Jessica said. "You own the knowledge now." Freddie looked into the plastic bag. The heavy book sat there, a dense brick of information. It wasn't a dirty magazine. It wasn't a secret whispered in a locker room. It was a textbook. It had an ISBN number. It had an index. For the first time since the shower incident, the knot of shame in Freddie’s stomach loosened just a fraction more. It was just a subject. And he was a good student. "We have the manual," Freddie whispered, clutching the bag against his chest. "Now," Jessica said, turning toward the exit. "Let's go get your PolyPasses. I want to see you swipe onto a bus before we go home." The ID Office was tucked into a corner of the Student Union, smelling of warm plastic and lamination chemicals. Since it was summer orientation season, the line was short—mostly transfer students and a few confused freshmen who had lost their cards during the first week of Session 1. "Next," the camera operator called out. She sat behind a beige counter, looking bored, her finger hovering over a capture button. Jessica went first. She stood on the tape mark on the floor. Flash. "Done," the operator said. "Next." Paige stepped up. She smoothed her hair, offered a polite, closed-mouth smile. Flash. "Next." Freddie stepped onto the tape. He looked at the camera lens. It looked like a mechanical eye. He didn't smile; that felt performative. He just looked at the lens, ensuring his eyes were open and his head was level. Flash. The sudden burst of light left a purple afterimage in his vision, but he didn't flinch. He held his ground. They moved to the waiting area. Behind the counter, a specialized printer began to whir. Zzzzt-clack. Zzzzt-clack. It was a rhythmic, industrial sound—the sound of identity being manufactured. Five minutes later, the operator handed three warm plastic cards across the counter. "Don't punch a hole in them," she recited the standard warning. "It breaks the antenna coil. If you lose it, it is ten dollars to replace." Freddie took his card. It was still warm from the printer. It was sleek. The background was a deep Maroon with Orange accents. CPI POLYPASS. His name was printed in raised, black thermal lettering: FREDDIE AVERY. His photo was to the right—he looked serious, alert, and present. He ran his thumb over the raised letters of his name. It was tactile proof of his existence in the system. He flipped it over. A thick black magnetic stripe ran across the top. A barcode sat at the bottom. "Access granted," he whispered. He looked at Jessica. "This works on the bus?" "Swipe and ride," Jessica confirmed, sliding her own card into her wallet. "Starting right now. It is your key to the city. It opens the library, it gets you into the gym—if you ever wanted to go there—and it pays the fare." Freddie slid the card into the front pocket of his jeans. He patted it. It wasn't just plastic. It was mobility. "Phase Two," Jessica announced as they walked out of Newman Hall into the bright sunshine. She pointed across the massive, grassy expanse of the Drillfield toward the imposing stone fortress on the hill: Burruss Hall. "We have the IDs. Now we have to pay the toll." "Tuition?" Paige asked. "Tuition," Jessica confirmed. "Summer classes aren't covered by standard financial aid packages. The Pell Grant doesn't run in July. This is a cash-on-the-barrelhead transaction." She patted her purse. "Luckily, the Avery Grant is liquid." They walked across the grass. Freddie watched the heavy limestone buildings loom closer. "Burruss Hall," Freddie noted. "Administrative Command." "Exactly," Jessica said. "The Office of the Bursar is on the first floor. They want their money before you sit in the chair." The final stop was a quieter building near the edge of the Drillfield. They entered the office marked SERVICES FOR STUDENTS WITH DISABILITIES (SSD). It was carpeted, quiet, and smelled of lavender—a deliberate choice, Freddie suspected, to lower anxiety. A receptionist looked up from a desk. "Welcome to SSD. How can I help you?" "Intake," Jessica said, placing the thick manila envelope on the desk. "This is Freddie Avery. Incoming Freshman, starting Session 2. We have his documentation for Cerebral Palsy and ADHD." The receptionist took the folder. She opened it, scanning the medical records from the Virginia Beach school system. "Everything looks standard here," she said. "We can set up your accommodations letter for the summer session today. Extended time on tests, note-taking assistance... the usual suite." She turned to her computer. "We need to schedule an intake interview to finalize the plan. Is Monday at 10:00 AM acceptable?" Freddie nodded. "Monday is acceptable." Then, he hesitated. He looked at Jessica, then at Paige. They both nodded slightly. Go ahead. Freddie turned back to the receptionist. He cleared his throat. "There is... another variable," Freddie said. The receptionist stopped typing. She looked at him with patient, open eyes. "Yes?" "My sisters and I... we suspect I am Autistic," Freddie said. The word felt heavy in the quiet room, but saying it out loud didn't cause the walls to collapse. "I do not have a diagnosis on file. The data is... empirical observation. I would like a recommendation for a provider who can perform an evaluation." The receptionist smiled warmly. She opened a drawer and pulled out a separate pamphlet. "We work closely with the Psychological Services Center right here on campus, and there is a specialist in Blacksburg, Dr. Aris Thorne, who handles adult diagnoses. He is excellent." She wrote a name and number on a sticky note and attached it to the pamphlet. "Call him. Tell him SSD sent you. It can take a few weeks to get an appointment, but having the referral helps." "Thank you," Freddie said, taking the paper. It felt like a treasure map. He looked at the sticky note, then at his sisters standing behind him. A critical logical gap occurred to him. He was eighteen. Legally, he was a sealed database. But his operating system required external administrators. "One query," Freddie said, looking back at the receptionist. "I am eighteen. My records are encrypted by privacy laws, correct?" "That is correct," the receptionist confirmed. "FERPA laws protect your educational and medical records. We cannot discuss them with anyone but you." "That is a flaw in the architecture," Freddie stated. "I require my support team to have full visibility. If I am non-verbal, or if I am in a crash state, they need to be able to speak for me. They need to be able to schedule appointments and view my grades." He pointed to Jessica and Paige. "They are the Admins. They need root access." The receptionist nodded, understanding immediately. She reached into a file sorter and pulled out a single sheet of paper. "You're looking for the FERPA Waiver and Release of Information form," she said, sliding it across the desk. "This authorizes us to communicate with designated individuals." Freddie didn't even read the fine print. He picked up the pen. He signed his name on the line: Freddie Avery. Then he checked the boxes: \X\ Full Access \X\ Financial \X\ Medical/Disability \X\ Academic He wrote the names in the authorized field, pressing hard to ensure the ink was permanent: Jessica Avery Paige Avery Ellen Avery He slid the paper back. "Access granted," Freddie said. "Do not lock them out." The receptionist stamped the form. FILED. "They are in the system, Freddie. You're all set. See you Monday at ten." They walked out of the building. The sun was high and bright. "Okay," Jessica said, putting her sunglasses on. "Now we go home." Paige spun the keys on her finger. "I'm driving." Freddie touched the pamphlet in his pocket. Dr. Aris Thorne. He had a name. He had a plan. And now, his Admins had the keys. "Let's go," Freddie said. "The King bed is waiting."

title: Part 3: The Medical Logistics
content: Paige navigated the Avalon smoothly down West Campus Drive, shifting from 2nd to 3rd gear with a satisfying thunk. "Clutch control is improving," Freddie noted from the passenger seat. "Thanks, Navigator." "Briefing on medical," Jessica said from the back seat. "Since we are not going back to the Beach, we need local providers. I am transferring our files." "Primary Care?" Paige asked. "There is a practice in Christiansburg near the hospital. But for the... specialized stuff," Jessica hesitated slightly, then pushed through. "I see a gynecologist in Riner. Dr. Halloway. She is quiet, she is efficient, and her office is in the middle of nowhere, so it is private." "Riner?" Freddie asked. "Route 8?" "Yes. And there is a bus," Jessica added, knowing his brain needed the transit connection. "Route 8 runs once an hour. It drops off right in front of her clinic." "Why do we need a special doctor?" Paige asked, glancing in the rearview mirror. "Because we are living in close quarters," Jessica said frankly. "And because periods are a variable we need to control. Dr. Halloway put me on the shot—the Cycle-Stop. One injection every three months. No pills to remember. No... mess." Paige thought about the King bed. She thought about the white sheets. She thought about the cramping that usually laid her out for two days a month. "No mess?" Paige asked. "It stops the cycle completely for most people," Jessica said. "It stabilizes the hormones. Less mood swings. Less pain." Paige shifted into 4th gear. "Sign me up. If I am going to be sleeping next to Freddie every night, I do not want to worry about... leaks. Or being crazy." "I will make the appointments," Jessica said. "We will take the bus down to Riner next week." Freddie looked out the window as they turned onto Pepper Street. The bus to Riner. The textbook on human sexuality. The shot. It was all maintenance. It was all keeping the machine running smoothly so they could just... live. "Systems normalizing," Freddie whispered. He touched the PolyPass in his pocket. The summer was just beginning, and they were already ahead of schedule.

title: Part 4: The Schematic
content: The silver Avalon crunched into the gravel driveway of 105 Pepper Street. The house was quiet, the air conditioner humming its steady, protective rhythm. They unloaded the cargo. Jessica carried the bag from the Bursar’s office (receipts and paperwork). Paige carried the PolyPasses. Freddie carried the books. He walked straight to the living room and sat on the beige carpet, using the coffee table as a desk. He pulled the heavy, glossy textbook out of the bag. Title: Human Sexuality: Biological and Psychosocial Perspectives. Weight: 4.2 lbs. Status: The Manual. He cracked the spine. The smell of new paper and binding glue wafted up—a sensory input he usually loved. He skipped the Preface. He skipped the Introduction. He went straight to Chapter 3: Anatomy and Physiology. Jessica and Paige sat on the sofa behind him, kicking off their shoes. "How is the data?" Jessica asked, opening a can of soda. "The diagrams are... two-dimensional," Freddie noted, tracing a line drawing of the female reproductive system with his finger. He frowned. The diagram was a cross-section. It was color-coded (pink for muscle, blue for veins, yellow for nerves), but it looked like a map of a subway system, not a biological entity. He looked up at the TV, which was off. He looked at the VCR. When he learned to wire the entertainment center, he didn't just look at the diagram in the manual. He looked at the ports on the back of the device. He traced the cables. He verified the input/output physically. Theory is useless without verification. He turned around to face his sisters. He held the book up, pointing to the diagram. "This schematic," Freddie stated, tapping the page. "It represents the internal and external architecture. But it is an abstraction. It is a drawing." "It is," Paige agreed. "It is a model." "I have difficulty translating 2D models into 3D reality without a reference point," Freddie admitted. "The 'Robert Virus' says looking is wrong. But the 'Science Class' protocol says verification is necessary." He looked at Jessica. "If we are to demystify the hardware... if I am to understand the mechanics so I do not freeze up or react with error..." Jessica set her soda down. She understood the request immediately. It wasn't about gratification. It was about calibration. He was an engineer trying to understand the engine. "You want to compare the schematic to the actual unit," Jessica stated flatly. "Affirmative," Freddie whispered. "Visual confirmation only. To map the vocabulary to the reality." Jessica looked at Paige. Paige nodded. She didn't look scared. She looked like she was ready to help him study for a test. "It is just biology, Freddie," Paige said. "We promised. No secrets. No shame." "Okay," Jessica said, standing up. She walked over to the windows and adjusted the blinds, ensuring they were fully closed. The room dimmed. "Class is in session," Jessica announced. "Bring the book." \NARRATIVE GAP: CLINICAL OBSERVATION & INSTRUCTION\ Time Elapsed: 45 Minutes

title: Part 5: Data Verified
content: The living room was bright again; Jessica had opened the blinds to let the afternoon sun wash over the carpet. The atmosphere in the room was calm. There was no tension. The air didn't feel heavy with secrets; it felt light, scrubbed clean of the mystery that usually plagued teenagers. Freddie sat on the sofa, the textbook open on his lap. He wasn't staring at the diagrams with confusion anymore. He was looking at them with recognition. The abstract lines of the cross-section now made sense. He could visualize how the 2D drawing translated into 3D space. Structure. Function. Design. Jessica was in the kitchen, making sandwiches. Paige was sitting next to Freddie on the sofa, reading her own copy of the textbook, highlighting a section on hormones. "The variance is significant," Freddie murmured, running his finger down a paragraph about biological diversity. "The book says 'average' dimensions, but the variance is standard." "Exactly," Paige said, not looking up from her highlighting. "Like how every car engine is basically the same design, but the layout varies by model year." "Correct," Freddie said. He closed the book. Thump. The sound was final. He leaned back into the cushions. The "Robert Virus"—the voice in his head that shouted Pervert! Wrong! Dirty!—was silent. It had been deleted. He had seen the reality. It wasn't a monster. It wasn't a glowing radioactive core of sin. It was just tissue. It was just plumbing. It was just his sisters. "Status?" Jessica called out from the kitchen, bringing a plate of sandwiches. Freddie looked at her. He didn't blush. He didn't look away. He looked her in the eye. "The mystery is resolved," Freddie stated calmly. "The hardware matches the documentation. I understand the mechanics." Jessica smiled, setting the plate down on the coffee table. "Good. That means when we get to class on July 7th, you won't be giggling in the back row like a freshman." "I do not giggle," Freddie said, picking up a sandwich. "I process." He took a bite. It tasted like ham and cheese. The world was simple again. He checked his mental inventory. Bus Routes: Memorized. Tuition: Paid. Anatomy: Verified. Bed: King Size. "We are operational," Freddie decided. "The system is stable." Paige leaned her head on his shoulder. "Systems go, Navigator."

title: Part 6: The Clear Curtain
content: The sun had finally dipped below the ridge, leaving the sky a bruised purple over the Iron City. Inside 105 Pepper Street, the lights were low, casting long shadows across the hallway. Jessica walked into the bathroom holding a plastic package she had picked up during their supply run to Valu-Mart. "Upgrade time," she announced. Freddie stood in the doorway, watching. He was wearing his orange hoodie over his boxers—his transition armor. He watched Jessica grip the old, opaque white shower curtain. Zip. Zip. Zip. The metal rings slid off the rod with a rhythmic clatter. The white curtain pooled on the floor like a deflated parachute. To Freddie, it looked like a wall coming down. Jessica tore open the new package. The smell of fresh vinyl filled the small room—a sharp, chemical scent that Freddie associated with "New" and "Clean." She unfolded it. It was heavy-duty, commercial-grade plastic. And it was completely transparent. She hung it up, hook by hook. "Visual confirmation," Jessica said, sliding it closed. The curtain rippled, but it didn't block anything. She stood inside the tub. Freddie could see her perfectly through the plastic—her silhouette, her face, the maroon CPI t-shirt she was wearing. "Water stays in," she said, tapping the liner with her fingernail. Tick-tick. "Data flows out." Freddie nodded slowly. His brain processed the variable. Old Curtain: Isolation. Unknown variables. Fear of abandonment. New Curtain: Containment. Visibility. Constant stream of data. "Logical compromise," Freddie whispered. "It maintains the moisture barrier but prevents visual disconnect." "Exactly," Paige said, appearing behind him holding her toothbrush. She looked through the clear plastic at Jessica. "No more open curtains. No more wet floors. But you never have to wonder if we left. We are right here." "Testing phase," Jessica said, stepping out of the tub. "You're up, Freddie. Let's verify the protocol." Freddie stepped into the bathroom. The "Robert Virus" attempted to run its startup script—You are eighteen. You cannot need help. This is wrong. But the script failed. He had read the manual. He had seen the diagrams. The body was just a machine. Washing it was just maintenance. He stripped off the orange hoodie and his boxers. He didn't rush. He placed them in the hamper. He stepped into the tub. He sat on the porcelain edge, just like yesterday. But today, he wasn't crashing. He was calibrating. He turned the water on. Warm spray hit his back. He looked through the clear liner. He could see the sink. He could see the mirror. He could see Paige standing right there, leaning against the counter, squeezing toothpaste onto her brush. She wasn't leaving. She was maintaining the perimeter. "Do you need assistance?" Paige asked, catching his eye through the plastic. Freddie paused. He could wash himself. His motor control was functional today. But the "Science Class" protocol wasn't just about utility; it was about desensitization. It was about proving, physically, that the shame was gone. "Affirmative," Freddie whispered. "Scrub assist." Paige set her toothbrush down. She didn't hesitate. She pulled the clear curtain back just enough to reach in. She picked up the washcloth and the bar of soap. She lathered it up until it was thick with white foam. "Arms up," Paige said gently. Freddie lifted his arms. Paige washed him. She started at his shoulders, working the warm, soapy cloth down his back in firm, circular motions. Scrub. Scrub. Scrub. It was rhythmic. It was tactile. It was the same deep pressure she applied when she hugged him, but transferred through the medium of the sponge. "Pressure okay?" Paige asked. "Optimal," Freddie said, closing his eyes. He felt the tension draining out of his trapezius muscles. He wasn't being "bathed like a baby." He was being cared for. She moved to his chest, scrubbing away the sweat of the day, the invisible residue of the bookstore anxiety, and the last clinging atoms of the "Robert Virus." She rinsed him off with the handheld sprayer. The warm water cascaded down his skin. "All clear," Paige announced, turning off the tap. She handed him the towel. "Dry off. Meet us in the Silo." Freddie stood up. He dried himself behind the clear curtain, watching Paige finish brushing her teeth. He wrapped the towel around his waist. He looked in the mirror. He looked clean. He looked stable. "Test successful," Freddie whispered to his reflection.

title: Part 7: The Silo
content: The door to the Master Bedroom clicked shut. The blackout curtains were drawn, sealing the room into a protective, cool twilight. The King Bed dominated the space. It was a massive, 76-inch plain of maroon jersey sheets—a landscape of safety. "Armor off," Jessica said, dropping her towel by the hamper. She climbed into the bed on the left side, pulling the sheet up to her waist. Paige followed suit, claiming the right side. Freddie stood by the edge of the bed. Yesterday, this moment had been terrifying. Yesterday, he had woken up screaming because he thought he had broken a rule. Today, he knew there were no rules. There was only the System they built. He dropped his towel. He didn't scramble to cover himself. He walked calmly to the side of the bed. He climbed into the center. He lay on his back. The mattress absorbed his weight. "Formation," Freddie whispered. Jessica rolled onto her side, pressing against his left arm. Paige rolled in from the right, resting her head on his shoulder, draping her arm over his chest to lock him in. They collapsed the empty space. They became a single thermal unit. Freddie closed his eyes. He ran a system diagnostic. Heart Rate: Nominal. Anxiety: Zero. Shame: Not Detected. He felt Paige’s breathing. He felt the weight of Jessica’s arm. It wasn't sexual. It wasn't weird. It was Gravity. It was the force that held him to the earth. "Textbooks on the nightstand?" Freddie asked into the dark. "Right there," Paige whispered. "Ready for class." "Good," Freddie said. He let out a long, slow breath. The static in his head—the white noise of fear that had been running in the background for eighteen years—finally went silent. He was safe. He was funded. He was understood. "Goodnight, Admins," Freddie whispered. "Goodnight, Navigator," they replied in unison.

title: Part 1: The Primary Node
content: The silver Horizon Avalon idled in the driveway of 105 Pepper Street. The morning was already hot, the air shimmering above the asphalt of Pepper Plaza across the street. Paige sat in the driver’s seat. She adjusted the rearview mirror, checking the sightlines. "Clutch in," she whispered. She shifted into Reverse. The gear stick clicked into place with mechanical precision. "We are mobile," Freddie confirmed from the passenger seat. He had his clipboard ready—a literal clipboard he had found in the Ops Room supplies. It held their insurance cards, the FERPA copies, and a list of objectives. "Destination: Montgomery General Internal Medicine," Jessica announced from the back seat. "Dr. Vance. He’s the primary node. He handles my physicals, and he’s the gateway to the specialists." Paige eased the car out of the driveway. Her clutch control was becoming muscle memory now; the car didn't even shudder. They turned onto the main road, heading toward the hospital district on the south side of Christiansburg. The waiting room smelled of antiseptic and old magazines. It was quiet, save for the low murmur of the receptionists behind the sliding glass window. They approached the desk as a unit. "Checking in," Jessica said. "Three appointments. Avery, Avery, and Avery." The receptionist blinked, looking at the three siblings who stood shoulder-to-shoulder. "New patients?" "I'm established," Jessica said. "They are new. Transfers from Virginia Beach." The receptionist handed over three heavy clipboards stacked with forms. "Update yours, and fill out the new patient packets for them. Insurance cards?" Freddie handed over the cards from his clipboard. He watched her scan them. Beep. "Okay," she said. "Have a seat. Bring the forms up when you're done." They sat in a row of chairs. Freddie looked at the stack of paper. Medical History. Family History. Surgical History. He uncapped his pen. He liked forms. Forms were binary. Yes/No. Check Box. Then he reached the last page: HIPAA Authorization & Release of Information. I hereby authorize this practice to release my protected health information to... "Hold," Freddie said. Jessica and Paige looked up from their own clipboards. "We need a policy decision," Freddie stated. "Standard protocol is privacy. My records are sealed." He looked at Jessica. "But you are the Admin. You need to know if the hardware fails." He looked at Paige. "You are the Anchor. You need to know if the chemicals are imbalanced." "And you need to know about us," Jessica countered. "If Paige has a reaction to the shot, or if I get sick during finals, you need to be able to talk to the doctor." "Redundancy," Freddie nodded. "Total transparency." He wrote in the blank lines on his form: 1. Jessica Avery (Sister) 2. Paige Avery (Sister) 3. Ellen Avery (Mother) He checked the box for \X\ ALL RECORDS. Paige watched him, then copied the list onto her form. Jessica did the same on her update form. "This is the Tri-Lateral Agreement," Freddie whispered, signing his name at the bottom. "If one unit goes down, the others have the schematic." Dr. Vance was a tall man with wire-rimmed glasses and a demeanor that was efficient but kind. He didn't blink when all three siblings crowded into the exam room. "Okay," Dr. Vance said, looking at the charts. "We’re doing intake for Freddie and Paige today?" "Affirmative," Freddie said from the exam table. He was sitting on the crinkly paper, legs dangling. "I require a maintenance check and referrals." "Let's start with the history," Dr. Vance said. "I see Cerebral Palsy and ADHD on the transfer file." "Spastic Diplegia," Freddie corrected. "Mild. Mostly affects the lower extremities. I require Baclofen for the spasticity." "And the ADHD?" "Ritalin," Freddie said. "Standard dosage. It maintains focus." Dr. Vance nodded, making notes. Then he looked at Jessica, then back to Freddie. "Anything else?" Freddie took a breath. He looked at Paige. She gave him a small nod. Use the manual. "There is a suspected discrepancy in the operating system," Freddie stated clearly. "Suspected?" Dr. Vance asked. "Autism," Freddie said. "My sisters and I have reviewed the diagnostic criteria. My sensory processing, social deficits, and reliance on routine match the profile. However, I lack a formal diagnosis code." Dr. Vance stopped writing. He looked at Freddie—really looked at him. He saw the lack of eye contact, the slight rocking, the precise, mechanical speech patterns. He looked at Jessica and Paige, who were standing guard like Secret Service agents. "I see," Dr. Vance said softly. "Well, you're in the right place. We can get that looked at." "We have a lead," Jessica interjected. "The Dean of Students recommended Dr. Aris Thorne in Blacksburg. But we need a referral for insurance." "Dr. Thorne is excellent," Dr. Vance agreed. "I'll write the referral today. 'Evaluation for Autism Spectrum Disorder.' That should get you in the door." "Thank you," Freddie said. "Now," Dr. Vance turned to Paige. "And for you?" Paige sat up straighter. "I need a referral too. To Dr. Halloway in Riner." "OB/GYN?" Dr. Vance asked. "Yes," Paige said. "I want to start the Cycle-Stop injection. Jessica is on it. We... we live in close quarters. We want to stabilize the variables." Dr. Vance didn't ask why siblings living together needed birth control. He was a doctor; he cared about health, not living arrangements. "Dr. Halloway is great," he said. "I'll put that referral in as well. Anything else?" "Just maintenance," Jessica said. "We want to make sure everyone is running at 100% before the semester starts." Dr. Vance finished his notes. "You guys have a good system here," he observed, tearing off the prescription slips for the referrals. He handed them to Freddie. "You're the keeper of the papers?" "I am the Archivist," Freddie said, taking them. They walked back to the Avalon. The sun was high overhead. Freddie held the referrals in his hand. Referral: Dr. Aris Thorne (Psychiatry/Neurology). Referral: Dr. Halloway (Gynecology). He looked at the papers. They weren't just slips of paper. They were patch notes. They were upgrades waiting to be installed. "We have the keys," Freddie said. "We have the keys," Paige agreed, unlocking the car. "Now let's go get some lunch. I'm starving." "Route 8 next?" Jessica asked. "Negative," Freddie said, checking the schedule in his head. "Today is Wednesday. We need to call Dr. Halloway first. But the bus run... that is a tactical necessity. We need to verify the route." "Next week," Jessica promised. "Next week, we ride to Riner."

title: Part 2: The Red Flag
content: The Silo was silent. The air conditioner hummed its steady, protective white noise. On the King Bed, the formation was holding. Freddie lay in the center, flanked by Jessica on his left and Paige on his right. The room was cool, the blackout curtains sealing them in a timeless dark. Paige shifted. It wasn't a normal sleep movement. It was a sharp, sudden jolt. She sat up, gasping softly. Her hand went to her thigh. "Oh," she whispered. "Oh no." Freddie woke up instantly. The sudden movement next to him triggered his proximity sensors. "Paige?" he mumbled, his voice thick with sleep. "Status?" Paige was already scrambling out of bed. She moved fast, her feet hitting the floor with urgency. In the faint light filtering from the streetlamp outside, Freddie saw her check her leg. There was a dark smear on her upper thigh. Blood. The "Robert Virus" surged. Injury. Attack. Danger. Panic spiked in his chest. His breathing hitched. "Paige!" he gasped, sitting up. "You are bleeding!" "I'm fine!" Paige hissed, rushing toward the door. "Just... bathroom. Go back to sleep." She disappeared into the hallway, closing the bathroom door with a click. Freddie couldn't go back to sleep. The image of the blood on her skin was burned into his retinas. He turned to the left. He shook Jessica’s shoulder. "Jessica. Wake up. Emergency." Jessica groaned, rolling over. "What? What time is it?" "Paige is bleeding," Freddie said, his voice rising in pitch, the vibration of panic starting in his hands. "She stood up and there was blood. She ran to the bathroom. Is she injured?" Jessica was awake in an instant. She sat up, scanning the bed. She checked the sheet where Paige had been sleeping. It was clean. No transfer. "Okay," Jessica said, her voice dropping to a calm, command-level register. She put a hand on Freddie’s chest to steady him. "Freddie, listen. She isn't injured. She didn't cut herself." "I saw the blood," Freddie insisted, pointing at his own leg to indicate the location. "Femoral artery location. High volume risk." "No," Jessica said firmly. "It’s her cycle, Freddie. Her period." Freddie froze. "Period?" "Menstruation," Jessica clarified. "Remember the textbook? Chapter 4? The shedding of the uterine lining?" Freddie blinked. The data from yesterday’s reading session loaded into his RAM. Uterus. Endometrium. Monthly cycle. Bloody discharge. The panic wavered. It wasn't trauma. It was a function. "But... it is messy," Freddie whispered. "It looks like injury." "It does," Jessica agreed. "But it is just biology. She woke up because she felt it start. She’s in the bathroom taking care of it before it stains the sheets. That was a close call." The bathroom door opened. Paige walked back in. She wasn't nude anymore. She was wearing a pair of black cotton panties. She walked to the bed, looking tired but relieved. "Clear?" Jessica asked. "Clear," Paige confirmed, climbing back in. "Caught it just in time. No breach on the bedding." She settled back into her spot on Freddie’s right. Freddie looked at her. He looked at the black panties. "Status?" Freddie asked, his voice still trembling slightly. Paige offered a tired, reassuring smile. "Status is Red, Freddie. Literally. It’s just that time of the month." She saw the fear still lingering in his eyes. She took his hand and placed it on her stomach, right over her belly button. "I am not hurt," she promised. "My body is just doing a system reset. It’s annoying, and tomorrow it’s going to hurt, but I’m okay." Freddie felt the warmth of her skin. He felt the steady rise and fall of her breathing. Not trauma. Maintenance. "Pain levels?" he asked. "Zero right now," Paige said. "But Day Two is usually the bad one. I might need the Cycle-Ease and the heating pad tomorrow." "And pressure," Jessica added from the other side. "Don't forget the squeeze." "I can provide pressure," Freddie stated immediately. The mission parameters had changed from 'Rescue' to 'Support.' He could do Support. "I know," Paige whispered. "That’s why you're the best." She pulled the sheet up. "Panties are mandatory for the next five days," she noted. "Containment protocol." "Understood," Freddie said. "Hygiene standard." He lay back down between them. Jessica draped her arm over him again. Paige snuggled close, her head back on his shoulder. The black cotton barrier was there, but the warmth was the same. The fear evaporated. It wasn't a crisis. It was just life. And now that he knew what it was—now that he had seen the reality of it without the shame—he didn't have to be scared. "This is why we need the doctor in Riner," Paige mumbled into his shoulder, her eyes already closing. "Get on the shot. Stop the bleeding." "Efficiency," Freddie whispered. "Upgrade the system." "Sleep," Jessica commanded gently. "Sleep," Freddie agreed. He closed his eyes. The King Bed held them all—the biology, the anxiety, and the safety of the truth. Here is Part 3 of the narrative, detailing the trip to Riner and the medical appointments.

title: Part 3: The Maintenance Run
content: The morning at 105 Pepper Street started earlier than the alarm clock intended. Around 3:00 AM, Paige had woken up with the familiar, dull ache of cramps, signaling the start of her cycle—and the "Red Flag" status Freddie had learned to recognize. While the timing meant a groggy start to the day, it was actually serendipitous for the logistics of the morning. They had 9:00 AM appointments at the clinic in Riner. Blue Ridge Transit’s Route 8 was the only link between the two towns, a lifeline designed primarily to shuttle seniors from the rural hills into Christiansburg. It ran on a strict hourly pulse, leaving Pepper Plaza at 45 minutes past the hour. "Strategy," Jessica announced, checking her watch in the kitchen. "The 8:45 AM bus gets us there at 9:05 AM. That is too tight for intake paperwork. We take the 7:45 AM departure." They left the Base at 7:35 AM. It was a short walk—diagonally across the street to the Pepper Plaza Transit Center. The morning air was humid, but the view of the mountains was clear. The bus pulled into the sawtooth bay right on time. It was smaller than the massive articulated buses used for the university runs, better suited for the winding state roads. The amber destination sign glowed against the morning sun: 8 RINER They boarded, swiping their newly minted PolyPasses. The bus was mostly empty, save for a few locals heading out to the farms. The ride was deceptively short but scenic. As soon as the bus left the commercial density of Christiansburg, the landscape opened up. They rolled down SR-8, passing rolling farmland, misty cow pastures, and scattered farmhouses. For twenty minutes, Freddie watched the telephone poles whip by, counting the intervals. It was a quiet, rhythmic transition from the "Iron City" to the country. "Next stop," the driver announced. "Riner Road and Union Valley." The bus slowed, pulling over to the side of the highway at the intersection of SR-8 and SR-669. They stepped off onto the gravel shoulder. "Landmarks," Jessica pointed out. Directly in front of them, at 4021 Riner Rd, stood a boxy, metal-sided building with a yellow sign: Riner Value Mart. It was the only retail anchor in sight. "Target is across the street," Jessica said, pointing to the other side of the highway. "1917 Union Valley Road." The geography here was tricky. The medical building was built directly into the steep hillside. From the bus stop at the top of the hill, they were looking at the roof and the second floor of the brick structure. "We have to go down," Paige noted, clutching her stomach slightly as a cramp hit. They waited for a break in the traffic on SR-8—mostly pickup trucks and landscaping trailers—and crossed the highway. They navigated the sidewalk that sloped steeply downward, descending the hill to the main parking lot level. The entrance to Dr. Halloway’s office was on the first floor. Inside, the waiting room was quiet, smelling of sanitizer and potpourri. It was a small practice, far removed from the hustle of the hospital district. "Freddie," Jessica said, pointing to a comfortable chair in the corner. "This is your post. You hold the perimeter." "Acknowledged," Freddie said, sitting down. He pulled a book from his bag, happy to be the silent sentry while his sisters handled the biological maintenance. Jessica and Paige went to the check-in window. Jessica was a regular; she simply signed her name. Paige, however, had the new patient clipboard to navigate. They were called back quickly. For Jessica, the appointment was routine clockwork. She knew the drill: a quick vitals check, a brief chat with Dr. Halloway, and the administration of the Cycle-Stop injection. It was a quick pinch, and she was protected for another three months. For Paige, the consultation took longer. Dr. Halloway, a woman with a kind face and efficiency that matched Jessica’s, reviewed Paige’s file. "So, we're looking to start the Cycle-Stop today?" Dr. Halloway asked. "Yes," Paige said. "My sister is on it. We live together. We want to... synchronize the systems." "That makes sense," Dr. Halloway nodded. "Now, usually we have to wait to administer the first shot to ensure you aren't pregnant. We prefer to give it during the first five days of your menstrual cycle." Paige blinked. "I started at 3:00 AM today." "Perfect timing," Dr. Halloway smiled, grabbing a pair of gloves. "Since you are on Day 1, we can do this right now. You’ll be effective immediately, though we always say give it a week to be safe. This should help with the cramping you mentioned, too. Eventually, it might stop the bleeding altogether." "That is the goal," Paige said, exhaling in relief. Ten minutes later, Paige walked out of the exam room, rubbing her arm. She felt lighter. The anxiety about "leaks" and "mess" in the King Bed was gone. She had the patch. They collected Freddie from the lobby at 9:45 AM. "Mission complete?" Freddie asked, standing up. "Systems updated," Jessica confirmed. "Let's catch the ride home." They walked back out into the humidity, trudging back up the steep hill to SR-8. They crossed the street to the return stop, located near 4010 Riner Rd, just down from the intersection. They checked the schedule posted on the sign. The bus departed from Auburn High School nearby at 10:15 AM. A few minutes later, the white bus appeared over the crest of the hill. The destination sign had flipped for the return leg: 8 CHRISTIANSBURG They boarded, taking their seats in the cool air conditioning. As the bus wound its way back through the farmland toward Pepper Plaza, Freddie watched his sisters. They were relaxed. The medical logistics were handled. The "Base" was fully operational. "Next stop," Freddie whispered to himself as the bus rolled on. "Home."\`

title: Part 1: Ground Rules
content: The fluorescent lights of the classroom hummed, a stark contrast to the humid warmth of a Blacksburg summer afternoon outside. This was HPE 204: Dimensions of Human Sexuality. For Freddie, this class was a strategic maneuver. The university’s Health and Physical Education requirement was mandatory for graduation, usually filled by sweating through tennis, jogging, or swimming. With his cerebral palsy, those options ranged from "difficult" to "logistical nightmare." But HPE 204 counted for the same credit, and the only muscle he had to exercise here was his brain. He sat in the second row, the sweet spot for serious students who didn’t want to appear eager. Flanking him were Paige and Jessica, the three of them claiming a block of desks like a defensive line. "I give it ten minutes before the frat boys in the back row crack," Jessica whispered, leaning in from Freddie's left. She had her notebook open but her pen was capped, her eyes scanning the room with amused cynicism. "Five," Paige countered from his right. She had already written the date and the course title at the top of her page in neat, architectural block letters. "Look at them. They’re already vibrating." She wasn’t wrong. The room was set for thirty, and while half the class looked like Freddie—students checking a box for a degree requirement—the other half were the types who had seen the word "Sexuality" in the course catalog and assumed this would be an easy A or a comedy hour. The door shut with a heavy click, and Dr. Aris Thorne walked to the podium. She was a woman who radiated a clinical, no-nonsense authority. She didn’t smile. She didn’t try to be cool. She set a stack of syllabi on the desk and looked over her glasses at the room. "Welcome to Dimensions of Human Sexuality," Dr. Thorne said. Her voice was calm but projected to the back corners of the room without a microphone. "Let us establish the ground rules immediately." The shuffling of backpacks ceased. "In this room, there are no secrets," she began, pacing slowly in front of the whiteboard. "We are studying human biology, psychology, and sociology. We will treat these subjects with the scientific dignity they deserve. If you are here to giggle, drop the class now. There is a waiting list of students who actually need this credit." Freddie adjusted his posture, grateful for the sturdy desk chair. He saw Paige nod in approval. "I will use proper terminology," Dr. Thorne continued. "You will hear words like 'penis,' 'vulva,' 'intercourse,' and 'masturbation' frequently. However..." She paused, picking up a dry-erase marker. "You are entering a world where you may be educators, healthcare providers, or counselors. The people you interact with will not always use textbooks terms." She turned and wrote a single word on the board: Terminology. "We will learn the clinical definitions," she said, facing them again. "But we will also introduce and discuss the slang. The street terms. The words you hear in movies and locker rooms. Not because I want you to use them in your papers, but because when a patient or a student comes to you confused and uses those words, you need to know exactly what they are talking about without flinching." From the back row, a stifled snort broke the silence. It was the distinct sound of someone trying to hold back a laugh and failing. Dr. Thorne didn't even look up from her notes. "I assume that was a involuntary reflex," she said dryly. "Get it out of your system now. By Chapter 3, the novelty will have worn off." Jessica leaned toward Freddie, her voice barely a breath. "She's good." "She has to be," Freddie whispered back. "This is a safe space," Dr. Thorne said, her eyes locking on the back row. "Questions are encouraged. Ignorance is expected—that is why you are here. But disrespect will result in an immediate ejection. We are discussing the mechanics of human life. You will respect the subject, and you will respect each other." She tapped the stack of papers on her desk. "Syllabuses are coming around. We start with anatomy on Wednesday. I suggest you do the reading. If you are uncomfortable discussing the human body, the registrar closes at 5:00 PM." Freddie took a syllabus as the pile passed him, handing the rest to Paige. He glanced at the course schedule. It was dense, clinical, and thorough. It was exactly what he needed to get his degree without worrying about his legs giving out on a track. He uncapped his pen. He was ready to work.

title: Part 2: Zero Tolerance
content: Dr. Thorne moved through the syllabus with the efficiency of a surgeon. She didn’t pace; she planted herself behind the podium and let the weight of the topics settle over the room. "Week four covers reproductive anatomy," she said, tapping the document. "Week five, the physiology of sexual response. Week six, we begin our unit on contraception and STI prevention. Do not assume you know this material because you took a health class in ninth grade. The statistics suggest otherwise." She flipped a page. "Regarding visual aids: We will be viewing diagrams and clinical photography. These are medical images. They are not pornography. If you cannot distinguish between the two, you will struggle to pass the midterm." The room was silent, save for the scratching of pens. Freddie appreciated the bluntness. There was no ambiguity here. Then, Dr. Thorne reached the section on sexual dysfunction. "We will discuss common issues ranging from erectile dysfunction to vaginismus..." A sharp, high-pitched giggle erupted from the third row. It wasn’t a cough disguised as a laugh. It was a full-blown, open-mouthed cackle. A girl with blonde highlights and a popped collar—who had spent the last ten minutes whispering to her neighbor—had apparently found the medical terminology hilarious. She was exactly the type Freddie had clocked earlier: someone who signed up hoping for an "easy A" and perhaps some titillating live demonstrations, treating a university course like a bachelorette party. The silence that followed was absolute. Dr. Thorne stopped mid-sentence. She didn’t sigh. She didn’t scold. She simply pointed a manicured finger at the door. "Out," she said. Her voice was level, devoid of anger but terrifyingly final. The girl blinked, her smile faltering. "What? I was just—" "You were disrupting my lecture and disrespecting the material," Dr. Thorne said. "Pack your bag. You are dropped from the course effective immediately. I will email the registrar before this class ends." "But—" "Now." The girl’s face flushed a deep crimson. The reality of losing three credits in the first twenty minutes of the semester seemed to crash down on her. She shoved her notebook into her bag, the sound of the zipper loud in the quiet room. She stood up, smoothing her skirt, trying to salvage some scrap of dignity by pretending she didn't care. She walked down the aisle, chin held high, passing the second row. As she came abreast of Freddie, she paused. She had seen him walk in earlier, noting the uneven rhythm of his gait, the way his foot dragged slightly, and how heavily he leaned on the blonde girl next to him for stability. In her mind, she did the quick, cruel calculus of the immature: Disability means desperation. She slowed her pace and locked eyes with him. Her expression shifted from embarrassment to a bizarre, heavy-lidded sultry gaze—an exaggerated, "I want you" look. It was performative and predatory, a smirk that said, I bet you’d take whatever you could get. She winked, then pushed through the double doors, letting them slam behind her. Freddie stared at the closed door, his stomach turning. He wasn't flattered; he was insulted. She had looked at him and seen an easy target, a lonely guy who would be grateful for the attention of a girl who just got kicked out of sex ed. She couldn't have been more wrong. He felt a hand slide firmly onto his forearm, squeezing with a familiar, grounding pressure. It was Paige. She didn't look at the door; she was looking at him, her blue eyes calm and knowing. On his other side, Jessica shifted in her seat, her shoulder pressing solidly against his, creating a physical barrier of support. Freddie let out a breath, the tension in his spastic muscles easing under Paige's touch. He didn't need the validation of a stranger looking for a rebound. He had Paige, his twin and safe person. He had Jessica, his rock. He had five other sisters back home in Virginia Beach who made up his entire world. He had more love and support in his life than that girl would likely ever understand. He glanced at Paige, offering a small, dismissive shrug. She smiled—a tiny, private expression that said, I know. She’s gone. You’re safe. "As I was saying," Dr. Thorne continued, her voice slicing through the lingering awkwardness. "Vaginismus. Now, let’s turn to page four regarding the attendance policy..."

title: Part 3: Safe Harbor
content: The rest of the lecture blurred into a stream of biological terms and syllabus dates. Dr. Thorne didn’t let the tension linger; she buried it under a mountain of academic expectations. By the time she capped her marker and announced, "Class dismissed," the incident with the girl felt like a distant memory to everyone—except the three people in the second row. As the room erupted into the sound of zippers and shuffling feet, Freddie didn't move immediately. This was part of the routine. The adrenaline spike from the confrontation, combined with sitting still for fifty minutes in a rigid desk chair, meant his legs would be seized up. The spasticity always hit harder after stress. "Take your time," Jessica said, her voice low and steady. She stood up first, smoothing the front of her dark green top. She turned to face the aisle, effectively becoming a human shield against the rush of students trying to exit. Her posture was relaxed but firm—the Matriarch holding the line. No one was going to push past her to rush Freddie. On his right, Paige shifted her backpack to her outside shoulder, leaving her left side clear. She stood up and turned toward him, her expression softening into that familiar, easy smile—the same one she’d worn in family photos since they were kids. "Ready?" she asked. Freddie nodded, gripping the edge of the desk to lever himself up. His right leg dragged, the muscle tight and resisting the command to straighten. He wobbled for a fraction of a second, a moment of vulnerability that usually made him grit his teeth in frustration. But the moment he swayed, Paige was there. She didn't make a big deal out of it. She simply stepped into his space, offering her shoulder as a solid, immovable anchor. Freddie wrapped his arm around her, pulling her close. To an outsider, it might have looked like a simple side-hug between siblings. To Freddie, it was a structural necessity. He leaned his weight onto her, exhaling sharply as the tension in his lower back released. This was their default state. The grey cotton of her shirt against his arm, the scent of her shampoo, the way she instinctively braced her stance to support him—it was deep pressure therapy in motion. "You okay?" Paige murmured, her voice vibrating against his side. "Yeah," Freddie said, the tightness in his chest finally unspooling. "Just stiff." "I got you." Jessica glanced back at them, doing a quick visual check. Seeing Freddie secure against Paige, she nodded—a quick, professional confirmation that the "server" was stable. "Let's get out of here," Jessica said, finally stepping aside to open the path. "I need coffee, and if we hurry, we can beat the rush at the student center." They walked out together, a tight formation against the chaos of the hallway. Freddie moved with his distinct, uneven gait, heavily leaning on Paige with every other step. He wasn't hiding the limp, and he wasn't hiding the affection. If anyone else in the hallway looked at him with pity or mockery, he didn't notice. He was too busy holding onto the sister who made the world stop spinning.

title: Part 4: The Predator
content: The journey from the classroom door to the building lobby was only fifty yards, but to Freddie, it felt like a forced march across a gravity-heavy planet. His arms were draped heavily over his sisters’ shoulders. To his left, Jessica bore his weight, her shoulder pressing into his armpit. She was wearing a maroon CPI t-shirt emblazoned with the school mascot—The Forger—a muscular, bearded blacksmith raising a hammer. The graphic seemed to mock the current situation; while the painted man on her chest was made of iron, Freddie felt like he was made of wet sand. To his right was Paige. She was wearing a plain navy blue t-shirt that was, objectively, a size too small. The fabric pulled tight across her chest and shoulders, outlining her bust in a way that usually made Freddie avert his gaze out of respect. But right now, he wasn't looking at her geometry; he was relying on her structure. She gripped his waist firmly, her hip locking against his thigh with every step to prevent his knee from buckling. Freddie himself wore a simple tan t-shirt that fit perfectly, though it was currently damp with the sweat of exertion. "Almost there," Paige whispered, adjusting her grip on his belt loop. "The bench is at twelve o'clock. Visual confirmation." They rounded the corner into the lobby. The air was cooler here, the sunlight streaming in through the glass walls. "Target acquired," Jessica murmured. "Preparing for docking procedure." But the path to the bench was blocked. Leaning against a pillar, right in the center of the lobby, was the girl. She hadn't left the building. She was waiting. Her arms were crossed over her chest, pushing up her cleavage in a way that seemed calculated. She was popping gum with a rhythmic snap-crack that cut through the lobby noise. When she saw them emerge—Freddie sagging between his sisters, his face pale—her eyes lit up. She didn't see three college students moving as a unit. She didn't see the Forger on Jessica’s shirt or the family resemblance in their faces. She saw a target. She saw a guy who, in her estimation, probably spent his Saturday nights alone and would be grateful for a scrap of attention from someone like her. She pushed off the pillar and stepped directly into their path. "Hey," she purred. Her voice had dropped an octave from the shriek she’d used in class. It was now smoky, suggestive. The Avery unit came to a halt. Freddie blinked, trying to clear the sweat from his eyes. He looked at her, then past her to the bench. "Obstruction," Freddie whispered to Paige. "Path blocked." The girl ignored the women holding him up. To her, they were background noise—staff, aides, maybe volunteers from the disability office. She scanned over Paige’s tight navy shirt with a dismissive sneer, writing her off completely. "Rough class, huh?" the girl said, stepping closer, invading Freddie's personal space. She smelled of cheap vanilla perfume and ambition. "That teacher is such a prude. I bet you were bored out of your mind." Freddie frowned. "The material was... standard," he rasped. "She enforced the syllabus." The girl laughed, tossing her hair. "You're funny. I like that." She looked him up and down, her gaze lingering on his denim-clad legs, then moving up to his eyes with a predatory smirk. "You look like you’ve had a hard day," she said, lowering her voice to a conspiratorial whisper. "You look tense. Maybe you need someone to help you... relax?" She reached out, her hand aiming for the tan fabric of his chest. "I was thinking, since I got kicked out, maybe I need a private tutor? Someone to show me the... practical application?" Jessica stiffened. Her grip on Freddie’s waist tightened. The Forger on her shirt seemed to glare. Freddie stared at the girl. His brain attempted to parse the data. Input: Girl from class. Status: Expelled. Action: Blocking the bench. Dialogue: Illogical. Suggestive. "I am not a tutor," Freddie said flatly. "I am a student. And I require a seat. My legs are failing." The girl pouted, a theatrical expression. "Aww, poor baby. Your legs hurt?" She took another step, virtually chest-to-chest with him now. "I bet I can make you forget all about your legs. I bet I can make you feel real good." She shot a dismissive glance at Paige and Jessica. "Why don't you ditch the help? We can go to my dorm. It's close." The silence that followed was heavy. "The help?" Jessica repeated. Her voice was ice cold. The girl rolled her eyes. "Yeah. The nurses. The aides. Whatever. You guys can go. I’ve got him from here." She reached for Freddie’s arm, trying to pull him away from Paige’s navy-clad shoulder. That was a tactical error. Paige didn't let go. She clamped down on Freddie’s bicep like a vice. She didn't look at the girl with anger; she looked at her with the pity one reserves for a mosquito about to hit a bug zapper. "He isn't going anywhere," Paige said pleasantly. "Excuse me?" the girl snapped, her mask slipping. "I'm talking to him. Not you." "And he is talking to you," Jessica interjected, stepping forward slightly, effectively using her shoulder to box the girl out. "He said he needs to sit down. You are in the way." "He wants to go with me," the girl insisted, looking at Freddie with that same sultry, desperate look. "Don't you, tiger? You want to have some fun? You want to know what a real woman feels like?" Freddie looked at her. He looked at the heavy makeup and the popped collar. Then he looked at the two women holding him up. He looked at Jessica in her maroon school colors, the architect of his safety. He looked at Paige in her tight navy tee, the anchor of his sanity. These were the women who bathed him when he couldn't move, who slept next to him to keep the nightmares away, who learned an entire medical textbook just to make him feel safe. He knew exactly what a real woman felt like. He was holding two of them. "No," Freddie said. His voice wasn't loud, but it was clear. "I do not want 'fun.' I want stability. And you represent chaos." The girl’s mouth fell open. "Chaos?" she sputtered. "Variable rejected," Freddie confirmed. "Please move. I need the bench." He didn't wait for her to move. He gave the signal—a slight lean forward. "Forward," Jessica commanded. The phalanx moved. They didn't walk around her; they walked through the space she was occupying. The girl had to scramble backward, her sneakers squeaking on the tile, to avoid being run over by the sheer momentum of the Avery unit. She stood there in the middle of the lobby, mouth agape, as the three siblings bypassed her completely. They reached the bench. Paige and Jessica coordinated the descent, lowering Freddie gently until he was seated. He leaned back against the wall, closing his eyes, letting out a long, ragged exhale. "Safe," Freddie whispered. "Safe," Paige confirmed, sitting next to him and wrapping her arm around his shoulders. The girl watched them for a moment, her face twisting into a sneer of rejection. She huffed, spun on her heel, and stormed out the front door, muttering something about "freaks." Jessica watched her go, brushing a piece of lint off her Forger t-shirt. Then she sat on Freddie’s other side. "She thought we were staff," Jessica noted dryly. "Nurses." "She thought I was desperate," Freddie corrected, opening one eye. "She calculated that disability equals a zero-sum game for romantic selection. She assumed I would take any input provided." "She sucks at math," Paige said, resting her head on his shoulder. "Agreed," Freddie said, closing his eye again. He felt the warmth of his sisters on both sides—maroon on the left, navy on the right. The bench was hard, the lobby was bright, but the perimeter was secure. "Five minutes," Freddie requested. "Then the bus." "Take ten," Jessica said, crossing her legs in her blue jeans. "We aren't going anywhere."

title: Part 5: Geometry and Physics
content: The lobby bench was hard wood, but to Freddie, it felt like a recharge station. He sat in the middle, eyes closed, letting his breathing sync with the steady rise and fall of Paige’s chest against his right side. "Heart rate decelerating," Freddie murmured. "System cooling." "Good," Paige whispered, keeping her arm firmly around his shoulders. "We’ll sit here as long as it takes." But the peace was short-lived. The heavy glass doors of the lecture hall swung open again, releasing the stragglers—the students who had hung back to pack their bags or avoid the initial crush. Among them was a boy Freddie had noted earlier in the back row. He was wearing a polo shirt with the collar flipped up—a fashion choice Freddie found illogical as it offered no neck protection—and he had spent the majority of the lecture snickering at the diagrams. He stopped when he saw them on the bench. His eyes didn't go to Freddie. They didn't go to Jessica. They went straight to Paige. Specifically, they went to the navy blue t-shirt. Freddie opened his eyes. He saw the vector of the boy’s gaze. It was a direct line of sight to Paige’s chest, where the tight fabric struggled to contain her anatomy. Freddie felt a spike of protective irritation. He knew the shirt was too small; it was an error in the laundry cycle, not an invitation. But the boy didn't see an error. He saw an opportunity. He sauntered over, ignoring the fact that Paige was clearly engaged in a support maneuver. "Hey," the boy said, stopping right in front of her. He leaned against the wall, trying to look casual. "You were in the second row, right? The one taking all the notes?" Paige looked up. Her expression was flat. She tightened her grip on Freddie’s shoulder. "I was." "I noticed," the boy smirked, his eyes dropping to her neckline again. "Hard to miss. That shirt is doing a lot of heavy lifting. I respect the effort." Jessica sat up straight on Freddie’s left, her eyes narrowing behind her glasses. She opened her mouth to eviscerate him, but Paige squeezed Freddie’s arm, signaling Hold. "Can I help you?" Paige asked, her voice dropping to a temperature that could freeze nitrogen. "Just thought you might want a study partner," the boy said, stepping closer. "That class looks... intense. I figured maybe we could compare notes. Grab a drink? You look like you could use a break from..." He gestured vaguely at Freddie, waving a hand as if Freddie were a piece of luggage or a confusing piece of furniture. "...whatever this is." Freddie felt a sudden, sharp jolt of recognition. The data retrieval system in his brain spun up. He accessed a file from Freshman Year, September 1999. Subject: Jason. Snare Drummer. Incident: Concession Stand. Dialogue: "He's a big boy... cut the cord... it's embarrassing." This was the same algorithm. Different face, same code. Freddie lifted his head. He looked at the boy. "This," Freddie stated, pointing to himself, "is her brother. And she is not 'babysitting.' She is anchoring." The boy laughed, a dismissive bark. "Brother? Right. Look, man, no offense, but she looks a little cramped. I'm just offering to give her some space." He looked back at Paige, flashing a winning smile. "Come on. Ditch the family reunion. Let me buy you a coffee. I bet you're fun when you aren't weighted down." Paige didn't smile back. She didn't blush. She didn't look flattered. She gently removed her arm from Freddie’s shoulders, but she didn't stand up. She shifted her weight, turning her body so she was facing the boy directly. The tight navy shirt stretched across her chest, but she didn't cross her arms to hide it. She used her geometry as armor. "I had a boyfriend once," Paige said conversationally. Her tone was light, dangerously so. "Back in high school. His name was Jason. He played the snare drum." The boy blinked, confused by the non-sequitur. "Uh. Cool?" "He thought the same thing you do," Paige continued. "He thought that because I love my brother, because I take care of him, that I must be desperate for an 'out.' He thought that if he made fun of Freddie, I would laugh along to prove I was cool." She stood up. She wasn't tall, but in that moment, she looked ten feet high. "I dumped him in front of the entire football team," Paige said, her voice turning into steel. "Because he made one mistake. He disrespected the Unit." She took a step toward the boy. "Freddie isn't weight. He's my gravity. And you?" She looked him up and down, unimpressed. "You're just noise." The boy’s smirk vanished. He looked at Paige, then at Freddie (who was watching with a look of clinical satisfaction), and finally at Jessica, who was inspecting her fingernails like she was deciding which one to use to cut his throat. "Whatever," the boy muttered, his ego bruised. "You're all weirdos. Enjoy your... group therapy." He turned to leave, but he found his path blocked. Dr. Thorne was standing there. She had exited the classroom quietly, holding her stack of files. She had heard the last part of the exchange. She looked at the boy over the rim of her glasses. "Mr. Henderson," Dr. Thorne said. Her voice was calm, but it carried the weight of the Dean's office. "I was just leaving," the boy stammered. "You are," Dr. Thorne agreed. "And you won't be coming back." "What?" "I heard your comment," Dr. Thorne said. "And I observed your conduct. Harassing students in the lobby after class constitutes a violation of the safe space policy I outlined thirty minutes ago." She pulled a pen from her pocket and made a mark on her roster. "I suggest you visit the registrar immediately, Mr. Henderson. You have been dropped from HPE 204. I will not have students who treat anatomy like a joke and my classroom like a pickup bar." The boy’s face went pale. He looked at Paige, then at the professor. He realized, too late, that he had walked into a minefield. He fled. The double doors swung shut behind him. Dr. Thorne watched him go, then turned to the bench. She looked at Freddie. "The 'Jason Protocol'?" she asked, raising an eyebrow. "It is a highly effective filter," Freddie confirmed. "It removes incompatible variables from the social circle." "I can see that," Dr. Thorne smiled faintly. She nodded to Paige. "Good geometry." Paige grinned, sitting back down and wrapping her arm around Freddie again. "Thanks, Doc." "Rest up," Dr. Thorne said, walking toward her office. "Wednesday's lecture is on Physiology. It’s dense." Freddie leaned back against the wall. The lobby was quiet again. The threats—the girl, the boy—had been neutralized. "Two for two," Jessica noted. "We are clearing the roster." "Efficiency," Freddie whispered, closing his eyes. "Now... can we catch the bus?" "Yeah," Paige said, squeezing him tight. "Let's go home."

title: Part 6: The Safe Zone
content: The walk to the CPI Transit Center was a silent march. The adrenaline from the confrontation in the lobby was fading, replaced by the heavy, humid weight of a Virginia afternoon. A white-and-maroon bus was already idling in the loop, its diesel engine rumbling with a deep, patient rhythm. The destination sign glowed amber: 1 FALLING BRANCH "That’s us," Jessica said, her voice tired. "Let’s get out of here." They boarded. Freddie pulled his PolyPass from his pocket and held it up for the driver to see. The driver gave a quick nod of acknowledgment—a visual check, no beep, no machine. Just a flash of plastic to prove he belonged. Jessica and Paige flashed their IDs behind him, and they moved to the back of the bus, finding a row of empty seats near the rear exit door. Freddie slid in next to the window. Paige sat in the middle. Jessica took the aisle seat, effectively boxing them in. As the bus hissed and pulled away from the curb, merging into the campus traffic, Paige let out a long, frustrated sigh. She slumped in her seat, crossing her arms over her chest—not to hold Freddie this time, but to hide herself. She looked down at the navy blue t-shirt. It was tight. She knew it was tight. It was a laundry error, a remnant from high school that had accidentally made it into the college rotation. But looking at the way the fabric pulled across her chest, she felt a sudden, burning wave of resentment. "I hate it," Paige muttered, tugging at the hem of the shirt. "The fabric?" Freddie asked, looking at her. "Is the texture abrasive?" "No," Paige said, shaking her head. She looked out the window at the passing stone buildings of the university. "I hate that I can't just... exist. I hate that I walk into a room to learn about anatomy, and some jerk thinks I'm there to be the anatomy." She turned to Freddie. Her eyes were wet, frustrated tears gathering in the corners. "He didn't even look at my face, Freddie. He looked at my chest. He talked to my t-shirt. It’s like... it’s like the rest of me didn't even matter. I was just a shape to him." Freddie processed the data. He recalled the boy's gaze in the lobby—the vector, the smirk, the comments about "heavy lifting." "He reduced you to geometry," Freddie stated. "He ignored the architecture." "Exactly," Paige whispered. She wiped her eyes. "It’s exhausting. Being looked at like... like meat." Freddie wasn't looking at her chest. He never did. And he never will. He had seen her naked—in the shower, in the King Bed—and even then, stripped of all fabric, he would not stare at her chest. He would always lock his eyes to her eyes, overriding his natural autistic urge to look away, specifically out of respect. His eyes were focused entirely on her face, scanning her expression for data on her emotional state. His hand was resting on his own knee, tapping a slow, rhythmic pattern. He wasn't assessing her curves; he was assessing her stability. To Freddie, she wasn't a collection of "parts." She wasn't "breasts" or "hips." She was Paige. She was the Anchor. She was the person who knew how to wash his hair without getting soap in his eyes. She was the weight that stopped the world from spinning. She was his sister. The relief of that realization hit Paige harder than the anger. In a world full of boys who only saw what was under her shirt, Freddie was the one man who only cared about what was in her heart. "Come here," Paige whispered. She didn't wait for him to initiate. She leaned forward and wrapped her arms around him. It wasn't a protective hug this time; it was a seeking one. She buried her face in the hollow of his neck, breathing in the scent of his laundry detergent and the faint, metallic smell of the bus. She pressed herself against him. Her chest was pressed against his arm, but there was no weirdness. There was no tension. Freddie reacted instantly. He didn't pull away. He didn't get awkward. He lifted his arm and wrapped it around her shoulders, pulling her in tighter. He rested his chin on the top of her head. "Pressure applied," Freddie murmured. "Yeah," Paige breathed, closing her eyes. "Pressure applied." She felt safe. She felt human. For the first time all day, she didn't feel like an object. She felt like a person who was loved. "You are not geometry," Freddie said softly, his voice vibrating against her hair. "You are the structural integrity of the system. You are the Safe Person." Paige squeezed him, a fierce, bone-crushing hug that poured all her gratitude into him. "And you're mine," she whispered. "My safe person." Jessica watched them from the aisle seat. She saw the way the other passengers on the bus glanced at them—a guy and a girl hugging intensely in the back row. Let them look, Jessica thought. They didn't know the code. They didn't know that this wasn't romance; it was survival. "Next stop," the automated voice announced. "Pepper Plaza." Paige pulled back, but she didn't let go of his hand. She looked down at her shirt one last time, then shrugged. "I'm burning this shirt when we get home," she decided. "Illogical," Freddie countered, adjusting his glasses. "Cotton is a useful material. Use it for rags. Cleaning the Avalon." Paige laughed, a real, genuine sound that chased the shadows away. "Okay. Rags it is." The bus hissed to a halt. The doors opened. They stepped out into the sunshine of Christiansburg, leaving the predators and the geometry behind, walking toward the safety of the Base.

title: Part 7: The Incorrect Variable
content: Newman Hall was the living room of the university. While the library was for silence and the labs were for code, Newman was for noise, food, and decompression. Freddie sat on a low, plush sofa in the main atrium. He physically could not sit at the high-top tables near the café; the bar-stool height required a climb his spastic diplegia made dangerous, and his balance was too precarious for a seat without a back. The sofa was the only viable option. He had the emergency brake engaged and was currently in "Recharge Mode." His legs were stretched out on the coffee table (a minor violation of etiquette he ignored). Paige sat next to him, reading a paperback. Freddie was lying with his head in her lap. It was a public display of intimacy that most siblings abandoned in middle school. But for the Avery Unit, it was functional. The weight of her hand resting on his chest provided the necessary pressure to keep his heart rate steady in the bustling student center. "Page turn," Freddie murmured, hearing the rustle of paper above him. "Chapter four," Paige replied softly, tracing a pattern on his shoulder with her thumb. A shadow fell across them. Freddie opened his eyes. He saw a pair of designer jeans, a tight pink top, and a face that was trying very hard to look friendly. It was the girl from Monday. The one Dr. Thorne had ejected. "Hey," she said. She didn't sound aggressive today. She sounded... rehearsed. Freddie tensed. He felt Paige’s hand stop moving on his chest. "I didn't catch your name the other day," the girl said, shifting her weight to one hip. "I'm Krystal. With a K." Freddie sat up slowly. He didn't want to engage, but the social contract required an acknowledgment of a direct address. He swung his legs off the table. "Freddie," he stated. "Freddie," Krystal repeated, testing the word like it was a flavor. "That’s a nice name. Look, Freddie, I wanted to apologize. For Monday. I came on a little strong in the lobby." She glanced at Paige, then back to Freddie. She offered a smile that didn't quite reach her eyes. "I figured maybe we got off on the wrong foot. I wanted to see if I could buy you a coffee? There’s a place right over there." She pointed to the Espresso Bar in the corner. "My treat. No strings attached. Just... getting to know you." Freddie processed the offer. Input: Coffee. Variable: Caffeine causes tremors. Variable: Bitter taste profile. Conclusion: Incompatible. "I do not drink coffee," Freddie said flatly. "It induces kinetic instability." Krystal blinked. "Oh. Okay. Well, they have tea? Or soda?" "I drink hot chocolate," Freddie corrected. "With whole milk. But I do not require a beverage at this time." He turned his body away from her, rotating toward Paige. He lifted his arm and wrapped it around Paige’s waist, pulling himself into her side. He buried his face in her shoulder, further engaging the "emergency brake" protocol. It was a clear, non-verbal signal: I am occupied. I am safe. Go away. Krystal watched the hug. She saw the way Freddie clung to the girl in the navy t-shirt. She saw the way the girl instinctively wrapped her arms around him, resting her chin on his head. To Krystal, this wasn't a signal of rejection. It was a signal of dependency. She's good, Krystal thought, assessing Paige. Very hands-on. Probably one of those specialized aides for the severe cases. "That's sweet," Krystal said, her voice dripping with a condescending kind of sympathy. "She takes good care of you, huh?" Freddie pulled back slightly. "She is essential," he said into Paige’s shirt. "I bet," Krystal nodded. She stepped closer, lowering her voice so "the help" wouldn't hear (even though Paige was literally holding him). "But hey... does she have to be there all the time? I mean, surely you get some free time? When you aren't... doing therapy?" Paige looked up. Her expression was unreadable. She tightened her grip on Freddie. "He isn't in therapy," Paige said calmly. "He's resting." "Right, right," Krystal waved a hand dismissively. "Resting. Look, Freddie... I'm just saying. If you ever want a break... from the routine..." She pulled a small piece of paper from her pocket—a slip of notebook paper with a phone number written in purple gel ink. She tucked it boldly into the pocket of Freddie’s orange hoodie. "Call me," Krystal whispered. "I bet I can show you some things that aren't in your textbook." She straightened up, waiting for a reaction. She expected a blush, a smile, or for him to push the girl away now that a "better option" was available. Instead, Freddie stared at the slip of paper in his pocket like it was a contaminant. He looked at Paige. "She thinks you are an employee," Freddie whispered. "She thinks you're a project," Paige countered. Freddie shoved the paper deeper into his pocket to hide it, then leaned back into Paige, closing his eyes again. He assumed the interaction was over. But Krystal didn't leave. She stood over them, hands on her hips, her posture aggressive. She watched the way Paige resumed stroking Freddie’s hair—a gentle, rhythmic motion that seemed to melt the tension right out of his body. She watched the way Freddie settled deeper into her lap, turning his face inward toward her stomach, completely ignoring the "hot girl" standing right there. It infuriated her. "You know," Krystal said, her voice losing its sugary coating and becoming tight with genuine annoyance. "You're really possessive. It’s not cute. He’s a grown man, not a pet." Paige stopped stroking Freddie’s hair. She slowly lifted her gaze. She didn't look angry anymore; she looked genuinely baffled. She studied Krystal’s face—the heavy eyeliner, the plucked brows, the sheer determination to ignore reality. Then she looked down at Freddie. They had the same dark, thick hair. They wore identical black-rimmed glasses. They had the same nose—a slightly upturned Avery trait inherited from their mother. They even had the same jawline. To anyone paying attention, they looked like two versions of the same person. "Are you blind?" Paige asked quietly. Krystal blinked. "Excuse me?" "Look at his face," Paige commanded, pointing a finger at Freddie. "Then look at mine. Really look." Krystal frowned. She looked down at Freddie, who opened his eyes to peer up at her through his lenses. Then she looked at Paige. She saw the eyes. Dark brown. Identical. She saw the nose.
