Jessica shifted, pulling the duvet tighter around his shoulders. "Inside the circle," she whispered, echoing the song. "That's us. The perimeter is sealed." "So let the painted smile fall down You're standing on your native ground You're home... you're finally home" A tear leaked out of the corner of Freddie’s eye, sliding hot into his hairline. The painted smile. The mask he had worn for the Dean. The mask he had worn for Vanessa. The desperate, grinning attempt to be a "good student" while he was dying inside. It crumbled. "The mask you wore is on the floor You don't need it anymore The silence has no power here We'll banish every single fear..." The song continued, the singer’s voice gaining power, urging him to let go. "Just let it go, the heavy load At the ending of this lonely road Just lean on us, we'll hold the line..." And then, the line that broke him. "Your broken heart will mend with time" Freddie made a sound—half-sob, half-gasp. His heart was broken. It wasn't just the fear or the exhaustion. It was the heartbreak of having his autonomy stolen, of being treated like an object, of being discarded in a bus terminal. It felt shattered. But the song didn't say it was fixed. It said it would mend. With time. "Did you hear that?" Paige whispered, her face pressing into his shoulder. "It’ll mend, Freddie. We have time. We have all the time." The guitar solo soared, a high, crying melody that sounded like relief. It sounded like the feeling of the hot water hitting his back. It sounded like Jessica’s arm across his chest. "You're home... you're finally home We are your sanctuary... you're not alone." The song faded out into a gentle reverb. The room was silent again, but the silence wasn't empty anymore. It was filled with the resonance of the music. Freddie lay perfectly still, sandwiched between the two people who shared his DNA, his history, and his soul. The radio hummed with low static. "Data received," Freddie whispered, his voice thick. "Message... acknowledged." "Status?" Jessica asked, her voice fierce and protective in the dark. Freddie took a breath. It didn't shudder this time. "Safe," Freddie said. "I am safe."

title: Part 6: The Signal Cut
content: The reverb of "Sanctuary" had barely faded when the DJ’s voice returned, slick and energetic, jarring against the heavy emotional air in the room. "That was Mirage, holding you close. But sometimes, you gotta fight your way out of the dark before you can find the light. Here’s a track that starts in the gutter and ends in the sky. This is 'Haven City' by Steel Horizon." The speaker thumped. A heavy, distorted drum machine kicked in—thud-clank, thud-clank—accompanied by a pulsing, predatory synth-bass. Freddie flinched. The sound was too close to the memory of the Pathfinder bus engine idling in the terminal. It sounded like the headache that had been splitting his skull for three days. "Off," Freddie gasped. "Turn it off." Jessica moved instantly. Her hand slapped down on the snooze/off button. Click. The driving drums and wailing guitars were severed instantly. The silence that rushed back into the room was heavy, ringing in their ears. Freddie lay panting, his chest heaving against Paige’s side. He squeezed his eyes shut, trying to banish the afterimage of the music. "Input overload," Freddie whispered. "System... saturation." "We know," Jessica soothed, smoothing the hair back from his forehead. "We pushed it too fast. No more radio." They lay there for a long time, letting Freddie’s heart rate settle. The room was just a room again. The smell of verbena soap was grounding. The warmth of his sisters was real. Freddie took a deep breath. He thought about the lyrics he had almost heard. Take me home. He thought about the house on Pepper Street. He thought about safety. But then, he thought about the map in his head. Currently, the sector labeled "Seattle" was a corrupted file. It contained only pain: the bus terminal, the rain, the feeling of being dragged across a bathroom floor. If he left now, that data would be permanent. Seattle would always be a monster. He opened his eyes. He looked at Jessica. Then he looked at Paige. "I have... a request," Freddie whispered. "Anything," Jessica said instantly. "We can call the airline right now. We can be on a plane tonight." "Negative," Freddie said. He shifted, trying to sit up. "I do not want to evacuate." Paige frowned, helping him prop himself up against the headboard. "You don't?" "If we leave now," Freddie said, his voice trembling but gaining strength, "the data remains corrupted. Vanessa wins. She defined this location as a prison." He looked at his hands. "I want to redefine the location," Freddie stated. "I want to overwrite the bad data with good data. I want... I want to be a tourist." Jessica and Paige exchanged a look. It was a look of pure relief and pride. "Okay," Jessica smiled. "Tourist Protocol. Let's plan it." "Living room," Freddie requested. "I require... the sofa configuration." They helped him out of bed. They moved to the small sitting area of the suite. Freddie sat in the middle of the beige loveseat. Paige sat on his right; Jessica sat on his left. Freddie wrapped his arm around Paige’s waist. He wrapped his other arm around Jessica’s waist. He pulled them both in tight, anchoring himself in the center of the unit. "Secure," Freddie breathed. "Now. Show me the options." Paige grinned. She reached for her bag on the floor and pulled out a stack of glossy brochures she had grabbed from the lobby rack days ago. "I was hoping you'd say that," Paige said. She spread them out on the coffee table. She picked up the first one. It showed a sleek, white tower rising above the city, crowned with a flying saucer-shaped observation deck. "The Seattle Sky-Spire," Paige announced. "It’s 605 feet tall. Elevators take forty-one seconds to reach the top. It has a rotating floor." Freddie leaned forward, adjusting his glasses. He traced the curve of the tower on the paper. "It looks like a docking pylon," Freddie whispered. "From Stellar Voyage." "It does," Paige agreed. "And from up there? The bus station looks like a toy. You can look down on it. You can see the grid." "Elevation," Freddie nodded. "Perspective." Jessica picked up another brochure. THE BAYFRONT AQUARIUM. "And this," Jessica said. "It's built on a pier. They have a dome room under the water. Blue lights. Quiet tunnels. Fish moving in perfect, silent orbits. It’s sensory soothing, Freddie. It’s a tank." Freddie looked at the blue picture. He imagined the silence. He imagined the water. "Biological systems," Freddie noted. "Predictable movement." He looked at his sisters. They weren't looking at him with pity. They were looking at him like he was the Captain planning a shore leave mission. "I want to do this," Freddie said firmly. "I want to go to the Spire. I want to go to the Aquarium. I want to remember Seattle as the place where we went. Not the place where she took me." "Then we stay," Jessica declared. "We have the rental car. We have the suite. We extend the stay for three days." "Operation: Decompression," Paige named it. "We reclaim the map." "Reclaim the map," Freddie echoed. He squeezed them both tighter. The fear of the city outside the window began to fade, replaced by the anticipation of a new schematic. "Tomorrow," Freddie said. "We execute the itinerary." "Tomorrow," Jessica agreed. Safe in the sandwich configuration, holding the promise of a new memory in his mind, Freddie Avery closed his eyes. He wasn't running away. He was rewriting the code. The decision to stay had settled over the room like a fresh blanket, but the emotional exertion of the "overwrite" discussion had drained Freddie’s remaining battery. He sat in the middle of the beige loveseat, his arms still wrapped around both sisters, his breathing slowly syncing with theirs. "Wait," Paige said suddenly, her eyes widening. "We forgot the fuel." "Fuel?" Freddie murmured. "The Comfort Fuel," Paige said. "Jessica bought the canister. White Hot Chocolate. With the little marshmallows." Jessica stood up instantly. "You're right. Critical oversight. I'll deploy the beverages." Paige started to shift, intending to help, but Jessica put a hand on her shoulder. "Negative," Jessica commanded softly. "You stay. Maintain the anchor." Jessica knew the schematic. If she left, Freddie would have an open flank. If Paige left too, he would be adrift. He needed at least one point of contact to maintain structural integrity. "Understood," Paige said, settling back. Jessica walked to the kitchenette. As soon as her weight left the sofa cushion, Freddie reacted. The loss of the left-side pressure triggered a defensive reflex. He didn't sit up straight; he collapsed. "Brake," Freddie whispered. "Engaging." He slid sideways. He swung his legs up onto the sofa where Jessica had just been sitting. He laid his head down in Paige’s lap, curling his body into a tight C-shape against the back cushions. He buried his face in the soft fabric of her pajama shorts, hiding from the light, hiding from the room. "Brake engaged," Paige confirmed gently. She draped her left arm over his side, her hand coming to rest flat against the center of his chest, directly over his heart. She felt the rhythm—still a little fast, but slowing down. "I am... stationary," Freddie mumbled into her leg. "I know," Paige smoothed his hair. "You just stay there. We'll bring the fuel to the tank." In the kitchenette, Jessica worked with quiet efficiency. She heated the milk in the microwave—two minutes, stir, two minutes. She spooned the white powder into three mugs. She added the hot milk, stirring until it was a creamy, frothy white. She added a generous dollop of whipped cream from the can they had bought. She carried two mugs over to the living area. "Order up," Jessica said softly. She set the mugs on the coffee table, within easy reach of Freddie’s hand if he chose to extract it from the cocoon. "One for the Captain," she whispered. "One for the Anchor." She looked at the sofa. Freddie was fully extended, his legs taking up the cushion she had vacated. He was locked in. If she tried to sit back down, she would have to ask him to move his legs, and right now, asking him to move was like asking a stone to dance. "I'll be right back," Jessica said. She went back to the kitchen, retrieved her own mug, and returned. She looked at the available seating. The armchair was too far away. The other side of the sofa was occupied by Freddie’s feet. Jessica didn't hesitate. She didn't ask him to scoot. She respected the protocol. She sat down on the sturdy rectangular coffee table, directly facing them. She sat cross-legged, her knees brushing against the sofa cushion, creating a close, intimate circle. "Table seating," Jessica smiled, blowing on her cocoa. "Better view of the team anyway." Freddie peeled one eye open. He saw Jessica sitting right there, inches away, holding her mug. He saw the steam rising from his own mug on the table next to her hip. He reached out a hand—shaky but determined. "Refuel," Freddie whispered. Jessica picked up his mug and handed it to him. He took it, holding it close to his chest, letting the warmth seep into his hands. "Refueling," Freddie agreed. He took a sip. It was sweet, hot, and tasted like safety. He didn't sit up. He drank it right there in Paige’s lap, while Jessica watched over them from her perch on the table, the three of them locked in a quiet, perfect triangle of recovery. The white hot chocolate was warm in Freddie’s stomach, a soothing ballast against the cold rain streaking the windowpanes. He lay still on the beige loveseat, his legs still draped over the cushion where Jessica had been, his head heavy and secure in Paige’s lap. The "Emergency Brake" was fully engaged. He wasn't moving. He didn't want to move. Jessica sat on the coffee table, her knees brushing against the sofa, her own mug cradled in her hands. She wasn't rushing him. She was just... there. Freddie took a breath. The air smelled of cocoa and the faint, clean scent of Paige’s skin. It was time to clear the cache. "I need... to run a diagnostic," Freddie whispered, staring at the buttons on Paige’s pajama top. "On what?" Paige asked softly, her hand resuming its rhythmic stroke through his hair. "On the corruption," Freddie said. "The Vanessa Virus. I need to understand how the logic bomb was planted. I need to patch the security flaw so it... so it never happens again." He felt Paige tense slightly, then force herself to relax. "Okay," Jessica said, her voice calm and clinical. "Let's debug it. What did she say to you? What was the input?" Freddie closed his eyes. He replayed the scene in the lobby of Copernicus Hall. The way Vanessa had leaned in close. The way she had made her voice sound like she was the only one telling him the truth. "She said... she said you were leaving," Freddie murmured. "She said she heard you in the bathroom. That Jessica had an internship in New York. And Paige had a study abroad program in Italy." Paige stopped stroking his hair. "Italy?" "She said you turned them down," Freddie continued, his voice trembling. "She said you sacrificed your dreams because... because you couldn't leave me. She said I was the gravity well. The black hole. That if I didn't leave... you would eventually hate me for trapping you." He opened his eyes, looking up at Paige with a raw, terrifying vulnerability. "Is there... was there an Italy file?" Paige looked down at him. Her expression wasn't guilty. It was baffled. "Freddie," Paige said, shaking her head. "I looked at a brochure for Italy once. In the student center trash can. I picked it up because it had a pretty picture of a statue. I looked at it for ten seconds, thought 'Wow, that's a lot of walking,' and threw it back away." She leaned down, pressing her forehead against his. "There was no application," she whispered. "There was no acceptance letter. I never wanted to go to Italy. I don't speak Italian. I hate flying. And most importantly... you aren't there." "And New York?" Freddie asked, shifting his gaze to Jessica. Jessica snorted. It was a derisive, un-ladylike sound. "New York?" Jessica said. "The city that smells like garbage and has a cost of living that would bankrupt us in a week? No. Never. I applied for exactly zero internships in New York. My plan has always been to find a firm in Roanoke or Blacksburg so I can drive or take the bus home every night." She reached out and squeezed his ankle, which was resting near her on the sofa. "Vanessa made it up," Jessica stated firmly. "She took a tiny fragment of data—maybe she saw me reading a magazine about New York—and she weaponized it. She built a fiction designed to target your specific insecurity: that you are a burden." "It was... effective," Freddie admitted. "The logic held. I believed I was a constraint." "You aren't a constraint," Paige said fiercely. "You're the Point of Origin. You're where the map starts." She adjusted her position, pulling him tighter against her stomach. "Freddie, listen to me. I don't want to go to Europe. I don't want to go backpacking to 'find myself.' I know exactly where I am." She looked around the small hotel room—the stocked kitchenette, the blackout curtains, the massive bed where they had all slept in a pile. "My priority... my dream... isn't a place," Paige said. "It's a state. It's waking up in the morning, rolling over, and touching your arm. It's feeling you breathe. It's knowing—knowing—that you are safe." She looked him in the eye. "When I wake up and you're there, sandwiched between us... that is the best moment of my day. Every single time. I don't want to wake up in Rome alone. I want to wake up in Christiansburg with you." "Forever?" Freddie whispered. "Forever," Paige promised. "Even... even when we are old?" Freddie asked. "The social contract suggests that siblings separate. That you find... partners." "We found our partners," Jessica said simply. "We found each other. The Avery Unit is a closed system, Freddie. We don't need external variables." She leaned forward on the coffee table. "I want the King bed," Jessica declared. "I want the sandwich configuration. I want to sleep next to you for the rest of my life because it stops my nightmares too. It’s not just for you, Freddie. We need it. We need the weight." Freddie processed this. The data was overwriting the Vanessa Virus. Vanessa's Logic: He is a burden holding them back. New Logic: He is the anchor keeping them grounded. They want to be held. The "trap" wasn't real. The "sacrifice" wasn't real. "So," Freddie said, his voice gaining a little strength. "New York is deleted. Italy is deleted." "Purged," Paige confirmed. "And the bed... is permanent architecture?" "Permanent," Jessica agreed. "We buy a new mattress every ten years if we have to. But the formation stays." Freddie let out a long, shuddering breath. He felt the last of the poison leave his system. He wasn't a jailer. He was a brother. He snuggled deeper into Paige’s lap, pressing his face against her stomach. He felt the tension leave his legs. "Patch installed," Freddie whispered. "System secure." "Good," Paige said, resting her hand over his heart again. "Now, stay right there. The Emergency Brake is still active. We aren't moving until you say so." "I say... never," Freddie mumbled, closing his eyes. "Never works for us," Jessica smiled, picking up her mug. Safe in the lap of his sister, guarded by the other, Freddie Avery finally stopped running. The virus was gone. The code was clean. And the Unit was unbreakable. The afternoon light behind the curtains had faded to evening grey, and the quiet conversation about Italy and New York had settled the dust in Freddie's mind. The "Vanessa Virus" had been quarantined, if not fully deleted. But another system was now sending urgent alerts. Gurgle. Freddie’s stomach growled—a low, persistent rumble that vibrated against Paige’s thigh. "Status check," Paige whispered, a smile touching her lips. "Fuel levels... critical," Freddie admitted. His voice was stronger now, less like a ghost and more like a tired man waking up. He shifted. For the first time in hours, he didn't just burrow deeper; he tried to sit up. The "Emergency Brake" was disengaging. "Assist?" Paige asked, feeling him struggle against the gravity of exhaustion. "Affirmative," Freddie said. "I wish to... participate. I want to sit at the table." Paige placed a hand on his back and another on his shoulder, leveraging him up while he pushed weakly against the cushions. He swayed for a second once he was vertical, blinking behind his glasses. "Steady," Jessica said from her perch on the coffee table. She stood up, stretching her legs. "Okay, Captain. Table it is." They flanked him for the short migration. It was only ten feet from the sofa to the small, round dining table near the kitchenette, but they moved like a security detail. Jessica took his left arm, Paige took his right. They didn't drag him; they just offered a solid framework he could lean on. Freddie sat in one of the dining chairs. It was firm, upright. It felt like a return to civilization. "Menu options?" Freddie asked, looking at the kitchenette. "I'm cooking," Jessica announced, tying her hair back. "You stay right there with Paige. I’ve got the supplies." She opened the freezer. She pulled out the bag they had bought at Market Street Grocery. Crispy Chicken Strips. She opened the cupboard. Creamy Macaroni & Cheese (the deluxe kind with the foil pouch of liquid gold, not the powder). "Comfort Protocol," Jessica winked. "Chicken and Mac. Zero spice. Maximum cheese." "Acceptable," Freddie said, watching her work. "High caloric density." Paige sat in the chair next to him, turning it slightly so her knees brushed his. She kept her hand on his forearm, a constant tactile reminder that he wasn't alone. While the water boiled and the oven preheated, Jessica laid out the new mission parameters. "Okay," Jessica said, stirring the macaroni. "If we're doing the tourist thing tomorrow, we need a transport plan. I don't want to drive the rental car downtown. Parking is a nightmare, and the traffic is chaos." "Agreed," Freddie said. "Urban driving introduces stress variables." Paige pulled a transit map from the stack of brochures. TRANSIT AUTHORITY OF THE PUGET SOUND (TAPS). "Look at this," Paige said, spreading the map on the table. "They have a unified zone downtown. It’s called the Ride Free Area." Freddie leaned in, adjusting his glasses. He traced the shaded box on the map. "Ride Free?" "Between 6 AM and 7 PM," Paige read. "Any bus trip that starts and ends inside this zone is zero fare. You just hop on." "Frictionless entry," Freddie noted approvingly. "No payment interaction required." "And look," Jessica pointed with a wooden spoon. "Our hotel is here, on Stewart. We're inside the zone. We can catch any bus right outside the door and ride it all the way to the waterfront or the retail core without spending a dime." "Efficient," Freddie said. Paige traced a line north. "The zone ends here at Battery Street. If we get off at the last stop, we're only a few blocks from the Sky-Spire." She looked at the scale of the map. Then she looked at Freddie. "It's about a six-block walk," Paige estimated. "From the bus stop to the Spire." Freddie frowned. He ran a diagnostic on his legs. They were stiff, sore, and currently running on reserve power. Six blocks on city pavement was a marathon. "Range anxiety," Freddie whispered. "Six blocks is... significant." "We don't have to walk it," Jessica called out from the stove, dumping the cheese sauce into the pot. "There's a relay." She pointed to a blue line on the map. THE METRO-RAIL. "It's an elevated train," Jessica explained. "It runs from the downtown mall directly to the Seattle Exposition Park. It drops you right at the base of the Spire. It’s a two-minute ride." "A monorail?" Freddie asked, his eyes lighting up. "Elevated transit?" "Exactly," Paige said. "We take the free bus to the mall. We take the elevator up to the platform. We ride the train to the Spire. Minimal walking." "And if we do walk," Jessica added, bringing the plates to the table, "we break it up. We stop at every bench. We stop at every coffee shop—well, for us to get coffee, you can get water. We aren't in a rush, Freddie. If you need to sit, we sit. If you need to stop, we stop." She set a plate in front of him. Steaming mac and cheese. Three golden chicken strips. "We move at your pace," Paige promised, squeezing his arm. "The Captain sets the speed." Freddie looked at the food. He looked at the map. He looked at his sisters. "The Metro-Rail," Freddie decided, picking up his fork. "That is the optimal vector." He took a bite of the chicken. It was hot, mild, and safe. "Tomorrow," Freddie said, chewing slowly. "We take the train." "Tomorrow," Jessica agreed, clinking her fork against his. They ate in the quiet hotel room, the map of the city spread out between them, plotting a course for a day that would replace the grey memory of the bus station with the bright, elevated view of a family that had found its way back to each other. The dinner plates were pushed aside, empty save for a few streaks of cheese sauce. The map of Seattle was still spread out on the table, promising a future of monorails and space needles. Freddie sat back in his chair. His stomach was full. The "Emergency Brake" was disengaged, and his systems were coming back online. But as the adrenaline of the planning session faded, a different sensation took over. He felt... sticky. Not with the grime of the bus—that had been scrubbed away earlier—but with the lingering, phantom residue of the day’s stress. He felt the need to be submerged again. To be held by the water and his sisters simultaneously. He looked at Jessica, who was stacking the plates. He looked at Paige, who was folding a napkin. They were all nude. In the soft light of the hotel room, stripped of the jeans and hoodies and armor of the outside world, it didn't feel exposed. It felt honest. It meant there were no hidden weapons, no hidden agendas. Just skin. Just the Unit. Freddie cleared his throat. The "Admin" voice he usually used for requests—I require hygiene protocol—felt wrong. It felt too cold for the warmth in his chest. "Jessica?" Freddie said softly. "Paige?" They both stopped and looked at him instantly. "System report?" Jessica asked. "Systems are... grateful," Freddie whispered. He looked down at his hands. "I have a request. A... favor." "Name it," Paige said. "Could I... please... have a bath?" Freddie asked. The word please felt heavy and sweet on his tongue. "Not a scrub. Just... a bath. With both of you?" He looked up, his eyes wide behind his glasses. "I want to feel the water," he stammered, the emotion breaking through his usual cadence. "And I want you there. Please. If you don't mind." Jessica’s expression softened into something incredibly tender. She reached out and touched his cheek. "You never have to say 'please' for that, Freddie," she said. "But yes. Absolutely." "We'd love to," Paige added, standing up and taking his hand. "Let's go to the spa." The hotel bathroom was dim, lit only by the light spilling in from the kitchenette. Jessica started the water. She didn't make it scalding hot this time; she made it warm, a gentle, enveloping temperature. She poured in a little of the hotel’s complimentary bubble bath—something she usually dismissed as frivolous, but tonight, it seemed necessary. "Ready, Captain?" Paige asked. "Ready," Freddie said. "Thank you." They helped him into the tub. He slid into the bubbles, the water rising to his chest. He sighed, a long, trembling sound of pure contentment. Jessica knelt on the bathmat to his left. Paige knelt to his right. They didn't grab scrub brushes or medical saline this time. They grabbed soft washcloths. "Arms up," Paige whispered playfully. Freddie lifted his arms. Paige began to wash his left arm. She moved slowly, the cloth gliding over his skin in long, soothing strokes. "Thank you, Paige," Freddie whispered, watching her hand. "Thank you for finding me." "I'll always find you," Paige said, her voice thick. She kissed his wet shoulder. Jessica took his right hand. She washed his fingers, one by one, massaging the stiffness out of his knuckles where he had gripped the wheelchair armrests for so long. "Thank you, Jessica," Freddie said, turning his head to look at her. "Thank you for the plane. For the food. For... everything." "It's just logistics, Freddie," Jessica smiled, squeezing his soapy hand. "That's what I do." "It is not just logistics," Freddie corrected gently. "It is love. Thank you." They washed his chest. They washed his neck. They were careful of his lower back, washing around the dressing with infinite tenderness. It wasn't a medical procedure. It was a ritual. With every stroke of the cloth, they were telling him: You are here. You are ours. You are safe. Freddie closed his eyes. He listened to the water lapping against the porcelain. He felt the steam on his face. He felt four hands touching him, caring for him, asking for nothing in return. He thought about Vanessa. She had wanted to take. She had wanted to own. His sisters just wanted him to be clean. "I am... so happy," Freddie whispered, the words bubbling up from a place deep inside him. "I am overwhelmed with data... but it is good data." "Good data," Jessica agreed, rinsing the soap from his back with a cup. "Okay," Paige said softly. "One last rinse." She took the handheld shower wand. She turned it to a gentle spray. She rinsed the bubbles away, leaving his skin warm and clean. "All done," Paige announced. Freddie looked at them. They were wet from the splashing, their hair frizzy in the humidity, kneeling on the hard tile floor just to be close to him. "Thank you," Freddie said again. He didn't know how else to say it. The vocabulary of the "Iron City" didn't have a word for this feeling. "You're welcome, Freddie," Jessica said. "Now. Let's get you dry. The King bed is waiting." They helped him stand. They wrapped him in warm towels. And as they walked him back to the "Silo," Freddie realized that the "Robert Virus"—the voice that said he was broken—was silent. He wasn't broken. He was just loved. The hotel room was dim, illuminated only by the microwave clock and the faint sliver of city light bleeding around the edges of the blackout curtains. The air conditioner hummed a steady, low-frequency drone that scrubbed the room of silence. They moved from the bathroom to the sleeping area. They didn't bother with pajamas. The "Armor" had been discarded in the hamper. Tonight, after the bath, after the confession about Italy, and after the decision to stay, clothing felt like unnecessary friction. "Bedtime," Jessica announced softly. She walked to the massive King bed and pulled back the heavy white duvet. "Positions," she murmured. Freddie climbed in first. He moved to the dead center of the mattress. The sheets were cool and smooth against his clean skin—a sharp contrast to the grit of the denim he had worn for three days. He lay back, sinking into the pillows. Jessica climbed in on his left—the side closest to the door. She was the Shield. She lay on her side, pressing her back against his arm, her legs tangling with his. Paige climbed in on his right—the side against the wall. She was the Anchor. She curled into him, resting her head on his shoulder, draping her arm across his chest to lock him in. They collapsed the 76 inches of space. They became a single thermal mass in the center of the bed. "Pressure check?" Jessica asked from the dark. "Optimal," Freddie breathed. He felt the weight of Paige’s arm. He felt the warmth of Jessica’s back. It was a heavy, grounding sensation that pinned him to the earth. He closed his eyes. Usually, the darkness brought the static—the replay of the trauma. But tonight, the static was quiet. His mind drifted to tomorrow. "Tomorrow," Freddie whispered into the quiet room. "The bus." He felt Paige tense slightly against his side. "You okay with that? We can take a taxi if you want." "No," Freddie said immediately. "I want the bus." He visualized the map they had looked at during dinner. The Ride Free Area. The Tunnel. "Vanessa made the bus a prison," Freddie murmured. "She made it a cage." He squeezed Paige’s hand where it rested on his chest. He nudged Jessica with his elbow. "But tomorrow... the bus is a vehicle," Freddie stated. "Because the crew is correct." "The crew is correct," Jessica agreed, reaching back to squeeze his hand. "We're riding with you, Freddie. We're riding the electric bus in the tunnel. It's going to be quiet. It's going to be smooth." "And if you get scared," Paige promised, kissing his shoulder, "we get off. We pull the cord. We stop. You have the control." Freddie smiled in the dark. That was the variable that changed the equation. Control. "I am looking forward to it," Freddie admitted. "I want to see the tunnel." "We'll see it," Paige said. "Now sleep, Captain. We have a big day." "Goodnight, Anchor," Freddie whispered. "Goodnight, Shield." "Goodnight, Freddie." Safe in the sandwich configuration, clean, fed, and held by the only people who mattered, Freddie Avery let go. The bus ride of the past was over. The bus ride of the future—the tourist ride, the family ride—was waiting. He slept without dreaming.

title: Part 1: Fueling the Expedition
content: The blackout curtains held the line against the morning, maintaining the protective twilight of the "Silo," but the digital clock on the microwave insisted it was time to start the day. Freddie woke up in the center of the King bed. He was warm. He was compressed. He was safe. To his left, Jessica was already stirring, checking her watch with the efficiency of a shift commander. To his right, Paige was still deeply asleep, her arm thrown over his chest like a seatbelt, anchoring him to the mattress. "Morning, Captain," Jessica whispered, sitting up and stretching. "Morning," Freddie rasped. He ran a diagnostic. His back was stiff from the injury, throbbing with a dull ache where the skin was healing, but the "static" in his head was low. The anxiety that usually greeted him upon waking—Where am I? Is she here?—was absent. He knew exactly where he was. He was with the Unit. "Weather check," Jessica announced, sliding out of bed. She walked to the window and cracked the heavy curtains just an inch. A beam of bright, clean sunlight sliced into the room, illuminating dust motes dancing in the air. "Visual confirmation," Jessica smiled, looking back at them. "Blue skies. High of 65 degrees. Perfect visibility for the Spire." "65 degrees," Freddie noted, sitting up carefully. "Low humidity. Optimal." They moved with the easy rhythm of a team that had lived in close quarters for years. There was no scrambling for modesty, no hiding behind doors. They simply moved from the bed to the bathroom to the kitchenette, getting dressed in comfortable layers for a day of walking. Freddie put on fresh jeans, wincing slightly as the waistband settled near the bandage on his lower back, and a soft grey t-shirt. He tied his orange hoodie around his waist—just in case the temperature dropped or he needed the armor. Jessica took command of the stove. The kitchenette was small, but she treated it like a restaurant line. "Order up," Jessica said, cracking eggs into a bowl. "The Captain needs protein for the climb." She whisked the eggs with a fork. She added diced ham, cheddar cheese, and mushrooms she had prepped the night before from their Market Street run. "Omelet," Freddie said, watching the pan sizzle. "Structural integrity looks good." "Wheat toast," Paige added, popping two slices into the toaster. "Grape jelly. And..." She held up the canister. "White Hot Chocolate." "Essential," Freddie agreed. For themselves, the sisters opted for something lighter but equally fueling. "Yogurt parfaits," Jessica said, setting out bowls of vanilla yogurt, granola, and sliced strawberries. "And coffee. Lots of coffee." They sat at the small round table. The map of Seattle was spread out under their plates like a tablecloth. Freddie cut into his omelet. It was fluffy, hot, and savory. He took a bite of toast with grape jelly—sweet and crunchy. He took a sip of the white hot chocolate—creamy and soothing. "Fuel status?" Paige asked, crunching on granola. "Tanks filling," Freddie said. He pointed to the map with his fork. "Vector confirmed," he stated. "We exit the hotel. We enter the Transit Tunnel at Convention Place. We board the bus. We transfer to the Metro-Rail at Westlake Center. We proceed to the Sky-Spire." "And the bus ride?" Jessica asked gently, watching him over her coffee mug. Freddie paused. He thought about the Pathfinder. He thought about the vibration, the smell, the fear. Then he looked at the map. He saw the "Ride Free Area" box. He saw the tunnel line. "The bus is electric," Freddie reminded himself. "It is a dual-mode. It runs on overhead wires in the tunnel. It is silent. It is clean." He looked at Paige. "And the crew is correct," he added. Paige smiled, reaching over to squeeze his hand. "The crew is ready." "Then we launch," Freddie said, finishing his chocolate. "Tourist Protocol is active." They cleared the table. They grabbed their bags (water, cameras, jackets). They walked out the door of Room 412, not as refugees fleeing a crime scene, but as explorers stepping out into a brand new world.

title: Part 2: The Mode Switch
content: The walk from the Cascade Suites to the transit station was short—just a few blocks through the crisp, sunny Seattle morning. The air smelled of rain-washed pavement and coffee, a sharp contrast to the diesel fumes of the Pathfinder terminal across the street. They arrived at Convention Place Station, the northern terminus of the Downtown Seattle Transit Tunnel. It wasn't a dark, underground hole; it was a sunken, open-air plaza where the city streets dipped down to meet the subway level. "There," Freddie said, pointing to the dedicated bus lane. "The insertion point." They watched as a massive, articulated bus—painted in the teal, yellow, and white livery of the Transit Authority of the Puget Sound (TAPS)—rolled into the station from the street. The diesel engine was rumbling, a low, familiar growl. "Wait," Freddie whispered, holding up a hand. "Watch the transformation." The bus came to a halt at the designated "changeover" line. The driver engaged the parking brake. Then, the magic happened. The roar of the diesel engine cut out abruptly. Silence descended on the bay. With a mechanical whir, two long poles rose from the roof of the bus. They extended upward until they made contact with the thick copper wires strung overhead. Snap-hiss. The connection was made. The bus hummed to life—not with a roar, but with a high-pitched, electric whine. "Mode switch complete," Freddie beamed, his eyes wide behind his glasses. "Diesel propulsion offline. Electric traction online. It is a hybrid organism." "That is pretty cool," Paige admitted, squeezing his arm. "It's like it plugged itself in." "It is cleaner," Freddie noted approvingly. "No exhaust in the tunnel. Smart engineering." The bus pulled forward to the boarding platform, gliding silently now. The doors folded open. "Ride Free Area," Jessica reminded them. "We just walk on." They stepped aboard. Freddie took a window seat near the articulation joint. Paige sat next to him; Jessica took the seat across the aisle. The interior didn't smell like the Pathfinder. It smelled of ozone and electricity. "Next stop," the automated voice announced, crisp and clear. "Westlake Station." The bus accelerated. It plunged into the dark mouth of the tunnel. Freddie tensed for a microsecond, expecting the shaking, the noise, the claustrophobia. But the ride was smooth. The electric motor provided a constant, linear acceleration with zero vibration. The tunnel walls whipped by, illuminated by the bus's headlights, but it felt controlled. It felt like a spaceship launching from a bay. "Status?" Paige whispered, leaning close. Freddie looked out at the tunnel lights. He felt the smooth glide of the tires on the dedicated roadway. "Silent running," Freddie whispered back, relaxing into the seat. "This is... acceptable." The bus glided to a halt at Westlake Station. They stepped off onto the mezzanine platform. "Upstairs," Jessica said, pointing to the signs. "To the Monorail." They took the escalator up, rising from the subterranean tunnel into the light-filled atrium of the Westlake Center mall. "Level 3," Freddie recited from the research. "The station is integrated into the architecture." They reached the Monorail platform. And there it was. The Metro-Rail. It wasn't a bus. It wasn't a train. It was a retro-futuristic red streak sitting on a concrete beam high above the street. It looked like something out of a 1960s sci-fi cover—The World of Tomorrow. "Target acquired," Freddie grinned. "The Monorail. Built for the 1962 World's Fair." "It looks fast," Paige said. "It travels the one-mile track in exactly two minutes," Freddie said. "It is a dedicated point-to-point shuttle." They bought their tickets (\$1.50 each). They boarded the red train. The windows were massive, curving up into the roof to offer a panoramic view of the sky. Freddie sat right at the front. He looked down through the windshield at the concrete beam stretching out ahead of them, threading between the skyscrapers. "Ready for launch?" Jessica asked from the seat behind him. "Ready," Freddie said. The doors slid shut. The Metro-Rail surged forward. They were flying above the traffic, above the noise, gliding on a beam of concrete toward the white needle piercing the blue sky in the distance. "Destination," Freddie announced, watching the tower grow larger in the window. "The Sky-Spire."

title: Part 3: The Observation Deck
content: The Metro-Rail glided into the station at the base of the tower. They stepped off the train and walked through the park, craning their necks to look up. The Sky-Spire rose 605 feet into the air, a slender white stalk supporting a massive, saucer-shaped top house. It looked impossible. It looked like a spaceship tethered to the ground. "Architecture check," Freddie murmured, shielding his eyes. "Tripod legs. Tapered waist. It is structurally efficient." They bought their tickets and queued for the elevator. "High velocity," Freddie warned as the doors closed. "This elevator travels at 10 miles per hour. It ascends 520 feet in 41 seconds." The lift shot up. Through the glass window, the ground fell away instantly. The trees shrank to bushes, then to dots. The cars became toys. Freddie gripped the rail, but he didn't look away. He watched the city grid reveal itself. Ding. The doors opened on the Observation Deck. They stepped out. The view was panoramic. To the west, the Elliott Bay glittered in the sun, ferries cutting white wakes across the blue water. To the east, the skyscrapers of downtown stood like glass cliffs. And in the distance, the massive, snow-capped cone of Mount Rainier floated above the horizon like a cloud. "Oh wow," Paige breathed. They walked out onto the open-air deck. The wind whipped around them, but the heavy wire cage kept them safe. Freddie walked to the edge. He looked down. He saw the grid of the streets. He saw the tiny, ant-like buses moving in straight lines. And he saw the roof of the Pathfinder terminal. From down there, it had been a prison. From up here, it was just a grey rectangle. It was small. It was insignificant. "Perspective," Freddie whispered. "What do you see?" Jessica asked, standing on his left side. "I see the map," Freddie said. "It is just data. It is manageable." He pointed down at the terminal. "That is where I was," Freddie said. "Down in the noise." He looked at his sisters. They were standing in the sun, hair blowing in the wind, smiling at him. "This is where I am," Freddie said. "Above the static." "This is where you belong," Paige said, leaning her head on his shoulder. "High ground." Freddie took a deep breath of the thin, clean air. He felt the vibration of the tower in the wind—a subtle sway designed to handle storms. It bends, he thought. But it does not break. "I like the elevation," Freddie decided. "The Overwrite is successful. Seattle is not a trap. It is a launchpad." "Good," Jessica grinned. "Now let's go inside. I think the rotating restaurant has lunch." "Rotation?" Freddie asked. "One revolution every 47 minutes," Jessica promised. "Slow and steady." "Acceptable," Freddie smiled. They went back inside, leaving the view of the bus station behind, trading the grey memory for a lunch in the sky.

title: Part 4: The Deep Blue
content: The "Metro-Rail" ride back from the Sky-Spire had been smooth, but the transition to the waterfront was a physical trial. They navigated the "Hill Climb" elevators at the public market, descending from the city streets to the pier level. By the time they reached Alaskan Way, Freddie’s gait had deteriorated. The adrenaline of the morning's ascent had burned off, leaving behind the heavy, grinding reality of his spastic diplegia. His right foot dragged slightly with every step. He was leaning heavily on Paige, his arm draped over her shoulders, his breathing shallow and tight. "Target acquired," Jessica announced, pointing to the large wooden structure of Pier 59. "The Bayfront Aquarium." "Low light protocol," Freddie rasped, trying to sound like the Captain, but his voice was thin. "We’re going under." They entered the lobby. It was cool and smelled of brine, a welcome relief from the sun, but the queue for tickets was long. Freddie swayed, gripping Paige’s waist to stay upright. "Status check?" Paige whispered, looking up at him with concern. "Legs... critical," Freddie admitted, staring at the floor. "Battery low." Jessica looked around the lobby while waiting in line. She saw the ticket counters, the gift shop, and the eager families. Then, out of the corner of her eye, she saw them. Tucked into an alcove near the coat check was a row of blue vinyl wheelchairs. They were standard-issue manual chairs, folded and waiting, with a sign above them: Complimentary Guest Use. Jessica stepped out of line. She walked over to the alcove and pulled one out. She locked the brakes and rolled it over to Freddie. "Freddie," Jessica said softly. Freddie looked down at the chair. He froze. The "Robert Virus" flared up instantly. Lazy. Giving up. What will people think? "No," Freddie whispered, backing up a step. "I can walk. I am not... invalid." "You aren't invalid," Jessica said firmly. "You're exhausted. You just walked a mile at the Sky-Spire. You've been on your feet for four hours." "Mom would say..." Freddie started, his voice trembling. "She would say I am quitting." "Mom isn't here," Paige cut in, her voice fierce. She turned to face him, grabbing both his hands. "She is three thousand miles away. We are here. And we say you are hurting." She squeezed his hands. "Look at me, Freddie. You are shaking. If you keep walking, you're going to crash. You're going to be in so much pain you won't even see the fish. Is that what you want?" "No," Freddie whispered. "I want to see the sharks." "Then sit down," Jessica said, her hand resting on the push handle. "Let us be the engine. You just be the Navigator." Freddie looked at the chair. He looked at Jessica’s determined face. He looked at Paige, who was nodding encouragement. "You promise?" Freddie asked, his voice small. "You won't... think less of me?" "Oh, Freddie," Paige said, pulling him into a tight, crushing hug right there in the lobby. "We could never think less of you. We think you're the strongest person we know. But even tanks need treads." Jessica joined the hug, wrapping her arms around his back. "Get in the chair, Captain. That's an order." Freddie let out a long breath. He nodded. "Okay," he whispered. "Chair protocol engaged." He turned and sat. The vinyl seat was cool. As he settled in, the weight came off his spine. The fire in his legs dimmed. He slumped slightly, the relief so profound it almost made him dizzy. "Better?" Jessica asked. "Much better," Freddie admitted. Jessica unlocked the brakes. "Then let's roll." They moved through the exhibits with a new, effortless rhythm. Jessica pushed the chair, her stride confident and smooth. She navigated the crowds like a pro, using the bulk of the chair to clear a path. Paige walked right beside him on the left. She didn't just walk; she connected. She rested her hand on the armrest, her fingers lacing through Freddie’s. It was a physical promise. I am right here. I am not letting go. They passed the jellyfish tank—a tall cylinder of blue light. Freddie leaned back in the chair, his head resting against the canvas, watching the jellies pulse. "No skeleton," Freddie murmured, relaxed. "Pure propulsion." "Like us," Paige smiled, squeezing his hand. "Just moving." They reached the Underwater Dome. The moving walkway carried them into the center of the massive glass sphere. Jessica locked the brakes in the middle of the tunnel. Fish swam everywhere—above them, beside them, below them. The light filtered through twenty feet of water, casting rippling patterns of teal and azure on Freddie’s face. He didn't have to worry about balance. He didn't have to worry about falling. He just sat there, safe in his rolling throne, holding his sister's hand. He looked up. A shark glided over the glass, its white belly visible. "It is a closed system," Freddie whispered. "Biological equilibrium." "It's peaceful," Paige said, leaning her head on his shoulder. "It is weightless," Freddie corrected. "In here... gravity is negotiable." He looked at his hand laced with Paige’s. He looked back at Jessica, who was leaning over the handles, smiling down at him. He realized then that the wheelchair wasn't a defeat. It was just another tool in the Avery inventory. It was a vehicle that let him stay in the fight. "I like the blue," Freddie decided. "It is the opposite of the bus." "Then we stay," Jessica said. "As long as you want. We just float." They stayed in the dome for an hour, the three of them suspended in the blue light, watching the fish circle in their endless, silent orbits, letting the cool water wash away the last of the red alert.

title: Part 5: The Wheelchair Epiphany
content: The hour in the Underwater Dome had been a total reset. The cool blue light, the silent circling of the sharks, and the weightless feeling of the water pressing against the glass had scrubbed the last of the bus vibration from Freddie's bones. But more importantly, the chair had worked. Freddie sat in the blue vinyl wheelchair, his legs relaxed for the first time in four days. He wasn't fighting gravity. He wasn't spending 60% of his processing power just trying to stay upright. He was just... looking. "Time to surface," Jessica announced gently, checking her watch. "The tank is closing." "Acknowledged," Freddie said. Jessica unlocked the brakes. She spun him around with an effortless pivot. As they rolled toward the exit, Paige didn't let go. She walked beside the chair, her hand still resting on the armrest, her fingers laced tightly through his. "You okay?" Paige asked, looking down at him. "I am... efficient," Freddie realized. "The energy cost of this excursion was minimal. If I had walked, I would be in system failure by now. But I am still operational." He looked at the wheels. He thought about Harper, his younger sister back in Virginia Beach. Harper was fourteen. She had cerebral palsy too—mild, like his, but painful. She walked with a limp. She fell a lot. And she was stuck with Ellen. Mom says we just need to try harder, Freddie thought bitterly. She says the chair is giving up. But looking at his sisters—Jessica pushing him without complaint, Paige holding his hand with pride—he realized Ellen was wrong. The chair wasn't giving up. It was a tool. It was a vehicle. "I have a hypothesis," Freddie said quietly as they emerged from the dark exhibit into the bright, overcast afternoon of the pier. "What's that?" Jessica asked, navigating the ramp down to the sidewalk. "The chair," Freddie said, tapping the armrest. "It is not a defeat. It is a strategy. Harper... she struggles. She hurts. Mom makes her walk everywhere." "I know," Paige said, her face darkening. "Mom thinks it builds character." "It builds pain," Freddie corrected. "I think... when we get back... we should tell her. We should tell Harper about the chair." "We'll do better than that," Jessica said firmly. "We'll buy her one." Freddie looked up, surprised. "We can?" "We have the Avery Grant," Jessica reminded him. "Aunt Marge left that money for 'Educational and Medical Necessities.' I think a titanium chariot for Harper counts as a necessity." Freddie smiled. He imagined Harper spinning in a chair like this, fast and purple (her favorite color), instead of limping behind them. "Purple," Freddie decided. "She would want purple." "Done," Paige agreed, squeezing his hand. "Project: Harper's Wheels is a go." They reached the curb. Jessica parked the chair. "Okay, Captain," she said. "We have to leave the rental here. But the lesson stands. If you need wheels, we get wheels." They helped him stand. His legs were stiff, but because he hadn't walked the aquarium, they weren't trembling. He felt strong enough to make the transit back. "One more thing," Paige said, stopping him before they started walking. She looked him dead in the eye, still holding his hand. "About what Vanessa said. About Italy. And New York." Freddie flinched. "We deleted that file." "I want to overwrite it," Paige said fiercely. "Listen to me. If Jessica gets a job in New York... we all go to New York. If I get a fellowship in Italy... we all go to Italy. If you get a job at NASA in Houston... we all go to Houston." She squeezed his fingers until his knuckles cracked. "We are a unit, Freddie. We move together. If one of us relocates, the headquarters relocates. No one gets left behind. Ever." Jessica stepped up on his other side. "I second that motion. The Avery Corporation is a package deal. You don't get one without the other two." Freddie looked at them. The fear that had been gnawing at him since the lobby—the fear that he was holding them back—evaporated. They weren't staying because they were stuck. They were staying because they were a team. "Agreed," Freddie whispered. "The Unit moves as one." "Good," Paige said. "Now let's get out of here. I need a nap."

title: Part 6: The Scar
content: They walked from Pier 59 back toward the Hill Climb elevator. The waterfront was noisy, smelling of diesel from the ferries and frying dough from the tourist stands. Above them, a massive, double-decked concrete structure loomed over the street, blocking out the sky. It roared with the sound of thousands of cars thundering overhead. The Alaskan Way Viaduct. Freddie stopped. He looked up at the grey, stained concrete underbelly of the highway. It was loud. It dripped water. It cut the city off from the sea like a prison wall. "Architecture check," Freddie muttered, wincing at the noise of a truck hitting an expansion joint above. "That structure is... hostile." "It's ugly," Jessica agreed. "It’s like a scar." "It is a barrier," Freddie corrected. "It severs the connection between the urban grid and the hydrological system. It is inefficient. It is loud. It should be removed." "Maybe they'll tear it down one day," Paige said, guiding him toward the elevator. "They should put it underground," Freddie decided. "Like the bus tunnel. Hide the noise. Open the view." They rode the elevator up to the market level, leaving the roar of the Viaduct behind. They walked to the TAPS bus stop on 1st Avenue. A teal-and-white trolleybus was approaching, its electric poles sparking slightly against the overhead wires. "Electric trolley," Freddie noted, pleased. "Route 10. It goes near the hotel." They boarded. The bus was quiet, humming with electric power. Freddie took a window seat. Paige sat next to him, re-establishing the anchor. Jessica sat across the aisle. Freddie looked out the window as they rolled through the city. He saw the buildings. He saw the people. He didn't see a prison anymore. He saw a city that had problems (the Viaduct) and solutions (the Tunnel). Just like him. He looked at his hand, still laced with Paige's. We move as a unit, he thought. Italy. New York. Or just back to the hotel. "Status?" Paige whispered. "Mobility verified," Freddie said. "The chair is... a valid option. I will consider acquisition." "We'll get you a fast one," Jessica promised from across the aisle. "Titanium. Matte black. Like a stealth fighter." Freddie smiled. "Stealth mode," he whispered. "I like that." The electric bus hummed up the street, carrying the Unit back to base, ready for the next day's mission.

title: Part 7: High Voltage
content: The door to Room 412 clicked shut, sealing out the hallway. Freddie wasn't walking. He was suspended between his sisters, his arms draped over their shoulders, his feet dragging slightly on the carpet. The "Hill Climb" from the waterfront—even with the elevator assist—had drained the last reserves of his physical battery. His legs were offline. "Easy," Jessica grunted, adjusting her grip on his waist. "Almost there. Sofa first, then we strip the gear." "You did good, Captain," Paige said, her voice breathless but proud. "See? If you had walked the aquarium, you would have collapsed on the pier. The chair saved your energy for the climb." Freddie nodded weakly, his head lolling against Paige’s shoulder. "Logic... confirmed. Chair was... efficient." They shuffled him into the main living area. To get to the sofa, they had to pass the large picture window. Jessica had left the curtains open earlier to let in the light. As they pivoted Freddie to lower him onto the beige cushions, his head turned. His gaze tracked past the sofa, through the glass, and down to the street below. He saw it. Directly across Stewart Street, inside the open-air bay of the terminal, a massive silver bus was idling. The logo on the side was unmistakable: Pathfinder. Blue diesel smoke curled up from its exhaust pipe, drifting toward the hotel window. The "Overwrite Protocol" failed. The "Good Data" from the aquarium vanished instantly, deleted by the raw, visceral trauma of the visual trigger. Freddie didn't see a vehicle. He saw a cage. He saw the miles of vibration. He saw the bathroom in Pasco. He saw Vanessa dragging him. "Ah!" Freddie yelped. It was a sharp, high-pitched sound of physical pain, as if he had been burned. Then, the air in his lungs compressed. A low, guttural rumble started deep in his chest, vibrating against Paige’s side. It rose in pitch and intensity until it tore out of his throat—a scream of absolute, primal terror. No! No! No! He violently recoiled, trying to twist away from the window, his body spasming so hard he nearly pulled his sisters down. "Freddie!" Jessica shouted, tightening her grip. "THE VESSEL!" Freddie shrieked, his eyes rolling back, lost in the static. "IT IS HERE! IT IS WAITING!" He wasn't in the hotel room anymore. He was back in the terminal. "Code Red!" Paige yelled. "Meltdown! Get him to the bed! NOW!" They abandoned the sofa. They hauled him toward the sleeping area, dragging him as his legs kicked out involuntarily. He was thrashing, fighting them, fighting the air, fighting the invisible restraints of his own mind. They reached the King bed. "Down!" Jessica commanded. They pushed him onto the mattress. Freddie scrambled, trying to curl into a ball, his hands clawing at his ears to block out the sound of the bus engine that only he could hear. He was hyperventilating, short, sharp gasps that sounded like a dying engine. "Restrain him!" Jessica shouted. Paige didn't hesitate. She climbed onto the bed. "On your back, Freddie!" Paige ordered, grabbing his shoulders and forcing him flat. He fought her. Let go! Trap! Trap! "It's me!" Paige screamed over his noise. "It's Paige!" She threw her leg over his hips. She climbed directly on top of him, straddling his waist, then lowered her entire body weight onto his. She pressed her chest against his chest, her stomach against his stomach. She wrapped her arms around his head, pinning his arms to his sides with her elbows. She locked her legs around his thighs. She became a human straitjacket. "Jessica!" Paige gasped. "Shield!" Jessica climbed onto the bed beside them. She didn't pin him; there wasn't room. She sat cross-legged right next to Freddie’s head, placing her hands firmly on his shoulders, adding her weight to the anchor. "We have you," Jessica said, her voice dropping to a low, commanding chant. "We have you. You are in the Silo. You are safe." Freddie bucked beneath Paige. He was strong—hysterical strength fueled by adrenaline. He arched his back, sobbing, a high, keen sound of misery. Get it off! Get it off! "I'm not getting off," Paige whispered fiercely into his ear. She pressed down harder, using gravity to compress his ribcage. "I am the ground wire, Freddie. Send the voltage to me." He was vibrating with electricity. His muscles were rock hard, firing random signals. He tried to turn his head, to bite, to scream, but Paige held him fast. "Breathe," Paige commanded. She exaggerated her own breathing, expanding her chest against his. In. Out. In. Out. "Match me. Find the rhythm." "Paige..." Freddie choked out, his voice broken. "Paige... Paige..." "I'm right here," she promised, locking her arms tighter. "It's Paige. It's just Paige. And Jessica. No one else. The bus is gone." "Vanessa..." he sobbed. "Deleted," Jessica said, stroking his hair with a firm, repetitive motion. "She is gone. She can't get in here. We are the firewall." They held him. They rode the wave of the meltdown. It was violent. It was loud. It was ugly. But they didn't let go. Ten minutes passed. Fifteen. Freddie’s thrashing began to slow. The screams turned into ragged, wet sobs. The electrical storm in his nerves began to ground out into Paige’s body. Twenty minutes. Freddie went limp. His head fell back against the pillow. His hands stopped clawing and uncurled. He lay there, gasping for air, sweat soaking his grey t-shirt. He was exhausted. Physically and mentally depleted. Paige felt his muscles release beneath her. She felt his heart rate drop from 'Critical' to just 'High.' But she didn't move. She knew the protocol. If she got up now—if she removed the weight too quickly—the sudden loss of pressure would trigger a rebound. His system was rebooting; it needed stability. "Holding," Paige whispered to Jessica. "Holding," Jessica confirmed. She kept her hands on his shoulders, wiping the sweat from his forehead with her thumb. Paige kept her arms locked around him. She kept her legs tangled with his. She pressed her cheek against his damp hair. "I'm staying right here," Paige murmured into his ear. "I'm staying until you tell me to move. You are the Captain. You give the signal." Freddie lay under the crushing, saving weight of his sister. He focused on the pressure. It was heavy. It was real. It was the only thing keeping him from floating away. He couldn't speak yet. The words were gone. So he just lay there, safe in the press, waiting for the world to stop spinning.

title: Part 8: The Silent Signal
content: The violence of the storm had passed, leaving behind a heavy, exhausted silence in the hotel room. Freddie lay flat on the mattress, pinned beneath the full weight of his sister. His chest heaved in shallow, ragged hitches, the aftershocks of the scream still rattling his ribs. Paige hadn't moved. She was still lying stomach-to-stomach on top of him, her legs hooked around his thighs, her arms locked around his head. She was a human blanket, heavy and hot and immovable. To his left, Jessica sat cross-legged, her hand resting firmly on his shoulder, her thumb rubbing a slow, rhythmic circle into his deltoid muscle. Safe, Freddie’s brain whispered. Safe. But the logic engine was firing misfires. He wanted to speak. He needed to issue a command. Evacuate, he screamed inside his head. Relocate Base. The perimeter is compromised. The enemy is across the street. He tried to force the words up his throat. He opened his mouth. Nothing. His vocal cords were paralyzed. The "Audio Driver" had crashed during the meltdown, severed by the sheer voltage of the panic. All that came out was a dry, clicking sound at the back of his throat. He squeezed his eyes shut. Tears leaked out, hot and fast. He couldn't tell them. He couldn't tell them that seeing the Pathfinder bus idling in the bay—the exact same model of vehicle that had been his prison for three days—had ripped the scab off his mind. He realized, with a sickening lurch of vertigo, that they had been sleeping here since Friday night. They had been sleeping directly across the street from the scene of the crime. Too close, his mind wailed. Too close to the cage. And then, the second wave hit. It wasn't the panic of the bus this time. It was the weight of the truth. He thought about the note on the counter in Christiansburg. I am setting you free. He thought about Vanessa’s voice in the lobby. They are trapped. You are the black hole. He had believed her. He had walked out the door. He had turned off his phone and left it in Christiansburg. He had almost thrown away the only two people in the universe who understood his code. I almost lost them, Freddie thought. I almost deleted the Unit. The guilt was a physical pain, sharper than the pressure sore on his back. It swamped him. He didn't fight Paige this time. He did the opposite. He freed his hands from where they were pinned at his sides. He reached up. He wrapped his arms around Paige’s back, clutching the fabric of her t-shirt in desperate, clawing handfuls. He pulled her down even harder against him. "Oh," Paige breathed, feeling the shift. "Round Two," Jessica whispered, her hand tightening on his shoulder. "Hold fast." They braced themselves, expecting another thrashing fit. But Freddie didn't thrash. He just broke. A new sound tore out of him—not a scream, but a high, keen whine of absolute misery. He buried his face in the crook of Paige’s neck, soaking her collar with tears. He shook, his whole body vibrating with the force of his remorse. I'm sorry, he tried to say. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. But he was mute. So he just cried. He cried for the boy on the bus. He cried for the sisters he had scared. He cried because he was safe, and he didn't feel like he deserved to be. Paige felt the shift instantly. This wasn't fight-or-flight. This was surrender. "I know," Paige whispered into his ear, her voice thick with emotion. She didn't pull away. She pressed down harder, maximizing the contact. "I know, Freddie. Let it out." She felt his arms crushing her ribs. He was holding onto her like she was the only solid thing in a dissolving world. "We've got you," Jessica murmured, leaning in close so her hair brushed his forehead. "We aren't going anywhere. You can't scare us off, Freddie. We're right here." Freddie sobbed, his chest heaving against Paige’s stomach. He tried to nod, tried to signal that he heard them, but his motor control was offline. He just held on. He locked his fingers together behind Paige’s back, creating an unbreakable loop. Don't let me go, he begged silently. Even if I try to leave... don't let me go. "Never," Paige whispered, as if she could hear his thoughts. "I've got you. I'm never letting go." She laid her cheek on top of his head. She closed her eyes. She settled her weight, prepared to lie there for an hour, a night, or a week—however long it took for the storm to pass and the Captain to find his voice again. Jessica kept her hand on his shoulder, the steady anchor in the sea. They stayed in the pile, three siblings on a hotel bed, riding out the aftershocks of a disaster they had survived together.

title: Part 9: The Restoration
content: The storm in the hotel room had passed, leaving behind a stillness that felt fragile but solidifying. Freddie lay beneath Paige, his chest rising and falling in a slow, rhythmic cadence that finally matched hers. The violent tremors that had racked his body twenty minutes ago had smoothed out into a low-level vibration of exhaustion. Paige was still lying fully on top of him, stomach to stomach, her legs hooked around his thighs, her arms locked around his shoulders. But the quality of the hold had changed. She wasn't restraining a thrashing patient anymore; she was hugging a brother who was holding on for dear life. She felt his arms tighten around her back, his fingers digging into her t-shirt, pulling her down. He likes the weight, Paige realized. He isn't fighting it. He needs it. She didn't move. She let her full weight settle, becoming a human gravity blanket. She pressed her cheek against his damp hair. "We stick together," Paige whispered into the silence, repeating the mantra. "The Unit is solid. No matter what." "Unconditional," Jessica added softly from her spot on the mattress beside them. She rested her hand on Freddie’s arm, her thumb rubbing a slow circle. "We don't leave. We don't quit. We just hold the line." Freddie squeezed his eyes shut. He couldn't speak—the audio driver was still offline—but he squeezed Paige’s ribs in response. Acknowledged. They lay there for a long time, the grey Seattle light fading outside the blackout curtains. The only sound was the air conditioner and the synchronized breathing of the three siblings. Then, a new sound broke the quiet. Gurgle-rumble. It was a deep, resonant protest from Freddie’s stomach. A second later, Paige’s stomach answered with a high-pitched growl of its own. Freddie’s eyes opened. He looked up at Paige. A flicker of awareness returned to his gaze—the "Captain" coming back online, realizing that the "Crew" was running on empty. He tapped Paige’s shoulder twice with his index finger. Tap-tap. The Signal. "Hungry?" Paige asked softly, lifting her head to look at him. Freddie nodded, a small, jerky movement against the pillow. "Okay," Paige said. "That means we have to move. Are you ready for the weight to lift?" Freddie hesitated. He liked the pressure. It was safe. But the biological imperative for fuel was becoming critical. He tapped her shoulder again. Proceed. "Slowly," Jessica commanded. Paige disengaged carefully. She unhooked her legs. She pushed herself up, sliding off him and settling onto the mattress at his side. The loss of pressure was jarring, but Freddie didn't panic. He immediately reached out and grabbed Paige’s hand, lacing their fingers together. "I'm here," Paige promised. "Dinner," Jessica announced, standing up from the bed. "I'm on mess duty." She looked at Freddie. He was lying flat, staring at the ceiling. If she went to the kitchenette, he wouldn't be able to see her. He would lose visual contact with one-third of the Unit. "Reorient," Jessica ordered. "Paige, help him turn. Head to the foot of the bed. Prop him up. I want him to have eyes on the kitchen." "Copy," Paige said. She helped Freddie shift. His legs were heavy and stiff, but together they rotated his body 180 degrees. He leaned back against a stack of pillows at the foot of the King bed. From this vantage point, he had a direct line of sight to the small kitchenette. "Visual confirmed?" Jessica asked, standing by the stove. Freddie nodded. He could see Jessica. He could feel Paige next to him, her arm wrapped around his waist, her head resting on his shoulder. The formation was broken, but the connection was intact. "Menu," Jessica mused, opening the fridge. "We need soft. We need comfort. We need... Grilled Cheese." She pulled out the loaf of soft white bread and the package of mild cheddar slices they had bought at Market Street Grocery. "And tomato soup," she added, grabbing a can from the cupboard. "Classic protocol." Freddie watched her work. The rhythm of her movements—buttering the bread, lighting the burner—was soothing. It was domestic. It was normal. His mind began to drift. He wondered about the time zone. 18:15 PM PST. That was 21:15 PM EST. Back in Virginia, the "Prime Time Block" would be starting. He thought about the show they watched on WNRV. The Local. The bar where "everybody knows your name." He wanted that. He wanted to hear the piano theme song. He wanted to see the wood-paneled bar where people were safe, where they were recognized, where they belonged. He looked at the TV mounted on the wall. He opened his mouth to ask for it. The Local, he tried to say. But his throat just clicked. The words were stuck behind the firewall of the meltdown. He felt a tear leak out of his eye in frustration. Paige felt the tension in his arm. She looked at him. She saw him staring at the blank TV screen with a longing that broke her heart. Tv? Paige guessed softly. Freddie nodded. "You want to watch something?" He nodded again. He tried to hum the theme song, but it came out as a shaky breath. "It's okay," Paige soothed, rubbing his arm. "We'll find something. Jessica, remote?" Jessica tossed the remote onto the bed. Paige picked it up. "Let's see what Seattle has," Paige said, pointing it at the screen. She turned it on. She cycled through the channels. News. Sports. Static. Then, she hit a channel showing a familiar, grainy image. A bar. A tall man drying a glass. A short man walking in the door. "NORM!" the TV audience shouted. Freddie’s breath hitched. They found it. Even here, on the other side of the continent, the signal existed. "The Local," Paige smiled. "Good call, Captain." She put the remote down. Freddie leaned his head against hers. He watched the show. He listened to the laugh track. "Soup's on," Jessica called out. She brought two plates over to the bed. Grilled cheese sandwiches, cut into triangles (no crusts), and mugs of tomato soup. She placed the tray on the mattress between them. "Eat," Jessica commanded gently. "Soft food. Easy chewing." Freddie picked up a triangle. It was warm. It was soft. He took a bite. The cheese was melted perfectly. He looked at the TV where the characters were raising a glass. He looked at Jessica, who had pulled the desk chair over to sit right next to the bed so she could eat with them. He looked at Paige, who was blowing on her soup. He couldn't say the words yet. He couldn't say Thank you or I love you or I'm sorry I tried to leave. But as he dipped his sandwich into the soup, surrounded by his sisters and the glow of the TV, Freddie knew one thing. He was in the place where everybody knew his name. And he was never leaving again.

title: Part 10: The Flight Plan
content: The episode of The Local ended, the piano notes fading into the hum of the air conditioner. The dinner plates were stacked on the nightstand. The city outside was dark, but inside the "Silo," the lighting was warm and low. "Shutdown sequence," Jessica whispered, turning off the TV. They prepared for sleep. There was no hesitation, no modesty. In the aftermath of the meltdown, clothes felt like barriers—layers of friction that prevented the necessary data transfer of heat and safety. They stripped down, leaving their clothes in piles on the floor, and climbed into the massive King bed. The configuration was absolute. Freddie lay in the center. He was exhausted, his body heavy and limp, but his eyes were alert. He watched his sisters settle in. Jessica took the left flank. She lay on her side, pressing her back against his, creating a solid wall between him and the door. Paige took the right flank. She curled into him, draping her leg over his thighs to pin him down, resting her head on his shoulder. She wrapped her arm across his chest, her hand finding Jessica’s hand in the dark. They interlaced their fingers over his heart, locking him in. "We've got you," Paige whispered, her breath warm against his neck. "Defenses are down. No armor. Just us." Freddie let out a long, shaky breath. He felt the skin-to-skin contact—arms, legs, ribs. It wasn't just warmth; it was verification. They are real. They are here. Paige closed her eyes, listening to his heart rate slow down. This was her favorite moment. It wasn't the sightseeing or the jokes; it was this. The moment when the tension left his body. If she could wake up tomorrow morning and know that he had slept through the night—that the night terrors hadn't found him—that would be the greatest victory of her life. Sleep, she willed him silently. Just sleep. But Freddie tapped her arm. Tap-tap. He pointed to the nightstand where Jessica’s laptop sat charging. "You want the computer?" Jessica asked, lifting her head. Freddie nodded. He opened his mouth to explain, but his throat clicked. The mutism was still holding the line. He pointed to his head, then to the machine. Input required. Jessica reached over and grabbed the MagnaByte. She opened it and set it on his stomach, resting it against his bent knees. Freddie opened Quantum Word. The screen glowed white in the dark room. He began to type. His fingers were slow, but deliberate. MISSION PLANNING: MONDAY He looked at them. VECTOR: NORTH. "North?" Paige asked, reading over his shoulder. "Why north?" Freddie typed. VANESSA'S AUNT = KENT. KENT = SOUTH. SOUTH IS COMPROMISED. NORTH IS CLEAN DATA. Jessica nodded, her expression fierce. "Logic is sound. We go North. What’s the target?" Freddie minimized the document and opened the web browser. He navigated to a map of the region north of Seattle—Snohomish County. He found it. A massive gray footprint near an airfield in Everett. The Aerospace Assembly Plant. He clicked the link. The largest building in the world by volume. Home of the 747. He typed again. AEROSPACE FACTORY. SYSTEMS TOUR. I WANT TO SEE THE MACHINE. "Airplanes," Jessica smiled. "Big ones. That works. We can drive the rental car up I-5." Freddie shook his head. He deleted the text. NEGATIVE. TRANSPORT MODE: BUS. Paige stiffened against his side. "Freddie... are you sure? After... everything?" Freddie looked at her. He saw the worry in her blue eyes. He typed fast, the keys clacking softly. PATHFINDER = PRISON. TAPS = FREEDOM. I NEED TO RECLAIM THE CODE. I NEED TO RIDE A BUS WITH THE UNIT. He looked at them. It was the only way to delete the trauma. He had to replace the memory of the old dog from hell with a memory of a clean bus ride with his sisters. He had to prove to himself that the vehicle wasn't the enemy. "You want to overwrite the file," Jessica realized. Freddie nodded. "Okay," Paige said, squeezing him tighter. "We take the bus. We take the commuter express from downtown. We hold your hand the whole way." Freddie smiled. He typed one last line. THANK YOU. END OF LINE. He closed the laptop. Jessica set it on the floor. The room went dark again. "We're going North," Jessica whispered into the silence. "Away from her. Away from the south." "And we're never leaving you," Paige promised, kissing his cheek. "I don't care if we have to move to the North Pole. We stick together. Always." Freddie closed his eyes. He imagined the massive factory. He imagined the bus ride. But mostly, he felt the weight of his sisters holding him down, keeping him safe from the gravity of the past. He slept. And for the first time in four days, he didn't dream of the road.

title: Part 11: The Northern Trajectory
content: The morning broke grey and misty—a classic Pacific Northwest start. Inside the hotel room, the mood was operational. The emotional storm of the previous day had washed away the panic, leaving behind a clear, hard resolve. They dressed for the mission. Freddie put on his jeans and the orange hoodie—reclaiming the armor. Paige and Jessica wore their rain shells. "Objective," Freddie stated, adjusting his glasses in the mirror. "North. Everett. The Factory." "Transport," Jessica replied, checking the TAPS schedule she had grabbed from the lobby rack. "We need the Regional Express Route 510. It’s a commuter line. High frequency. Professional ridership." "Where do we board?" Paige asked. Freddie consulted the map he had studied on the laptop. "The hotel is at 8th and Stewart," Freddie visualized. "The Pathfinder terminal is at 811 Stewart—directly across the street. The Route 510 Northbound stop is one block over. 9th Avenue and Howell Street." "One block," Jessica nodded. "We can do one block." 08:45 AM — Stewart Street They stepped out of the hotel lobby. The air was cool and wet. Directly across the street, the Pathfinder terminal was busy. A bus was idling in the bay, smoke curling from its exhaust. Freddie stopped. He looked at it. He felt Paige’s hand tighten around his. "Don't look," Paige whispered. "No," Freddie said. He looked at the bus. He looked at the dirty windows. He looked at the destination sign: PORTLAND. "It is just a machine," Freddie stated, his voice trembling slightly but firm. "It has no power. We are taking a different machine." He turned his back on the terminal. "Vector: North," he said. They walked one block east to 9th Avenue, then north to Howell. The bus stop sign was sleek and blue, marked TAPS Regional. 08:52 AM — 9th & Howell The bus rounded the corner. It wasn't a grey, dirty coach. It was a clean, white-and-teal articulated bus with the TAPS logo. 510 EVERETT "Boarding," Freddie whispered. He stepped up. He didn't look back. He paid the fare. He walked down the aisle. It smelled of wet raincoats and coffee. It was quiet. People were reading newspapers or looking at their phones. No one was shouting. No one was trapped. Freddie took a window seat on the right side.
