You bought the house in Redmond. I am not letting you drop that kind of cash on a birthday weekend." Cassandra didn't even blink. She pulled the laptop back toward her. She looked at me, her expression radiating the absolute, unyielding financial gravity of an executive who operated on the same floor as William Keswick. "David, it is a single line item in my operational budget," Cassandra stated, her voice calm and absolute. "It is already funded. The only question is, do you love the venue?" I looked at the screen again. The towering scale of the timber. The roaring walk-in fireplaces. The promise of absolute, impenetrable safety for my family. "It's perfect," I admitted quietly. "Then the decision is made," Cass said, turning her attention back to the keyboard. Without a single microsecond of hesitation, Cassandra Vance began filling out the digital booking contract. She agreed to pay the astronomical public price without requesting a single discount. She navigated the strict liability waivers, her legal mind appreciating the draconian, airtight language the Trust used to protect their property. When she reached the final payment gateway, she inputted her name as the primary billing contact: Cassandra Vance. "Booking confirmed," Cass announced, hitting the submit key. The screen flashed green, sealing our fate. "The Prospector's Keep is ours."

title: Part 1: The Checkpoint
content: The harsh fluorescent lights of the Norfolk International Airport departures terminal offered no comfort. It was Saturday morning, and the reality of the twenty-one-day bridge was officially here. We stood at the edge of the TSA security checkpoint. The glowing blue sign reading Ticketed Passengers Only Beyond This Point was a rigid, physical boundary line. Despite knowing the logic, and despite the absolute guarantee of December 17th, Casey’s processor was redlining. The tears she had managed to hold back since Thursday night finally spilled over. She buried her face into my chest, her arms locking around my waist in a vice grip. She was crying hard, the kind of quiet, desperate sobs that made my own chest ache. "It's only three weeks, Casey," I whispered, resting my chin on her head and wrapping my arms around her to provide as much deep-pressure grounding as I possibly could. My own eyes were burning. "Twenty-one days. And then I get you for the whole winter." "It's too long," Casey wept into my jacket. "It is going to feel incredibly long," Cass agreed gently, rolling her manual chair right up next to us. She reached out, resting her hand firmly on Casey’s back. "But the math doesn't lie, Casey. Every single hour that passes is an hour closer to the pack being back together. You can do this." Casey let out one last, shuddering breath and slowly untangled herself from my grip. She wiped her eyes, giving me a brave, fragile nod. Cass reached up, squeezing my hand tightly, before wheeling herself through the security line with Casey right behind her. I stood at the edge of the checkpoint, completely frozen, watching them until they disappeared around the corner toward the gates.

title: Part 2: The Firewall
content: The next three weeks moved in a surreal, regulatory blur. Moving back into Mom’s house in Virginia Beach was the safest logistical move. I threw all of my excess processing power into my classes, burying myself in textbooks and study guides to finish out the semester. But I wasn't alone. Over those three weeks, Meredith, Kate, Morgan, and David Delaney were at my house constantly, visiting me to keep me company. It felt incredible to just exist around them without having to flinch or constantly monitor my own body language. The women would casually hug me, lean against me on the couch, and press deep, lingering kisses to my lips when they arrived and when they left. If only Kristine knew just how deep the pack women actually went. Because of the absolute, barrier-free emotional intimacy of our pack, physical boundaries had dissolved a long time ago. Once we had all turned eighteen—long before I had ever met Kristine—that unconditional love had organically expanded to include deep, physical intimacy. I had already slept with Liz, Meredith, Morgan, and Kate. The only reason the Portsmouth Delaneys weren't on that list was simply logistics; the last time I had seen Erin, Megan, Shannon, and Kelly in Rhode Island, I was still seventeen. There was zero jealousy between any of the women, and because they were all strictly utilizing long-form birth control, there was no anxiety about consequences. It was simply the ultimate extension of pack bonding. Kristine thought a hug at the mall was a threat; she would have completely short-circuited if she knew the truth. Every single night, I was on the phone with Liz. Her voice became my primary tether, talking me down when the separation from her and Casey felt too heavy, while she powered through her own SVU finals in Dayton. But the perimeter Cassandra built was stronger than I knew. I had left my cell phone plugged into the charger on the kitchen counter when I stepped away to use the bathroom. I was washing my hands, the water running over the porcelain sink, completely oblivious to the fact that the screen in the other room had just lit up with Kristine Mercer’s name. Wendy Vance was wiping down the kitchen island when the phone started vibrating against the granite. She glanced at the caller ID. Cassandra’s tactical briefing from Thanksgiving had been absolute. She had laid out every single one of Kristine’s psychological maneuvers, but the detail that had completely enraged my mother was the kitchen incident. The sheer, predatory audacity of Kristine cooking completely naked in front of Casey—forcing my highly sensitive, youngest sister into an incredibly distressing and inappropriate situation—had crossed a line Wendy was not willing to forgive. My mother picked up the phone and pressed the green accept button. "David?" Kristine’s voice drifted through the speaker, coated in that familiar, sugary-sweet register she always used when she wanted something. "I miss you. Can we just talk about—" "David is not available," Wendy interrupted. Her voice wasn't raised, but it was forged from absolute, freezing steel. There was a sudden, jarring pause on the other end of the line. "Oh. Hi, Mrs. Vance. I was just hoping to catch David for a minute so we could clear some things up." "There is nothing to clear up, Kristine," Wendy fired back, her grip tightening on the phone. "And you will not be speaking to my son. Not today, not ever." "I... excuse me?" Kristine stammered, her customer-service mask slipping as she tried to recalibrate. "I just want to talk to my boyfriend." "He is not your boyfriend," Wendy stated, every syllable clipped and lethal. "And you listen to me very carefully. Cassandra told me exactly what happened on Thanksgiving. She told me exactly what you did in that apartment." The silence on Kristine's end was deafening. "Did you really think I wouldn't find out?" Wendy continued, her maternal fury finally uncoiling. "Did you think you could just strip down naked in the kitchen right in front of Casey and nobody was going to say anything? My youngest daughter was trapped in that room with you, and you intentionally subjected her to that disgusting, inappropriate display just to mark your territory." "I—that's not—" Kristine tried to stammer out a defense, her voice trembling as the reality of being caught completely leveled her. "Do not interrupt me," Wendy snapped, bringing the hammer down. "You tried to isolate my son, you tried to manipulate him, and you humiliated my daughter. You are toxic, you are deeply unwell, and you are entirely unwelcome in this family. If you ever try to contact David again, or if you ever come anywhere near him, Cassandra and I will make sure it is the biggest mistake of your life. Lose this number." I walked out of the bathroom just in time to see my mother pull the phone away from her ear, hit the red 'end call' button with extreme prejudice, and immediately navigate to the settings to permanently block the contact. She set the phone face-down on the counter, took a deep, steadying breath, and picked her dish towel back up as if she hadn't just completely obliterated my ex-girlfriend. She looked up and saw me standing in the hallway. "Spam call," Wendy said smoothly, though the fierce, protective fire was still burning brightly in her eyes. "I took care of it."

title: Part 1: Burton Station Road
content: The calendar eventually surrendered. On the afternoon of December 17th, the moment my final exam at the community college concluded, my mother was waiting for me in the parking lot. But Wendy Vance didn't drive us back to her house. She bypassed the highway exits for the main public terminal of Norfolk International Airport and instead navigated her standard sedan down Burton Station Road, pulling up to the discrete, heavily gated General Aviation terminal. I sat in the passenger seat, staring through the chain-link fence at the private tarmac. With Kristine’s toxic surveillance permanently eradicated from my life, Cassandra had absolutely zero reason to hide her leverage. She had completely abandoned the commercial charade. A sleek, twin-engine corporate jet touched down and taxied directly toward our gated perimeter. When the cabin door opened and the hydraulic accessible ramp deployed, Casey practically bounced down to the tarmac. She was clutching her duffel bag, her eyes wide with absolute, unfiltered awe. It was her first time ever flying on a private corporate jet, and the sheer scale of the luxury had left my seventeen-year-old sister completely stunned. Cassandra wheeled herself down the ramp right behind her, looking entirely composed and unbothered, her heavy messenger bag resting on her lap. I jumped out of Mom's car and met them at the gate. Casey collided with me, wrapping her arms fiercely around my neck for a massive, deep-pressure hug. The physical contact sent a shockwave of relief through my system. The twenty-one days of isolation were officially over. "This beats commercial First Class by a mile," Casey rasped into my shoulder, vibrating with excitement. "Quantum's logistics desk actually wanted to route our flight path into PVG over in Chesapeake," Cassandra noted casually, rolling up to the car and offering Mom a warm, familiar smile. "But I told them ORF was vastly superior. PVG is too far of a drive for you, Mom, especially with the High Rise Bridge traffic. Burton Station Road is much closer to home." "Well, I appreciate the executive override," Mom laughed, helping us load the bags into the trunk. We drove back to Virginia Beach, the east-coast consolidation of our pack finally underway. But the perimeter wasn't quite complete yet.

title: Part 2: The Flight Data
content: The drive back to Virginia Beach operated on a completely different frequency than the tense, quiet car rides of November. With Mom navigating the afternoon traffic and Cassandra sitting comfortably in the front passenger seat, the backseat belonged entirely to me and Casey. The moment the car doors closed, Casey leaned heavily against my shoulder, seeking her baseline physical grounding while simultaneously offloading a massive stream of rapid-fire data. She was practically vibrating with excitement, her hands animating every single detail of the cross-country flight. "David, you cannot even comprehend the logistical efficiency," Casey began, her voice slightly raspy but moving at lightning speed. "On Thanksgiving, we had to wait in that massive TSA line, take our shoes off, and sit at the gate with hundreds of people. The ambient noise alone was exhausting. But today? We just rolled straight up to the plane. There was zero friction." I laughed, wrapping my arm around her and pulling her closer. "Zero friction sounds exactly like a Cass operation." "It's entirely different architecture inside, too," Casey continued, her dark eyes wide as she twisted slightly to look at me. "Commercial First Class is just wider seats in rows. But the corporate jet has these massive, swiveling leather captain's chairs. You can actually turn around and face a mahogany table. Cass had her laptop out, doing Quantum server reviews, and I had an entire couch to myself in the back!" From the front seat, Cassandra glanced in the rearview mirror, offering a fond, satisfied smile as she listened to her younger sister break down the executive perks. "And the cabin pressure," Casey added, tapping my arm to emphasize the structural difference. "It's pressurized to a much lower altitude than a standard commercial airliner. My ears didn't pop once. There were no overhead announcements interrupting us, no strangers bumping into the armrests. Just total, uninterrupted quiet all the way across the country." "Did they at least give you those tiny bags of pretzels?" I joked, leaning my head against hers. Casey scoffed playfully, waving the idea away. "David, there was a dedicated flight attendant. For just the two of us. She brought out actual, hot catering on ceramic plates. I had a perfectly grilled chicken wrap and fresh fruit while we flew over the Rocky Mountains. It was flawless." I just sat there, smiling and absorbing her sheer, unfiltered joy. Hearing her completely dissect the mechanical and hospitality differences between the two flights was the exact anchor my system had been starving for. She wasn't carrying an ounce of the fear or hesitation that Kristine had forced into our environment just three weeks prior. "Well, get used to the layout, Case," Cassandra called back from the front seat, her tone completely matter-of-fact. "Because when we fly back to Washington on Monday, all four of us are getting on that exact same plane." Casey gasped, grabbing my hand and squeezing it tightly. "You and Liz are going to love it," she promised fiercely. "It's the ultimate perimeter."

title: Part 3: The Honorary Sister
content: By the time the winter sun had fully set over Virginia Beach, the anticipation in Mom's living room had reached a fever pitch. I was sitting on the sofa with Casey tucked securely against my side. We were watching a movie, but my internal clock was violently counting down the seconds. The twenty-one-day bridge was functionally over, but my system wouldn't fully settle until the final piece of the perimeter was physically in the room. Suddenly, a double set of headlights swept across the living room blinds. "She's here," I breathed, my heart hammering against my ribs. I practically bolted off the cushions. Under any other circumstance, abruptly breaking my physical proximity without warning would have sent Casey’s processor into an immediate tailspin. She relied on me as her primary anchor, and losing that deep-pressure contact usually triggered a wave of intense distress. But Liz Carter was the single, absolute exception to the rule. Liz was the only person on the planet who could pull my attention entirely away from Casey without causing my little sister to panic. Because Liz wasn't a threat to the pack—she was the pack. Casey didn't view Liz as someone taking her brother away; she viewed Liz as an extension of our safe space. Casey simply smiled, pulling her knees to her chest as I rushed for the front door. I threw the door open and sprinted down the concrete steps. Liz put her parents' sedan into park just as the heavy air brakes of a rented moving truck hissed loudly behind her, signaling that her mother and father had successfully completed the convoy from the Shenandoah Valley. Liz threw her car door open and ran across the driveway. We collided in the cold night air, her arms wrapping fiercely around my neck, pulling me into a breathless, desperate hug. The sheer relief of feeling her in my arms sent a massive, regulating shockwave through my entire system. "I've got you," Liz whispered fiercely into my ear, burying her face in my shoulder. "I told you I was coming." "I missed you so much," I choked out, refusing to let her go. When we finally pulled apart, the rest of the family was waiting on the porch. The dynamic was seamless. Even though Liz shared absolutely zero blood relation with us, the Vance family treated her exactly like a sister. Liz jogged up the steps and immediately knelt down to wrap Casey in a massive hug, which Casey happily returned. Cassandra wheeled forward, offering Liz a warm, deeply affectionate embrace, while my mother walked down the steps to greet Mr. and Mrs. Carter with open arms. The rest of the evening was a blur of joyous, insulated family time. We hauled a small mountain of delivery pizza boxes into the kitchen to feed both families. The Carters were incredibly supportive, treating Liz's cross-country move not as a disruption, but as the natural, inevitable evolution of our lives. As we all crowded into the living room with our paper plates, the layout of the pack naturally engaged. I sat on the floor, my back resting against the front of the sofa. Casey immediately sat down on my left side, leaning her weight against my ribs, while Liz sat on my right, resting her head on my shoulder. I was perfectly sandwiched between my favorite girl and my best friend, eating a slice of pizza while listening to Cassandra and Mr. Carter discuss the logistics of the moving truck. The perimeter was locked. My system was flawless. For the first time in what felt like a lifetime, I had absolutely everything I needed right in the palm of my hand.

title: Part 4: The Moving Logistics
content: With the pizza boxes cleared away, the conversation naturally shifted to the sheer mechanics of hauling Liz's life across the country. Mr. Carter pulled out a notepad, ready to outline the driving shifts for the rental truck, but Cassandra raised a hand, smoothly intercepting the planning phase. "You don't need to drive that truck to Washington," Cassandra stated, her executive tone cutting through the logistical chatter. "I have already retained a bonded, commercial moving service. They will be here tomorrow morning to take possession of the cargo. They are hauling everything to a climate-controlled storage facility I secured near the Federal Way apartment." Liz blinked, stunned by the frictionless solution. "Cass, you didn't have to do that." "The apartment is a two-bedroom layout, Liz. We don't have the square footage to absorb a truckload of furniture right now," Cassandra reasoned pragmatically. "Quantum's network handled the contracting. It is already paid for." With the immediate transit logistics resolved, the tone in the living room subtly shifted. The adults—Mom, Tom, and the Carters—were all sitting together, and Cassandra decided it was time to officially close out the operational debrief from the holiday. Cassandra didn't raise her voice, but she commanded the absolute attention of the room as she laid out exactly what had happened on Thanksgiving Day. Being mindful of the younger siblings in the room, she kept her language clinical and precise, summarizing the deeply inappropriate, territorial display Kristine had orchestrated in the kitchen. She explained the sheer hostility of the boundary violation, how Kristine had intentionally forced a minor into a highly distressing situation just to assert dominance over the apartment. As Cassandra spoke, I felt a heavy, residual spike of guilt hit my chest. I looked down at the floor, my shoulders slumping as the memory of the extraction washed over me. Liz intercepted the guilt instantly. She shifted on the floor, wrapping her arms securely around my neck, and immediately pulled Casey into the embrace from my other side. Casey didn't hesitate, burying her face against my shoulder as Liz locked us into a tight, three-way hug. "None of that was your fault, David," Liz whispered fiercely, her voice radiating absolute certainty. "She's right," Casey added softly, her cheek pressed against my collarbone. "I was never mad at you. I was just scared of her. But you're safe now." The absolute, unconditional forgiveness from the two women I loved most in the world completely pulverized the lingering shame. By the time ten o'clock rolled around, the travel exhaustion had finally caught up to all of us. Because my childhood bedroom and the room Casey had grown up in were both located on the second floor of the house, the stairs presented a hard, physical boundary. Cassandra’s severe 1999 axial load injury meant she couldn't navigate the staircase. "I'm claiming the sofa tonight," Cassandra announced, locking the brakes on her manual chair near the coffee table. "You three go get some sleep." I leaned down, wrapping my arms around my older sister for a long, grounding hug. Liz and Casey followed suit, exchanging warm, fiercely affectionate goodnights before the three of us headed for the stairs. We walked down the familiar upstairs hallway, stopping right between our two bedroom doors. Casey looked up at me, her dark eyes heavy with sleep but entirely free of the anxiety that had plagued her in November. We exchanged one last, deep-pressure hug. "Goodnight, David. Goodnight, Liz," Casey smiled, before slipping into her childhood bedroom and softly clicking the door shut. Liz took my hand, her fingers lacing naturally through mine, and followed me into my room. I shut the door, enclosing us in the quiet, absolute safety of my childhood sanctuary. It was the first time I was going to share a bed with anyone since the extraction, and the fact that it was my childhood best friend completely eradicated any lingering nervous tension. The transition into the space was seamless. Because we had spent virtually our entire lives in each other's orbits, there was zero hesitation or awkwardness. We moved around the room comfortably, getting undressed in front of each other just like we had countless times before, the vulnerability entirely natural. Liz pulled her t-shirt over her head, her eyes catching mine across the dim room. She paused, reading the quiet, shifting frequency of my baseline. "How are you feeling?" Liz asked softly, stepping closer. I swallowed hard, looking down at her. "I'm okay. I just... I really missed certain things we did last summer." Liz’s expression softened into a warm, profoundly understanding smile. She knew exactly what I meant. The deep, physical intimacy we had established before the fall semester had been a massive anchor for my system, and I had been entirely starved of that unconditional connection. She stepped directly into my space, resting her hands gently against my chest. "I'm still on my birth control, David," she murmured, her thumb lightly tracing my collarbone. "We have all the time in the world. We can go exactly at your pace." I nodded, a massive wave of relief and overwhelming affection crashing over me as I pulled her into a tight, grounding embrace. "My pace is right now." Liz wrapped her arms around my torso, her cheek resting against my bare chest. She didn't press for a kiss—we had never needed that specific physical mechanic to translate how we felt. Instead, she shifted just enough to glance over my shoulder toward the second-floor window. "Show me," Liz whispered softly, her fingers tracing a light, soothing pattern down my spine. "You haven't talked about the sky in months." Kristine had hated my astronomy hyperfixation, constantly shutting me down or rolling her eyes whenever I tried to explain orbital mechanics or constellation shifts. She had actively trained me to repress it. But Liz was deliberately pulling it back out, inviting my true baseline back into our shared space. I turned my head, following her gaze out the front window. From the second floor, looking out over the intersection of Pope and Delaney, the window faced directly southeast. The massive tree in the front yard had shed all its leaves for the winter, its bare branches acting like a dark silhouette framing the crisp, cloud-speckled night sky. The temperature outside had dropped into the low forties, but inside the room, anchored entirely by Liz's proximity, the cold didn't exist. "Orion," I murmured, the familiar, comforting data points easily flooding back into my processor as I looked at the southeast sky. "Right through the center branches. The three stars in the belt are perfectly aligned tonight. And just below it, you can barely see the faint glow... that's the Orion Nebula." "It's beautiful," Liz said, her voice a warm, steady hum against my collarbone. She pulled me down onto the mattress, the heavy winter blankets wrapping securely around us. As I settled into the familiar, deeply regulating weight of her body against mine, the astronomy data quietly faded into the background. I didn't need to look out the window anymore. The only thing left to process was the profound, absolute safety of my best friend, the quiet rustle of the sheets, and the undeniable reality that the isolation was finally over.

title: Part 1: The Morning Knock
content: The pale morning light filtering through the blinds of my childhood bedroom was the first thing to pull me out of sleep. Liz was a warm, heavy weight across my chest, her breathing perfectly steady in the quiet room. For the first time in three weeks, my internal processor wasn't running a frantic, defensive loop. I was completely, deeply anchored. Then, a soft, polite tapping echoed from the bedroom door. "David?" Casey’s slightly raspy morning voice filtered through the wood. "Are you guys awake?" "Yeah, we're awake," I called back, my voice still thick with sleep. "Just give us a second, Case!" Beside me, Liz’s eyes flew open. The haze of sleep vanished instantly as we both became acutely aware that we were completely bare beneath the heavy winter blankets. From the hallway, a sharp, unmistakable giggle vibrated through the drywall. "Take your time!" Casey chirped happily, entirely lacking any social filter. "I heard the muffled noises through the wall last night. I know exactly what you guys were doing!" Liz’s face instantly flushed a brilliant, furious shade of red, and she buried her face into the nearest pillow with a muffled groan. I felt a massive wave of heat crawl up the back of my own neck, my face burning as I realized my childhood bedroom shared a very thin wall with Casey’s. "We'll be right out, Casey!" I managed to shout back, my voice cracking slightly. We scrambled out from under the covers, frantically digging through our duffel bags for fresh clothes. Once we were both fully dressed and sufficiently decent, I walked over and pulled the bedroom door open. Casey didn't hesitate for a microsecond. She launched herself forward, wrapping her arms around my torso in a crushing, deep-pressure squeeze. I hugged her back just as fiercely, resting my chin on top of her head. "Good morning," Casey beamed, stepping back to pull Liz into a massive hug next. Her dark eyes were practically vibrating with excitement, the awkwardness of her hallway commentary completely overridden by her hyper-focus on the day's itinerary. "I am so ready to go to the airport. You guys are going to absolutely lose your minds when you see the corporate jet. It is the ultimate perimeter." "I can't wait," Liz laughed, her cheeks still slightly pink as she hugged my little sister back. "Let's go get some breakfast."

title: Part 2: The Flight Logistics
content: We headed downstairs, guided by the smell of bacon and pancakes filling the house. Mom and Tom were moving around the kitchen, pulling massive plates of food out of the oven to feed the crowded house one last time before our cross-country move. Cassandra was already stationed at the kitchen island. Her travel wheelchair was locked in place, and her silver laptop was open next to a steaming mug of dark roast coffee. "Good morning," Cass smiled warmly, closing her laptop as we walked into the room. I walked over and leaned down to give her a tight hug, which Liz and Casey immediately followed. The pack was fully assembled, and the ambient energy in the kitchen was perfectly synchronized. As we piled our paper plates high with breakfast and took our seats around the living room and kitchen island, Cass shifted smoothly into her logistical baseline. "Alright, let's review the transit architecture for today," Cassandra announced, looking directly at me and Liz. "We are not going to the main public terminal at Norfolk International. We are bypassing the commercial TSA lines entirely. Mom is going to drop us off at the private executive aviation facility on the far side of the airfield." Liz paused, her fork hovering over her plate. "Wait, we just walk right onto the tarmac?" "Exactly," Casey chimed in proudly, bouncing slightly on her heels. "Zero friction. No crowds, no waiting." "The pilots filed our flight plan an hour ago," Cass continued, adjusting her glasses. "We are flying direct on one of Quantum's long-range corporate jets. But we are not landing at Sea-Tac. Commercial hubs are a logistical nightmare, especially during the holiday rush." "So where are we landing?" I asked, my processor rapidly trying to map the Seattle-area airports. "BFI. Boeing Field," Cass stated with absolute executive finality. "It is a specialized airfield just south of downtown Seattle. It allows us to land, deplane directly into a waiting armored black-car, and be on the highway to the Federal Way apartment in under five minutes." I looked over at Liz. Her eyes were wide with quiet awe. For a couple of nineteen-year-old college students who had spent the last three weeks stressing over standard community college exams and highway driving routes, the sheer, staggering scale of Cassandra's corporate leverage was almost impossible to comprehend. "Boeing Field," I repeated, a massive grin breaking across my face. "Eat up," Cassandra smiled, reopening her silver laptop. "We have a plane to catch, and I want my family under my roof by dinner time."

title: Part 3: The Sovereign Airspace
content: Once we reached cruising altitude, the seatbelt sign chimed off, and the true scale of the aircraft's interior became apparent. It didn't feel like a plane; it felt like a high-end corporate boardroom wrapped in cream-colored leather and polished mahogany. Cassandra didn't waste a single minute. She wheeled herself away from the forward lockdown track and positioned her chair at the head of the massive mid-cabin conference table, flipping open her silver laptop. "David, Elizabeth, grab a seat," Cass instructed, her tone dropping into her familiar, efficient baseline. "We need to finalize your educational logistics before we land." Liz and I sank into the plush leather captain's chairs across from her. "You are both enrolling at Northwest Pacific University, specifically the main Seattle campus, for the Winter Quarter starting in January," Cass stated, pulling up a web browser. "I am paying your out-of-state tuition entirely out-of-pocket, so we don't have to wait a year for residency requirements. We just need to get your applications filed today." Liz stared at Cassandra’s screen, completely bewildered. "Wait... are we online right now? Up here?" "Enterprise-grade, in-flight satellite Wi-Fi," Casey chimed in from the window seat, entirely used to her sister's bleeding-edge tech ecosystem. "Quantum doesn't do dead zones." Liz just shook her head in quiet awe. Cass efficiently guided us through the NPU portal, helping us set up our student accounts and walking us through the application forms. When it came to the permanent residence section, she dictated her Federal Way apartment address for both of us, officially locking in our new West Coast perimeter. As soon as the forms were complete, Cass pulled a sleek card from her wallet and paid both application fees directly over the secure connection. By the time the applications were submitted, the smell of roasted chicken and fresh vegetables began wafting from the forward galley. It was lunchtime. For Liz and me, eating a hot, high-end catered meal on a private jet was a surreal, staggering first. For Casey, it was just her second time experiencing Quantum's aviation hospitality, but she dug in with just as much enthusiasm. As I ate, I looked around the mahogany table. Liz was sitting next to me, our knees touching. Casey was happily chatting about her high school classes. Cassandra was sipping a sparkling water, reviewing a deployment spreadsheet. My internal processor ran a quick diagnostic and returned absolute, profound peace. The pack was reunited for good. And the absolute best part? There was no Kristine. I let out a sudden, involuntary laugh. "What's so funny?" Liz asked, pausing with her fork halfway to her mouth. "I just pictured Kristine's face," I chuckled, shaking my head. "If she could see me right now. She probably thought I'd be stuck flying commercial into SEA in coach. Instead, I'm eating roasted chicken on a private corporate jet flying direct to Boeing Field." Cassandra offered a sharp, satisfied smirk without looking up from her screen. "Let her imagine whatever she wants. She no longer exists on our grid." Cass wiped her mouth with a linen napkin and pushed her plate aside. "Alright, I have to actually get some work done for the rest of this flight. When we land at BFI, Quantum has a wheelchair-accessible van waiting on the tarmac to take us down to the Federal Way apartment." "Is that how you normally get around?" I asked, looking at the sheer luxury of our current setup. "A private driver in a customized van?" "Absolutely not," Cass replied immediately, her disdain for operational friction bleeding through. "There are rumors floating around Building 33 that I'm being groomed as William Keswick's heir, which is ridiculous. I'm twenty-six years old and I've only been at the company for four years. But even if I had access to a dedicated driver every day, I wouldn't use it. You have to book it, schedule it, and hope dispatch doesn't screw up the timing. I much prefer the city bus. I can just show up at the bus stop on my own schedule, deploy the ramp, and ride. True autonomy doesn't require a reservation."

title: Part 4: The Global Reach
content: With Cassandra fully locked into her executive workflow at the conference table, Casey took it upon herself to act as our official tour guide. "Come here, I have to show you guys the back," Casey whispered loudly, grabbing my hand and pulling me and Liz toward the aft section of the cabin. She led us past another set of plush captain's chairs and gestured proudly to a long, luxurious leather divan that took up an entire wall of the lounge. "It folds out into a completely flat bed," Casey explained, her eyes wide with excitement. "Because this jet is built for ultra-long-haul flights. Cass and I have already taken it to Tokyo, London, and Sydney. You just go to sleep, and when you wake up, you're on another continent." "That is unbelievable," Liz breathed, gently running her hand over the premium leather. "Where else can it go? Could we go to Dubai?" From the mid-cabin conference table, without breaking her typing rhythm or even looking away from her glowing screen, Cassandra’s voice drifted back to us. "Veto," Cass stated with absolute, glacial finality. "We are not flying to the Middle East. As long as I am the one charting the flight plans, I will not subject the women in this pack to countries where our basic human rights and autonomies are treated as conditional. We have the range to go anywhere on the planet; we'll stick to grids where we are legally respected." Casey grinned at me, entirely used to her sister's fiercely protective, unyielding worldview. "Well, Europe it is, then."

title: Part 5: The I-5 Crawl
content: A few hours later, the heavy winter clouds of the Pacific Northwest parted just enough for the jet to break through the gray canopy. We banked smoothly over the Seattle skyline, bypassing the commercial chaos of Sea-Tac entirely, and touched down on the long runway at Boeing Field. The transfer was an absolute masterpiece of logistics. The jet taxied directly to a private hangar, the mechanical ramp deployed, and Cassandra wheeled herself effortlessly down to the wet tarmac. The Quantum wheelchair-accessible van was idling ten feet away. Within minutes, the driver had engaged the motorized lift, secured Cass inside, loaded our luggage, and we were pulling out of the airfield gates. Liz and I exchanged a look of pure amazement in the backseat. We hadn't stood in a single line, touched a single piece of luggage, or waited for a single shuttle. But as the van merged onto Interstate 5 South, the reality of Seattle's geography immediately hit us. The early winter sunset was already plunging the city into a dreary twilight. As we approached the massive, sprawling interchange where I-5 collided with I-405 and State Route 518 in Tukwila, all southbound lanes were gridlocked in a sea of red brake lights. "Massive collision ahead on the Interstate," the driver announced over his shoulder, tapping the GPS display on the dashboard. "I-5 South is completely blocked. I'm taking the SR-518 exit to reroute us onto SR-99. We can take 99 all the way down into Federal Way. It's going to be stop-and-go for a while." "Don't worry about the traffic," Cassandra noted from the front, watching the endless line of cars with complete apathy. She had fully anticipated the delay. "We are inside the perimeter now. We don't have to be anywhere else." I leaned my head back against the plush leather seat, Casey resting warmly against my shoulder, and watched the Seattle rain streak across the tinted windows. My phone was resting on my thigh. I looked down at the blank screen, and then over at Liz. For the first time since September, my heart wasn't racing. I didn't have a low-level, background anxiety constantly monitoring the environment to see who was watching. My operational protocols were completely offline. "I don't have to hide my phone anymore," I whispered into the quiet hum of the van. Liz turned to look at me, her expression softening. "No," she said gently. "You don't." "It's weird," I admitted, my voice tight as the sheer gravity of the last few months finally hit me. "I spent the entire fall treating you like a classified document. I partitioned my entire life just to keep Kristine from crying. I honestly thought I was just being a good boyfriend, making compromises to protect her." "She wasn't asking for compromises, Davey," Liz said, reaching over to squeeze my hand. "She was asking for control. You don't have to protect anyone's insecurities ever again." From the front seat, Cassandra didn't turn around, but her voice drifted back to us with clinical precision. "Your firewall was mathematically flawed from the beginning, David. You cannot stabilize a toxic algorithm by feeding it more isolation. The only solution is a hard sever." "I know," I breathed, feeling the last remaining knot in my chest finally dissolve. I didn't care how bad the traffic was on Pacific Highway. The rain was drumming against the roof, the heater was running, and I was sitting right next to my best friend without looking over my shoulder. My pack was finally, permanently, home.

title: Part 1: The Social Boundary
content: By the time the Quantum van finally escaped the gridlock of Pacific Highway and pulled up to the Federal Way apartment complex, the winter sun had completely set. We hauled our luggage out of the vehicle, thanked the driver, and took the elevator up to Cassandra's floor. The moment the front door unlocked and our heavy travel bags were dropped onto the living room floor, Casey’s excitement reached a boiling point. She didn't even take her winter coat off. She simply grabbed my hand, her grip incredibly tight, and physically dragged me down the short hallway. "Come here, you have to see my room!" Casey insisted, pulling me through the second doorway. I stumbled in behind her, laughing as she dramatically gestured to her space. It was a perfectly organized, cozy room that clearly belonged to a seventeen-year-old, but the centerpiece was a massive, incredibly comfortable-looking queen-sized bed. "Look at how much space there is!" Casey beamed, dropping my hand and bouncing backward onto the mattress. She looked up at me, her dark eyes shining with the pure, unadulterated hope of having her safe person back in her daily routine. "David, you should just sleep in here with me tonight. It'll be exactly like when we were kids. We can just pile up all the blankets and you can hold me." Before I could even process the logistics of the apartment's sleeping arrangements, the quiet hum of rubber tires on the carpet signaled Cassandra's arrival. Cass wheeled herself into the doorway, with Liz stepping in right behind her. Cass’s expression was incredibly gentle, but her executive baseline was fully engaged. "He can't do that, Case," Cassandra said softly, parking her manual chair in the doorframe. Casey’s face immediately fell, her brow furrowing in confusion. "Why not? The bed is huge. He fits." "It has nothing to do with the square footage," Cassandra explained, navigating the emotional landmine with absolute precision. "It has to do with how the outside world interprets things, Casey. I personally have absolutely no issue with you two sharing a bed. Even Liz is entirely okay with it. We all know there is absolutely nothing inappropriate about you needing deep-pressure comfort from your brother." Cassandra wheeled forward just an inch, making sure she had Casey's complete understanding. "But you are seventeen years old, and David is a nineteen-year-old legal adult. If someone outside this family were to find out, they might assume inappropriate things are happening. We cannot risk anyone misunderstanding the situation and causing trouble for David or for you. It's just a social boundary we have to respect for now." Casey stared at Cassandra, the heavy reality of the outside world's perception sinking in. She understood the math. The perimeter had to remain absolutely flawless to protect David. Liz stepped around Cassandra's chair, walking over to the edge of the queen bed. She sat down next to Casey, wrapping an arm warmly around my little sister's shoulders. "But here is the best part about the calendar," Liz smiled, bumping her shoulder gently against Casey's. "You were born on May 25th, 1987. Which means that on May 25th of this coming year, you are officially turning eighteen. The absolute second you are a legal adult, no one can say a word about it. Those rules will no longer matter. Until then, we just have to play it safe." Casey took a deep breath, processing the data, and finally gave a small, resolute nod. "Okay. May 25th."

title: Part 2: Comfort Food and The Ledger
content: Casey eagerly grabbed one end of the heavy sofa cushions while Liz took the other. Together, we dragged the mattress frame out from the depths of the couch. The metal springs groaned, unfolding to take up nearly the entire footprint of the small living room. "I think we just leave this out permanently," I suggested, tossing a heavy blanket over the mattress. "It’s going to be a tight squeeze in this apartment for the next few weeks, but it saves us having to fold it up every single morning." "Agreed," Liz smiled, smoothing the sheets down. "We'll see how apartment living goes. I honestly don't care if it takes up the whole floor, as long as we're all together." Right on cue, Cassandra wheeled herself out of the kitchen, carefully balancing a tray on her lap. "Dinner is served," she announced, a warm, genuine smile breaking across her face. She handed out massive, steaming bowls of the ultimate childhood comfort food: thick macaroni and cheese mixed with sliced, cheesy hot dogs. But it was the drinks she passed out next that made my processor stall for a fraction of a second. She handed me a tall, ice-cold glass of whole milk. For the last three months, Kristine’s lactose intolerance had dictated every item in the pantry, forcing me to eat dry cereal and completely eliminating milk from my diet. Sitting on the edge of the pulled-out sofa bed, holding a glass of milk and a bowl of mac and cheese, the stark contrast between Kristine’s restrictive control and my sister's unconditional hospitality hit me like a wave. I took a long drink, feeling a profound sense of relief wash over my system. We all sat cross-legged on the edge of the mattress and the floor, eating in comfortable, easy silence for a few minutes before Cassandra shifted into her logistical baseline. "Now that we are all physically consolidated, we need to update the financial architecture," Cassandra explained, setting her bowl on the end table. She looked directly at me. "David, I am officially stopping the ACH transfers." I blinked, momentarily surprised. While I had been isolated in Virginia, she had been using Quantum's internal payroll portal to automatically route a portion of her pay directly into my checking account via ACH transfer. "I am not cutting off your support," Cassandra clarified instantly, sensing my momentary confusion. "This is strictly a maneuver to bypass the IRS. Because the annual total I was sending you exceeded the IRS gift tax exclusion limit for 2005, my CPA firm had to silently file Form 709 in the background. Every dollar over the limit deducts the excess from my lifetime exemption. I refuse to needlessly burn through that cap." "So how does it work now?" Liz asked, genuinely fascinated by how Cassandra treated the federal tax code like a solvable software bug. "Now that David is living under my roof, the legal classification changes," Cass explained smoothly. "I will simply absorb your daily living expenses directly at the point of sale. However, I am not always going to be at your side. You and Liz will be on the NPU campus taking classes, and you will need to buy lunch, supplies, and your monthly TAPS Passes." Cassandra pulled two sleek, metallic cards from her pocket and set them on the table. "I have already ordered authorized user cards in both of your names," Cass stated. "They are linked directly to my primary accounts. If you need something, you swipe the card. It bypasses the gift tax entirely and ensures you maintain total operational autonomy when I am at work." "Thank you, Cass," I said softly, completely overwhelmed by the sheer, friction-less safety net she had engineered for us. "Speaking of school," Casey chimed in proudly, practically vibrating with excitement as she scooped up a bite of hot dogs. "I got my progress reports back yesterday. Straight A's in every single class. My calculus teacher said I have the highest average in the district." "That is incredible, Case!" Liz beamed, reaching over to give Casey a high-five. "You are going to completely destroy college next year." "I expect nothing less," Cass smiled, radiating absolute pride for our younger sister. "What about you, Cass?" I asked, leaning back against the sofa cushions. "What's going on at Quantum? Any big deployments?" Cassandra, who works in Building 33 alongside Quantum's founder William Keswick, let out a rare, exasperated sigh and rolled her eyes. "The deployments are fine," she dismissed, waving her hand. "It is the internal rumor mill that is currently malfunctioning. Half the executive suite is whispering that Keswick is secretly grooming me to be the next CEO of Quantum." Liz choked slightly on her milk, her eyes going wide. "Are they serious?" "They are, but I refuse to believe it," Cass stated flatly, shaking her head at the sheer mathematical improbability of the gossip. "I am twenty-six years old. I have only been with the company for four years. The idea that the board of directors would hand the keys to the largest tech empire on the planet to someone in her twenties is completely absurd. They are just rumors." I watched my older sister brush off the idea with pure, pragmatic logic. She might not have believed it, but as I looked at the flawlessly executed perimeter she had built around our pack—navigating family law, federal tax codes, and cross-country logistics without breaking a sweat—I knew exactly why William Keswick was watching her. If anyone was capable of running the empire, it was Cassandra Vance.

title: Part 3: The Evening Routine
content: By the time the dinner dishes were cleared from the kitchen island, a heavy, comfortable exhaustion had settled over the apartment. The adrenaline of the cross-country flight and the sheer relief of our consolidation had finally run its course. "Alright," Cassandra announced, wheeling herself away from the kitchen counter. "Let's initiate the evening routine." The Federal Way apartment was efficiently laid out, but space was absolutely at a premium. There were exactly two bedrooms and two bathrooms. Cassandra’s master suite sat at the end of the hall, boasting a massive king-sized bed and a heavily modified ensuite bathroom. Casey’s room, with the large queen-sized bed she was so eager to share, sat adjacent to the standard hallway bathroom, which featured a standard sink, toilet, and a bath-and-shower combo unit. Casey lingered in the hallway, looking longingly from her bedroom door to the living room where my duffel bag sat on the pull-out sofa. "I know it feels arbitrary, Case," I said gently, stepping over to give her a quick hug. "But the rules are absolute. Just until you turn eighteen." "May 25th," Casey recited, giving a small, resilient nod. "I know. No loopholes for Tom." "Exactly," Cassandra agreed, smoothly establishing the logistical boundaries for the night. "To ensure the perimeter remains legally and visually flawless, Casey will use her bedroom and the hallway bathroom to change. David and Liz, grab your bags and come into the master suite with me. We keep the sightlines entirely separated." Casey grabbed her pajamas and disappeared into her room, clicking the door shut. Liz and I hoisted our duffel bags and followed Cassandra down the hall into the master bedroom. The space was dominated by the sprawling king-sized mattress. "You two are more than welcome to share this bed with me if the living room sofa gets too uncomfortable," Cass offered, parking her chair near the doorway of her ensuite bathroom. "There is plenty of square footage." "We'll be fine in the living room for tonight," Liz smiled warmly, setting our bags on the edge of the mattress. "But we might take you up on that tomorrow. We're just happy to be here." Cassandra offered a grateful nod before looking over at me. Her executive mask dropped completely, leaving only the practical, unfiltered reality of our sibling dynamic. "David, I could use your help with the bathing and toileting tonight, if you don't mind," Cass asked quietly. "Of course," I nodded immediately, stepping into the ensuite bathroom behind her. Liz remained in the bedroom to unpack our sleepwear, entirely unfazed. She was a fully integrated member of the pack, and she understood that my physical presence was a functional asset to my sisters, not just an emotional one. Cassandra’s bathroom was a masterpiece of accessibility, retrofitted entirely to accommodate the permanent reality of her 1999 axial load injury. The space featured a custom roll-under sink, heavy-duty grab bars bolted directly into the wall studs next to the toilet, and an oversized shower stall equipped with a sturdy transfer bench. We had executed this routine dozens of times over the years. Because the hollow, pinned-together remnants of her heels and ankles simply could not support the weight of her body without catastrophic failure, transferring from the chair to the shower bench required immense upper-body strength and careful leverage. I acted as her physical anchor. I braced her chair, offered my arms for stability, and provided the secure, unyielding support she needed to safely navigate the transfers without exhausting her own system. It was a quiet, highly coordinated process built on absolute trust. I handed her the towels, secured her chair, and made sure she was completely safely situated before stepping out to give her privacy. Twenty minutes later, the entire apartment had successfully transitioned. The four of us emerged back into the living room, all dressed in comfortable, oversized pajamas. The heavy winter rain was still drumming a steady rhythm against the apartment windows, but inside, the thermal envelope was perfect. Liz and I climbed onto the sprawling pull-out sofa bed, pulling the heavy blankets over our laps. Casey immediately abandoned her bedroom, practically diving onto the mattress next to me. She curled her legs up, pressing her side firmly against my ribs, instantly locking into her deep-pressure baseline. Cassandra wheeled her chair right up to the edge of the mattress, resting her hand lightly on my knee to complete the circuit. I grabbed the television remote and flipped the screen on, the ambient glow washing over the dark living room. We didn't really care what was playing. For the first time in months, my processor was completely silent. The perimeter was secure, the legal boundaries were flawless, and the entire pack was finally anchored exactly where we belonged.

title: Part 4: The Blackout
content: By 9:30 PM, the quiet hum of the television was the only light source in the living room. Outside, the rain had been drumming a steady, predictable rhythm against the apartment windows. At first, it was just the standard, comforting drizzle of the Pacific Northwest winter. But within minutes, the atmospheric pressure violently shifted. The gentle tapping rapidly escalated into a deafening, torrential downpour that violently battered the glass. The sudden, intense spike in auditory sensory input caused my processor to instantly tense. Beside me on the sofa bed, Casey flinched, her grip tightening on my arm as the roar of the wind rattling the window panes grew significantly louder. Then, a massive, concussive crash echoed from the street outside, followed immediately by the sharp, electric crack of a transformer exploding. The television died instantly. The apartment plunged into absolute, pitch-black darkness. The sudden, violent sensory overload and the total loss of visual data pushed Casey over the edge. She let out a sharp, terrified gasp, burying her face into my chest and immediately starting to cry. Her system simply couldn't process the sudden chaos, and she shook violently against my ribs. "I've got you, Case, it's okay," I whispered rapidly, wrapping both of my arms around her trembling shoulders, trying to provide as much deep-pressure grounding as I could in the dark. "Nobody panic," Cassandra’s voice rang out. It was perfectly steady, cutting through the ambient roar of the storm with absolute executive authority. "It's just a blown transformer." "It's so loud," Casey sobbed into my shirt, terrified by the sheer volume of the storm outside. Cassandra didn't hesitate. In a crisis, standard operational protocols were immediately overridden by the prime directive: the absolute physical and emotional security of the pack. "Safety comes first, and we are staying together," Cassandra commanded in the darkness. "Everyone into my bedroom. Right now." Liz used the faint backlight of her cell phone to illuminate the floor. We carefully untangled ourselves from the sofa bed blankets. I kept one arm securely wrapped around Casey, guiding her down the dark hallway while Liz illuminated the path for Cassandra’s chair. We filed into the master suite, the sprawling king-sized mattress waiting in the center of the room. I sat down near the center of the bed, pulling Casey up right beside me. Liz climbed in on my other side, while Cassandra smoothly locked the brakes on her chair and transferred herself onto the edge of the mattress. Within seconds, all four of us were piled onto the massive bed, enveloped in the heavy wool blankets. Casey was still crying softly, clinging to my arm. Cassandra reached out in the dim light, resting her hand firmly on Casey’s shoulder. "Casey, listen to me," Cassandra said gently, her voice an anchor in the dark room. "This is an emergency protocol. We are doing this tonight because the power grid failed and safety comes first. But I need you to understand that this is an exception." Casey sniffled, looking up at our older sister. "This will not become the norm," Cassandra reminded her firmly, maintaining the absolute legal boundary required to keep our father away from us. "The rules still apply. We are only doing this tonight because of the storm." Casey wiped her wet cheeks with the back of her hand. She was sad, her system still craving the routine guarantee of always having this proximity, but her logical brain processed the math. She knew Cassandra wasn't rejecting her; she was protecting the perimeter from Tom's vindictive legal threats. "I understand," Casey cried softly, giving a small, resilient nod. "Just for tonight." "Just for tonight," Cassandra agreed, her voice softening into pure affection. She leaned back against the headboard, settling into the mattress. "Now come here." The pack completely consolidated. Casey pressed her back flush against my chest, her breathing hitching as the tears slowly subsided. I wrapped my arms securely around her, while Liz curled up tightly against my back. Cassandra rested against my shoulder, completing the circuit. The weight and proximity of all four of us acting as a single, grounded unit provided the ultimate deep-pressure regulation. The chaos of the outside world simply ceased to exist. Outside the bedroom walls, the wind howled and the Pacific Northwest rain battered the glass harder and heavier than before. But inside the dark apartment, entirely insulated by the unconditional love of the pack, the ambient noise faded into a steady lullaby. Surrounded by my sisters and my best friend, my processor finally went quiet, and we slowly drifted off to sleep.

title: Part 1: Pantry Logistics
content: The heavy wool blankets of the king-sized bed had created an absolutely flawless thermal envelope. When I finally blinked my eyes open, the digital alarm clock on Cassandra's nightstand was completely blank. The ambient, low-level hum of the apartment’s HVAC system was entirely absent, leaving the room blanketed in a heavy, insulated silence. I carefully shifted my weight. Casey was still curled up against my side, her breathing deep and even, while Liz was softly snoring against my shoulder. Cassandra was awake, her head propped up on a couple of pillows, quietly watching the gray morning light filter through the bedroom blinds. "Good morning," Cass whispered, her executive baseline already calmly assessing the situation. "The grid is still down." I gently untangled my arm from Casey, careful not to break her physical grounding too abruptly, and slipped out from under the covers. The air in the apartment had grown noticeably chillier overnight without the heater running. I walked over to the bedroom window and pulled back the blinds. The torrential, violent downpour from last night had burned itself out, leaving behind a steady, misty Pacific Northwest drizzle. Down the street, the cause of the blackout was immediately obvious. Half a dozen utility trucks, their amber lights flashing steadily in the gray morning, were clustered around a scorched utility pole. Linemen in bright yellow rain slickers were up in bucket trucks, physically wrestling with the blackened, blown-out remains of a massive transformer. "Utility company is already on it," I reported quietly, letting the blinds fall back into place. "Looks like they're replacing the whole transformer." "Then we are operating on emergency reserves for the morning," Cassandra stated, sitting up and stretching her arms. "Which means strict thermal discipline for the kitchen." By the time Liz and Casey started to stir, the apartment's operational protocols had been fully established. Because the ambient temperature inside was dropping, there was absolutely no reason to change out of our warm, oversized flannel pajamas. Casey rubbed her eyes, looking around the massive bed. She didn't have a meltdown about the change in routine. The deep-pressure sleep she had gotten while sandwiched between me and Liz had completely stabilized her processor. She was perfectly calm. "Is the power still out?" Casey asked, pulling a blanket around her shoulders. "It is," Cassandra nodded, sliding smoothly from the edge of the mattress into her manual chair. "Which brings us to rule number one for the day: nobody opens the refrigerator. Every time that door opens, we lose the cold envelope, and I refuse to let our groceries spoil. We are strictly utilizing dry assets this morning." We all shuffled out of the master bedroom and into the quiet, dim living room. Breakfast became an exercise in pantry logistics. Liz and I rummaged through the cupboards, pulling out boxes of dry cereal, foil-wrapped Pop-Tarts, and a handful of granola bars. Since we couldn't use the microwave or open the fridge for milk, we poured glasses of room-temperature bottled water and sat in a circle on the floor around the coffee table. It wasn't exactly a five-star Quantum corporate breakfast, but the vibe in the room was incredibly peaceful. Casey happily munched on a dry strawberry Pop-Tart, entirely unbothered by the lack of electricity. She was wearing a massive, fluffy sweater over her pajama pants, leaning back against the sofa bed frame with her knees pulled to her chest. "I kind of like it," Liz smiled, wrapping her hands around her glass of water. She was wearing one of my oversized t-shirts and a pair of thick sweatpants. "It forces us to just stop and exist. No schedules, no rushing." "It is definitely a forced operational pause," Cassandra agreed dryly, taking a bite of a granola bar. "But as long as the structural integrity of the roof holds and the utility crews keep working, I suppose a pajama day is an acceptable baseline."

title: Part 2: Circadian Logistics
content: As we sat on the floor of the dim living room, passing around boxes of dry oat flakes and frosted toaster pastries, the reality of our new geography started to set in. I took a bite of a generic, foil-wrapped pastry and looked across the coffee table at Casey. She was happily kicking her feet against the edge of the sofa bed, looking entirely well-rested despite the fact that she had practically lived on an airplane for the last forty-eight hours. "I don't understand how you two aren't completely dead on your feet," I said, glancing between Casey and Cassandra. "You flew from Seattle to Virginia on Friday, turned right back around, and flew from Virginia to Seattle on Saturday. My internal clock is completely fried, and you guys act like you just took a nap." Cassandra took a sip of her bottled water, her executive baseline effortlessly shifting to biological logistics. "It is basic circadian math, David," Cassandra explained, setting her water bottle down. "Casey and I experienced zero actual jet lag because our internal clocks never had time to decouple from the West Coast. We left Washington after school on Friday, and we were on the ground in Virginia for less than eighteen hours before we boarded the jet to come back. Our bodies never registered the Eastern Time Zone. We are dealing with standard travel fatigue, but chronologically, we are perfectly anchored." Liz rubbed her eyes, leaning her head against my shoulder. "That makes sense. Meanwhile, my body feels like it's almost noon, but it's not even nine in the morning here." "Traveling East to West is inherently easier on the human body than traveling West to East, because you are extending your day rather than compressing it," Cassandra noted, her tone analytical but warm. "However, you and David have lived your entire lives on Eastern Standard Time. You crossed three distinct time zones yesterday." "So how long until we stop feeling like we're operating on a delay?" I asked, finishing my dry breakfast. "The standard medical metric is roughly one day of adjustment for every time zone crossed," Cassandra calculated smoothly. "Since you gained three hours, your systems will require approximately three days to fully overwrite your old baseline. You will likely wake up entirely too early tomorrow and Monday, and hit a wall of exhaustion around seven in the evening. But by Tuesday, your internal clocks will be flawlessly synchronized with the Pacific grid." "Three days," Liz nodded, wrapping her arms around her knees. "I can handle three days. Especially since we don't have to be anywhere or do anything." "Exactly," Cassandra smiled, leaning back in her manual chair. "Which is precisely why we executed the extraction now, during the winter academic break. You have nearly a full month to acclimate to the apartment, the time zone, and the municipal transit grid before the spring semester begins at the university." Casey leaned over, resting her head firmly against my arm to engage her deep-pressure grounding. "And until then, we just get to hang out. No schedules. No Kristine. Just us." I looked around the dark, quiet apartment. The power was still out, the ambient temperature was slowly dropping, and our breakfast consisted entirely of dry pantry carbohydrates. But as Casey pressed against my side, and Liz held my hand, and Cassandra watched over us with absolute, unconditional protection, I realized my younger sister was entirely correct. The time zone didn't matter. The blackout didn't matter. The perimeter was secured, and for the next three days, my only operational objective was to adjust to being safe.

title: Part 3: The Eastside Expansion
content: We spent the rest of the morning in a massive, tangled cuddle puddle on the living room floor. With the ambient temperature still hovering on the chilly side, we had dragged the heavy wool blankets out from the master bedroom and created a makeshift nest around the sofa bed. Casey was completely anchored against my side, Liz was resting her head on my chest, and Cassandra sat with her back against the sofa frame, her legs stretched out under the blankets with us. It was perfectly quiet, the rain drumming steadily outside. The Federal Way apartment had been a brilliant tactical perimeter for Cassandra and Casey, but as I looked around the tight living room, the physical limitations of the space were obvious. "This apartment is a great temporary staging ground," Cassandra said softly, echoing my exact thoughts as she ran a hand gently through Casey's hair. "But it was only ever designed to hold two females. It was never meant to accommodate a pack of four adults." Liz tilted her head up, looking at Cass. "Are you thinking about renting a bigger place down here?" "No," Cassandra replied, her tone shifting into a quiet, calculated executive register. "I'm thinking about buying a house." Before any of us could process the sheer financial magnitude of that statement, a loud, mechanical clunk echoed from the utility closet down the hall. A second later, the steady, rhythmic whoosh of the HVAC system kicked on. The digital clock on the microwave lit up, blinking aggressively in the kitchen. Casey gasped happily. "The power!" "The grid is back online," Cassandra smiled, immediately shifting into operational mode. "Liz, grab my laptop from the kitchen island, please? The battery drained completely overnight, it needs to be hardwired into the wall." Liz untangled herself from the blankets and grabbed the silver laptop, bringing it over and plugging the heavy power brick into the nearest living room outlet. As the screen flared to life, Cassandra booted up her web browser and immediately pulled up a digital map of the Puget Sound region. "If we are going to purchase a permanent perimeter, we need to completely overhaul our geographic footprint," Cassandra explained, rotating the laptop so we could all see the screen. "Right now, I am commuting from deep south King County all the way up to the Quantum campus. It's functional, but it's not efficient. If we are buying a house, we are looking at the Eastside." "The Eastside?" I asked, looking at the map. "You mean across Lake Washington?" "Exactly," Cassandra nodded, tracing a finger over the digital map. "Cass, you're a high-level executive at one of the biggest tech companies on the planet," Liz pointed out, her eyes wide as she looked at the map's wealthy enclaves. "You could easily afford one of those massive waterfront mansions on Mercer Island. Or even Medina. Isn't that where all the tech billionaires live?" "Medina is highly optimal from a transit perspective," Cassandra conceded, pulling up the King County Metro route maps in a new tab to cross-reference the data. She tapped the screen to highlight the intersecting transit lines. - The Commute to Northwest Pacific University: "If we anchored in Medina, David and Liz could simply walk to the main road and catch the 271 bus going straight across the SR-520 floating bridge. It would drop you directly on the NPU campus in Seattle." - The Commute to Quantum: "At the exact same time, I could catch the 271 heading the opposite direction. It would take me to the Bellevue Transit Center, where I could easily transfer to an express route up to the Overlake Transit Center, right next to Building 33." "That is a flawless pipeline," I admitted, my processor instantly recognizing the beauty of the transit architecture. "One bus route serves the entire pack in opposite directions." Cassandra hummed in agreement, her fingers flying across the trackpad as she pulled up the regional real estate MLS listings. "Medina is statistically viable. But let's see what else is currently on the market—" She stopped. Her finger hovered over the trackpad. "Wait," Cassandra breathed, her executive baseline momentarily fracturing in pure surprise. She clicked on a newly populated listing, bringing up a photo of a sprawling, beautiful property surrounded by heavy Pacific Northwest evergreen trees. "What is it?" Casey asked, leaning over my arm to squint at the screen. "Look at the address," Cassandra said, tapping the screen. "It's not in Medina. It's in Redmond. It's just a few short blocks away from the Quantum campus. I wouldn't even need to take the bus to the Overlake Transit Center. I could literally roll from my front door to Building 33 in under ten minutes." I looked at the property details, then back at Cassandra. Her eyes were already running the logistical math, calculating property taxes, square footage, and accessibility modifications. "Should we check it out?" Liz asked, a massive grin spreading across her face. Cassandra closed all the transit tabs, leaving only the house listing glowing on the screen. "Yes. We absolutely should."

title: Part 4: The Tier-One Acquisition
content: Cassandra didn't just browse standard public real estate websites. The moment we decided on the Eastside, she closed the public tabs and logged directly into the highly exclusive Quantum Building 33 intranet wiki. "Standard real estate agents operate too slowly," Cassandra murmured, her eyes scanning the encrypted corporate directory. She bypassed the public real estate market entirely to locate a Tier-One real estate agent who specializes in acquisitions for high-net-worth tech executives. She clicked on a listing the agent's internal portal had flagged. It was exactly what she was looking for: a sprawling, 3,800-square-foot Pacific Northwest rambler situated right on the edge of the Quantum campus. "This is it," Cassandra stated, her eyes locking onto the property specs. "It fits the mandate perfectly. I require a single-family home on a flat lot, structurally suitable for commercial-grade ADA retrofitting, and located within a highly specific, transit-dense perimeter near the Overlake Transit Center in Redmond." "Are you going to call them?" Liz asked, peering over my shoulder at the screen. "It's Sunday afternoon. The real estate office is definitely closed." "I'll use their priority routing," Cassandra replied. She clicked an exclusive back-door email link maintained specifically for Quantum executives, designed to instantly flag the sender's corporate clearance level and bypass standard reception queues. Her fingers flew across the keyboard, drafting a polite but highly efficient message. From: Cassandra Vance To: Executive Acquisitions Desk Subject: Priority Inquiry - Redmond Property Good afternoon, I am looking to immediately view and acquire the 3,800-square-foot rambler adjacent to the Quantum campus. Please advise on your earliest availability to facilitate a private walk-through. I understand it is Sunday, so I am perfectly amenable to scheduling this for Monday morning if necessary. Best regards, Cassandra Vance She hit send and closed the mail client. "There. We'll likely hear back tomorrow morning once standard business hours resume—" Ping. Less than forty-five seconds after the email left her outbox, an alert flashed in the top right corner of Cassandra's screen. For the first time all weekend, Cassandra Vance looked genuinely shocked. Her executive baseline momentarily fractured into pure disbelief. "Well," Cassandra said, blinking at the screen. "I stand corrected." "Did they already reply?" Casey asked, laughing at our sister's rare moment of surprise. "They did," Cass nodded, opening the response. "Apparently, when you use the Building 33 portal, 'weekend hours' simply do not apply. The agent is offering to meet us at the property for a private walk-through in two hours." I looked at Liz, a massive grin breaking across my face. Our temporary Federal Way perimeter was already evolving into a permanent, sovereign fortress. "I guess we better get out of these pajamas," I smiled, tossing the heavy wool blankets aside.

title: Part 5: The Sunday Dispatch
content: The sudden, chaotic scramble to get out of our flannel pajamas and into respectable daytime clothes took less than ten minutes. But as I pulled a clean sweater over my head and walked back out to the living room, Cassandra was staring at the transit maps on her laptop with a deep, frustrated frown. "Is there a problem with the route?" I asked, grabbing my coat. "The Sunday municipal schedule is fundamentally flawed for an emergency deployment," Cassandra stated, snapping her laptop shut. "The 565 express route to Overlake only operates on weekdays. If we utilize the bus grid today, we would have to take the 174 local crawler all the way to the airport, transfer to the 560 to Bellevue, and then catch the 230 local into Redmond. It would take well over two hours. That is an unacceptable level of operational friction." She immediately pulled her cell phone from her purse and dialed a local dispatch number. "Yes, I need a minivan at the apartment complex on the corner of SR-99 and South 308th," Cassandra instructed the dispatcher, her voice crisp and authoritative. "No, it does not need a mechanical lift. I have a team with me to execute a manual transfer. Just send a standard minivan with an empty trunk. Thank you." She hung up and looked at us. "The dispatcher said fifteen minutes." "You don't care about the wheelchair ramp?" Liz asked, knowing how fiercely Cassandra usually guarded her physical autonomy. "Not today," Cass replied, wheeling herself toward the front door. "When it is just me traveling, I require a lift. But right now, I have my brother, my sister, and you. We can break down the chair and execute a manual transfer into a standard vehicle in under thirty seconds. We are prioritizing speed." Exactly fifteen minutes later, a standard yellow minivan pulled up to the lobby doors. We moved with synchronized precision. I opened the passenger door, and Liz and I securely braced Cassandra under her arms as she pivoted smoothly from her chair into the front seat. While Casey hopped into the back row, I quickly collapsed the manual chair, popped the wheels off, and shoved the entire frame into the trunk. As the cab merged onto Interstate 5 North to begin the forty-minute drive toward the Eastside, Cassandra double-checked her purse, ensuring her Quantum Blue Badge was securely clipped inside. "I have to admit," Cassandra murmured, looking out the window as we crossed the county line, "I am genuinely surprised." "By what?" Casey asked, leaning forward from the back seat. "The agent," Cass replied, shaking her head slightly. "I am perfectly aware of the leverage my clearance level carries inside Building 33. But the fact that this agent was willing to completely abandon his Sunday afternoon on fifteen minutes' notice just because a Quantum executive sent an email... it is staggering." "They know who they're dealing with," I smiled, leaning back against the seat. "They know you're not going to waste their time." Cassandra didn't reply, but a small, sharp smile pulled at the corner of her mouth. The skyline of downtown Seattle passed by on our left as the cab banked onto the SR-520 floating bridge, carrying us across the gray, choppy waters of Lake Washington and straight toward our permanent perimeter.

title: Part 6: The Redmond Compound Acquisition
content: The yellow cab pulled onto the sprawling, immaculately landscaped grounds of the Quantum campus. Instead of directing the driver to the residential address, Cassandra had him pull up directly in front of the massive, glass-fronted architecture of Building 33. "Why are we stopping at your office?" Casey asked as I paid the driver and hopped out to grab the wheelchair from the trunk. "Because a map only provides theoretical data," Cassandra explained, waiting for me to lock her wheels into place before I transferred her into the seat. "I need to physically test the commute perimeter." Once Cassandra was secure, we began the walk. The infrastructure was flawless—wide, fully paved sidewalks with perfect curb cutouts. Cassandra wheeled herself effortlessly under the heavy canopy of Pacific Northwest evergreens, maintaining a brisk, steady pace. Exactly eight minutes later, the commercial zoning of the tech campus faded seamlessly into a quiet, heavily wooded residential cul-de-sac. A sleek black luxury sedan was parked in the driveway of the property. A man in a sharp, tailored suit stood on the front porch, reviewing a dossier on his clipboard. He looked up as we approached, his eyes darting to the empty driveway and then back to us, visibly surprised that a high-level Quantum executive hadn't arrived via a private town car. "Ms. Vance?" the agent asked, stepping down the walkway to greet us. "I'm Marcus. I assumed you would be driving over." "I prefer to test my deployment routes manually," Cassandra replied smoothly, shaking his hand. "This is my brother David, my sister Casey, and Liz. Let's see the property." Marcus nodded, pulling out his keys. "It's a beautiful property—a sprawling, 3,800-square-foot Pacific Northwest rambler situated right on the edge of the Quantum campus. The seller currently has it listed for \$745,000. However, I need to be completely transparent: because it is dangerously underpriced during a massive Eastside tech money surge, a bidding war is absolutely guaranteed." He unlocked the front door and pushed it open, wincing slightly as he looked at the narrow entryway and the sunken living room. "Ms. Vance, I must warn you, the current layout is entirely inaccessible for your chair." "That is completely irrelevant," Cassandra stated, locking her wheels at the base of the front porch. She looked up at me and held out her arms. "David, transport mode." I grinned, crouching down in front of her chair.
