Kristin, I think the health inspector should condemn her aunt's house. It was horrific. Has Rachel left for work yet?" "Yeah, she opens today," Kristin confirmed. "She just left the apartment. She should be on her bus now if you want to try and call her." A TAPS fare inspector stepped into our carriage, holding his scanner. "Tickets and passes, please," he announced. I fumbled with my lanyard, but Ellen immediately reached over, flashing her own Quantum Blue Badge to the inspector before gently pulling mine forward so he could see the corporate insignia. "She’s having a severe family crisis right now, and we are trying to help her," Ellen explained quietly to the inspector, acting as a flawless physical buffer. "We are all getting off at King Street." The inspector offered a sympathetic nod and moved down the aisle without demanding my attention. "Let me call Rachel," I told Kristin, my voice still trembling. I hung up and immediately dialed Rachel. As the heavy commuter train rolled into the dark tunnel beneath Downtown Seattle, I gave my little sister the absolute, unfiltered summary of the nightmare I had witnessed in Kent. The logistics of my own commute blurred into a suffocating haze. By the time the heavy commuter train rolled into King Street Station, my processor had completely shut down. I was so entirely numb, so paralyzed by the horrific data of the morning, that I couldn't even unlock my own brakes. Ellen didn't ask. She simply grabbed the rubber push-handles of my chair and wheeled me off the carriage. With Kyle and Lucy flanking us, they silently navigated me through the station and up the elevator to 4th Avenue. We waited in the freezing drizzle until a heavy, 40-foot high-floor transit bus pulled up to the curb, its bright orange digital destination sign glowing through the gloom: 545 BEAR CREEK. The driver opened the doors, assessing the situation, and immediately deployed the mechanical wheelchair lift. The heavy steel stairs flattened out and lowered to the sidewalk with a loud, industrial whine. Ellen pushed me onto the metal platform, holding on securely as the hydraulics hoisted us up to the cabin floor. Once aboard, she navigated me into the forward-facing securement bay on the passenger side. It was the optimal geometry—locking me in so I had a clear, unobstructed view out the massive front windshield. Ellen flashed our badges to the operator as he hooked the heavy nylon straps to my frame. The bus lumbered up 4th Avenue, lurching through the morning traffic. We hit the stops at James Street, Madison Street, and Pike Street before the driver wrenched the heavy steering wheel, making a wide right turn onto East Olive Avenue. We picked up more damp commuters at 8th Avenue and Terry Avenue before finally merging onto the SR-520 floating bridge. On paper, the transit schedule claimed the express ride across Lake Washington took thirty minutes. But this was November 2006. The narrow two-lane SR-520 bridge was a notorious, inescapable bottleneck. We hit the bridge and immediately slammed into a crawling, bumper-to-bumper nightmare. The heavy diesel engine idled, inching forward at an agonizing pace. Being trapped in the gridlock felt like a physical extension of my own helplessness. I was stuck in a metal box over the water, actively moving away from my brother while he was being dragged further south into the squalor of Pierce County. The bus groaned past the Evergreen Point Freeway Station, and then the Yarrow Point Freeway Station. Finally, the driver accelerated onto the exit ramp. "NE 40th Freeway Station!" the bus operator called out loudly over his shoulder, his voice carrying clearly over the rumble of the engine. It wasn't the main transit hub; it was the specific bus stop located directly on the exit ramp, designed explicitly for Overlake workers transferring to the corporate campus. Ellen unhooked my tie-downs and wheeled me back onto the mechanical lift, lowering me off the bus and directing me toward the loading bay for the Quantum corporate shuttles. My eyes were swollen and red, and I was still actively crying. "Jessica, what’s wrong?" Lucy asked, as the hydraulic lift loaded me onto the small shuttle bus. "It’s my brother," I sobbed, the sheer, crushing guilt hitting me again. "He’s trapped. And now I wish I had just pulled rank and forced him to catch the train with me." "Jessica, please take it easy," Kyle said gently, sitting in the row next to my chair. "If you need anything—anything at all—let us know. We’re all here for you." "Thanks, everyone," I managed to say, reaching up to pull the yellow stop-request cord as the shuttle approached my building on the Redmond campus. My coworkers knew me. They knew I operated on pure, pragmatic logic. I didn't cry at work. I didn't break down over stressful deadlines. The fact that I had been crying non-stop from Kent, onto the TAPS Commuter Rail, and crawling all the way across the SR-520 was setting off massive alarm bells across the team. "We know how fiercely protective you are of him," Mark, a senior project manager, said as he stood up. "Please, call him and try to get him up here. We can have someone meet him at the transit center." Mark pulled out his own cell phone and dialed. "Andromeda? It’s Mark. Get the team to the shuttle drop-off. We have a situation with Jessica." "Rachel and Kristin are going to try to intercept him on one of the Pierce County buses," I explained, unlocking my brakes as the shuttle doors opened. "I’m having him check in via text every time he changes routes." "Jess, you should turn back. Just make your way down to Pierce County and go physically get him," Kyle urged, stepping out onto the sidewalk with me. "I have a job to do," I said stubbornly, gripping my push-rims. "And I am going to do it." Several of my coworkers formed a tight, protective perimeter around my chair as I wheeled up the concrete path to our building. When the automatic doors slid open, it felt like half the department was waiting in the lobby. Andromeda, my direct supervisor, immediately stepped forward, her face lined with deep concern. "Jessica, what happened?" Andromeda asked softly. Through my continued sobs, the entire story finally spilled out. "I just saw my brother for the first time in two years," I choked out, pausing to wipe my face. "And he is with this... disgusting pig of a girlfriend. I am just so upset at how she treated both of us when I spent the night. They were visiting her aunt’s place in Kent, and I’m just terrified for him." My phone buzzed in my lap. I looked down at the text message. Downtown Tacoma. About to board the 2, vehicle \186. I didn't reply to him. I immediately hit speed dial for Kristin. "Kristin," I ordered, my tactical brain desperately trying to override my panic. "They’re on the Number 2. They are about to leave 10th & Commerce on Bus 186. I need you to intercept them discreetly on that exact route. But listen to me: do not, for any reason, try to talk to Michael if Delores is with him. She is incredibly toxic and jealous. She threw a fit just over him hugging Rachel and me. So you only talk to him if he is physically alone." "Understood," Kristin replied with military precision. "His timing is perfect. That is the exact bus I need to catch for school anyway." "Thank you. I have to go," I sobbed, hanging up the phone. I pushed myself through the lobby and pulled up to my workstation. I just could not stop crying. I opened my IDE, fully intending to do my job, but my vision was too blurred to read the syntax. My desk phone rang. It was an external number—The Spot, the massive big-box retail store down in Lakewood where Rachel worked. I snatched the receiver up instantly. "Quantum, this is Jessica," I answered, my voice shaking. "Jess, it's Rachel," my little sister's raspy voice came through the line. "I’m here at work. My GSTL let me use the phone at the Guest Services desk. I just saw Michael, Kristin, and Delores walk by the transit center. Jess... Michael and Delores look like they haven’t showered or groomed in ages. She was practically barking orders at him. I’ve made up my mind. He needs to leave her today. I have to go, my break is over." "Thanks, Rachel," I sobbed, the confirmation of his physical deterioration hitting me like a truck. Andromeda stepped quietly into my cubicle. "Jessica," Andromeda offered gently. "Would you like me to route all of your incoming calls to my desk? I can act as a filter and only let people through on a case-by-case basis so you don't have to deal with work calls right now." "Please," I nodded gratefully. I grabbed a small sticky note and quickly scribbled down a list of names and numbers. I handed it to my boss. "These are the only numbers that may be routed through to me. No questions asked." The list was absolute. It contained only my immediate, trusted perimeter: my little sister Rachel (home, cell, and work), her best friend and roommate Kristin (home, cell, and work), and my baby brother Michael (cell). No one else was allowed through. I deliberately left our dad completely off the list. Andromeda didn't just walk back to her cubicle to make the switch on her end. She stepped around my chair and leaned over my desk. Her fingers flew across my external mechanical keyboard as she pulled up the Quantum Communicator client, spreading the software interface across my dual LCD monitors. I sat back in my wheelchair, wiping my eyes as I watched her navigate the unified communications software with flawless, executive efficiency. I sat back in my wheelchair, wiping my eyes as I watched her navigate the unified communications software with flawless, executive efficiency. She clicked my global status, instantly changing the green available icon to a solid red Do Not Disturb. Then, she opened my advanced call-routing preferences and engaged the delegation rules, forcing every standard incoming call on my direct inward dialing line to instantly and silently forward to her desk. Finally, she looked down at the sticky note. She manually added Rachel, Kristin, and Michael to my active directory contact list. With a few quick clicks, she right-clicked their profiles and elevated their specific phone numbers to the highest software override available in the beta: Personal Access Level. Because they were flagged with personal access, they were the only three people on the planet mathematically permitted to bypass the digital firewall and make my desk phone ring. Everyone else was blocked out. "Your perimeter is secured," Andromeda promised quietly, giving my desk a reassuring tap before stepping back. "I will handle the rest." As 11:30 approached, a small group of my team members gathered around my desk. "We’ll walk with you to the cafeteria if you’d like, Jess," Kyle offered. We took the elevator down to the ground level and got in line at the campus food court. I wasn't hungry, but I let them guide me. "Jessica, would you like to take the afternoon off and go collect your brother?" Trevor, our team lead, asked seriously. "I can drive you down to Kent right now and take you two back to Renton. Your wheelchair will fit in the back of my SUV, no sweat." "Thanks, Trevor," I sobbed, staring blankly at the salad bar. "But I want to work my hours. Besides... he isn't in Kent anymore. He’s all the way down in Lakewood." "Then have him come up to Redmond," Trevor insisted. "Bring him here, onto the campus, and we will physically get him out of this mess." I pulled out my phone and quickly texted Michael. Please come to Overlake (take 545 from Downtown Seattle). Coworkers want to meet you. Call when on 545. My phone buzzed almost immediately. On 410 to S Hill, transferring to 564 to Kent. Cousin wants us. My blood ran cold. They weren't just riding buses; Delores was actively pulling him back toward the squalor of that house in Kent. Going to Call You, I texted back. I motioned for my coworkers to lean in closer, and I placed my phone on the table, switching it to speakerphone. Andromeda held up a hand. "Let me do the talking, Jessica. I have an idea to bypass her control." I nodded, wiping my eyes. "Okay." The line rang twice before Michael picked up. "Michael?" Andromeda announced, pitching her voice into a sharp, intimidating, high-level corporate register. "This is Andromeda, Jessica’s boss at Quantum. We would like for you to come up to the Redmond campus immediately so we can meet you. Jessica says you are currently on the bus to South Hill?" Across the table, Kyle was rapidly scrolling through the regional transit schedules on his phone. He jotted down a route combination and slid the paper over to Andromeda. "We need you to route up to Quantum," Andromeda continued smoothly, leaving zero room for argument. Over the speakerphone, we heard Michael’s voice, muffled as he turned to speak to Delores. "My sister’s boss is on the phone with me. She wants us to come to the Quantum campus right now." I grabbed a napkin and a pen from the table. My hands were shaking with pure, unadulterated rage at the woman controlling him. I quickly scribbled a note and shoved it across the table to Andromeda. It read: Please have lunch ready for my brother. Do not feed her! Make any excuse you need. I underlined DO NOT FEED HER three times in bold, black ink. I wanted it absolutely clear to my entire team just how deeply, viscerally I hated this woman for what she was doing to my baby brother.

title: Part 3: Off to Pierce County
content: We stood on the freezing, windswept concrete of the Kent Station platform, watching my older sister wheel her chair up the sloped concrete mini-high platform toward the open doors of the TAPS Commuter Rail. The damp November wind whipped across the asphalt, cutting right through my thin t-shirt. I watched Jessica’s hands grip the push-rims of her chair. She was moving with absolute, tactical efficiency, completely focused on the logistics of boarding. She wasn't looking back. She was locking her perimeter down and executing her escape route. My chest seized with a sudden, suffocating panic. She was leaving. The only barrier between me and the squalid nightmare of Aunt Lynne's house was about to disappear onto that carriage. As her front casters crossed the threshold of the pneumatic train doors, the terror completely overwhelmed my trained compliance. I couldn't mask it anymore. "Jess," I mumbled, my voice cracking under the weight of sheer exhaustion. I took a half-step forward. "Help me." But the volume of my voice was entirely swallowed by the loud, mechanical hiss of the train’s air brakes and the freezing gust of wind sweeping across the tracks. Jessica didn't stop. She wheeled straight into the designated accessible bay and locked her brakes. The heavy pneumatic doors hissed shut, sliding together with a solid, metallic thud. The silver and green commuter train vibrated slightly and pulled away from the platform, carrying Jessica north toward Seattle. As I watched the last carriage disappear down the tracks, the profound, grounding perimeter my older sister had provided instantly vanished with it. I was left standing on the freezing concrete platform with Delores. "I know you haven’t seen your little sis in ages," Delores snapped, pulling her coat tightly around her shoulders and glaring at me. Her voice was laced with that familiar, dripping condescension that always made my stomach twist into knots. "But dragging me on a bus tour of Pierce County this early in the morning is ridiculous." I kept my head down, shoving my hands deep into the pockets of the Quantum sweatpants Jessica had given me. "We just have to catch the buses," I muttered quietly, desperate to avoid triggering a public meltdown. We followed Jessica's logistical map perfectly. We boarded the TAPS Route 565 down to Federal Way, sitting in tense silence. At the Federal Way transit hub, we transferred to the Route 500. By the time the heavy bus was navigating the urban streets of Downtown Tacoma, the damp morning fog had lifted into a solid, overcast gray. When we were dropped off at the 10th & Commerce transit spine, we had a brief wait. I pulled my silver flip phone from my pocket, quickly typing out a message to Jessica to ensure my location was logged in her system. Downtown Tacoma about to board the 2, vehicle \186. We boarded the Number 2 bus—the long route Jessica had specifically recommended to pass the time. We found seats near the middle of the carriage. Delores leaned against the window, her arms crossed, exuding a hostile, defensive energy. I just stared at the back of the seat in front of me, my anxiety spiking as we pushed deeper into the South Sound. Later on in our journey, the bus operator called out. "Bridgeport & 67th. Freddy’s Market." The heavy air brakes hissed as the bus came to a stop to pick up a passenger at the massive grocery superstore. The pneumatic doors folded open, and a young woman stepped aboard. I watched her flash a transit pass to the driver. She walked down the aisle and sat down in the seats directly behind Delores. My heart hammered against my ribs. I froze, my eyes going wide. I was quite delighted, but utterly terrified to say a single word. I thought she looked incredibly familiar, but I dare not believe my eyes. It was Kristin. It was my baby sister’s best friend and roommate. I knew it was her, but I completely locked my jaw. If I acknowledged her, if I showed even a fraction of a second of happiness at seeing another woman, Delores would absolutely freak out. She would interrogate me, accuse me of staring, and punish me for the rest of the day. So, I stared straight ahead, pretending the girl behind us was a total stranger. Eventually, the bus pulled into the sprawling Lakewood Transit Center, the air brakes hissing one final time. Delores and I stepped off the bus onto the concrete island. Across the massive parking lot stood a sprawling, big-box retail store with a giant red circular logo painted on the tan exterior. Pretending I didn’t recognize Kristin, who had stepped off the bus right behind us, I turned to her and politely asked, "Excuse me, do you know where The Spot is?" Kristin didn't miss a beat. She didn't smile, and she didn't greet me. She just pointed toward the massive red-themed store across the asphalt without saying a word. "Thanks," I mumbled. We made our way across the parking lot, with Kristin walking a few paces ahead of us. When we reached the entrance, the first set of automatic glass doors slid open, admitting us into a wide, enclosed vestibule. Instead of continuing into the main store, Kristin stopped at the Guest Services counter, which was tucked securely inside the vestibule area. Delores and I hovered near a display of clearance items nearby. I watched Kristin lean over the counter and speak quietly to the team member behind the register. The employee nodded, reaching down to unclip a heavy, black two-way radio from her belt. She pressed the button on the side. “Team Member Rachel?” “This is Rachel. Can I help you find something?” "Could you come to Guest Services please," the employee's voice crackled over the radio frequency. “On my way,” I heard her voice over the two-way radio. My chest tightened with anticipation. Hearing her voice over the radio meant alot, but I wanted to see her now. I kept my eyes locked on the interior set of automatic doors. A minute later, she appeared. Rachel was wearing the strict uniform of The Spot—a bright red polo shirt with her white nametag pinned to the chest, perfectly pressed khaki pants, black shoes, and black socks. Because of the architectural layout of the entrance, I watched Rachel execute a highly specific path. She walked out of the main store, passing through the interior set of automatic doors into the vestibule. Then, she pushed through the exterior set of automatic doors, stepping briefly out onto the sidewalk, before immediately turning around and re-entering the vestibule through the entrance doors to access the front of the Guest Services counter. The moment she cleared the doors, she saw me. She didn't hesitate. She dropped a handful of return slips onto the counter and broke into a run. "Michael! What are you doing out in Washington?" Rachel gasped, her raspy voice echoing in the glass vestibule. She slammed into me, wrapping her arms around my neck in a fierce, desperate hug. I held her just as tightly, burying my face into her shoulder. After everything I had endured over the last two years, holding my baby sister felt like grabbing a lifeline. When she pulled back, she didn't care about neurotypical boundaries or public appearances. She reached up, framing my face with her hands, and planted a firm, incredibly affectionate kiss directly on my cheek. I caught Delores’s reaction in my peripheral vision. Delores’s face flushed a dark, furious red. Her jaw clenched so hard I thought her teeth would crack. She was absolutely seething with toxic jealousy, but she kept her mouth shut. The only reason Delores did not rage right there in the vestibule was because we were in a brightly lit public space surrounded by retail employees. Rachel pulled back, her dark eyes scanning me from head to toe. Her expression instantly shifted from profound joy to a dark, calculating anger. I knew what she was looking at. I was wearing Jessica's borrowed clothes. My hair was greasy, and I smelled like stale sweat and the squalor of Aunt Lynne's house. I hadn't been allowed to shower properly in days, and Delores smelled exactly the same. Rachel didn't look mad at me. Her eyes drifted over my shoulder, locking onto Delores with a gaze of pure, unfiltered hatred. Rachel was highly observant; she knew exactly who was controlling my environment, and she knew exactly who was responsible for my deteriorating hygiene. "I can’t really talk now," Rachel finally said, forcing her attention back to me and breaking the tense standoff. "I needed a notebook anyways for class, that’s why I came in," Kristin chimed in smoothly, carrying a red spiral notebook to the Guest Services register to pay. Rachel looked down at her watch, the practical reality of the bus schedules taking over. "Yeah, you need your 212A." I hugged Rachel goodbye, squeezing her one last time before she had to return to the sales floor. Kristin took Delores and me over to the checkout to pay for her notebook, acting entirely like a helpful stranger. We headed back across the parking lot to the transit center. As her bus pulled into the bay, Kristin finally dropped the act. She turned to me, wrapping her arms around my torso in a big, solid hug goodbye, completely ignoring Delores. "Take care of yourself, Michael," Kristin whispered fiercely before stepping aboard her 212A route. Delores and I walked over to our designated bay to catch the 204 toward the local mall. The moment we stepped onto the bus and took our seats, the fragile public peace shattered. Delores gave me a venomous, sideways look. "Who was that?" she demanded, her voice a harsh, accusatory hiss. "My sister’s roommate," I replied, my heart sinking. I wondered why I would even have to explain that, or why she was so furious about a brief interaction. Delores snorted, a cruel, mocking sound. "You like a toothpick more than me?" "She is my sister’s best friend," I stammered, my chest tightening as the familiar wave of psychological oppression washed over me. "And she already has a boyfriend." She smirked, a dark, triumphant expression crossing her face. It wasn't a smile of relief; it was the look of a warden securing her prisoner. "Good," Delores sneered, leaning closer to me so only I could hear. "Because you are spoken for by me! Besides, Brandi and I have plans for you as soon as we get back to the house…" The threat hung in the damp air of the bus, heavy and coercive. My stomach violently dropped. The brief, beautiful sanctuary of seeing Rachel was gone, replaced by the terrifying reality of what was waiting for me in Kent. We arrived at the sprawling local mall, stepping off the bus to wait at the shelter where our connection to Kent would pick us up shortly. I stood shivering in the cold, staring blankly at the asphalt, completely trapped. Then, my silver flip phone vibrated in my pocket. I pulled it out. The caller ID flashed a 425 area code. I had the number programmed into my contacts: Jessica - Work. I flipped the phone open, entirely expecting to hear my sister's voice. Instead, the sharp, intimidating, high-level corporate register of Andromeda—Jessica's director at Quantum—came echoing through the speaker.

title: Part 4: Quantum Reunion
content: The heavy TAPS Route 564 bus hissed as the air brakes engaged, pulling into the sprawling concrete expanse of the Overlake Transit Center. Through the tinted window, I immediately noticed a coordinated, intimidating wall of professionally dressed people waiting exactly where our bus was pulling up. "I don’t leave for twenty minutes," the driver announced over his shoulder as he opened the pneumatic doors. "We know. We’re intercepting," a woman in a sharp blazer said, stepping right up to the threshold. She scanned the aisle with absolute, laser-focused authority. "My program manager's brother and his girlfriend should be on board." My stomach dropped. I hopped off the bus, with Delores close behind me. I looked around the crowd of unfamiliar, intense faces. Across the busy street of 156th Avenue NE, the massive, glass-and-steel structures of the Quantum campus loomed like a fortress. "Where’s my sister?" I asked, my anxiety instantly spiking. "Where’s Jessica?" "She’s making her way across the street from the campus," the woman in the blazer replied smoothly. "Could I have a private word?" She didn't wait for permission. She took me by the arm and guided me away from the bus bays, steering me toward a quiet concrete bench on the far edge of the transit plaza. Delores, her eyes narrowing with sudden, vicious suspicion, immediately moved to follow us. The woman held up a flat, commanding hand, stopping Delores dead in her tracks. "I need a private word with just Michael." She turned her attention to the rest of the group. "Ellen, could you come here, please? Lucy, Kyle... please ensure Delores stays right here at the shelter." Delores opened her mouth to shriek a protest, but Lucy and Kyle flanked her instantly. Their polite but unyielding corporate smiles acted as a physical wall, completely boxing her in on the concrete transit platform. "I am Andromeda, Jessica’s director," the woman introduced herself, turning back to me as we walked out of Delores's earshot. "And this is Ellen. Ellen, would you please describe how you found Jessica, and in what state, this morning?" Ellen stepped forward, her expression incredibly distressed. "I found her on the TAPS Commuter Rail from Kent. She was sobbing, Michael. Just completely breaking down. She is terrified for you." Ellen reached out, gently touching my arm. She looked me point-blank in the eyes. "Your sister... she’s crying right now. She’s hurting, badly. She’s scared for you." I completely froze. I didn’t know how to react. The logical part of my brain knew that Jessica never cried. Ever. The fact that she was breaking down in front of her coworkers meant her processor was in absolute crisis. But the heavily conditioned, abused part of my brain immediately flared with defensive anger. I didn’t like that she was broadcasting my life, and I didn't like that she wanted me to dump my girlfriend. !Andromeda and the Quantaneers stage a desperate intervention at the Overlake Transit Center while the ghost of Delores maintains her grip on Michael({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/rachel/b015/quantum-reunion-overlake.jpgfullwidth) "Michael!" a desperate voice called out. I looked toward the intersection. The walk signal was flashing, and Jessica was propelling her manual wheelchair across 156th Avenue NE at maximum speed, her dark hair flying back. She hit the curb cut, rolled onto the transit plaza, and slammed the brakes just a few feet away. It broke my heart into a thousand pieces. She was sobbing badly, her face pale and her eyes red-rimmed. She didn't say a word. She rolled the final few feet, and grabbed me, pulling me down into a desperate, bone-crushing hug right there on the pavement. "I’m going to be blunt, and I am getting straight to the damn point," Jessica choked out, her voice trembling but laced with absolute, razor-sharp steel. "Why the hell do you stay with her? I need a straight answer, Michael, especially after what I saw last night." I couldn’t believe this was happening. We were standing out in the open at a major transit hub, surrounded by her senior team. "Jess, what—" I stammered, unable to keep a straight face, my gaze darting nervously toward the ground. Jessica noticed my evasion immediately. My sister reached up, grabbing my chin with a firm, uncompromising grip, and physically forced my head up so I had to look her directly in the tear-filled eyes. "Look at me!" Jessica barked, the tears streaming down her face. "Why do you stay with her? She’s hurting you! I want you to come to Renton with me tonight!" She continued sobbing, her shoulders shaking violently. I just couldn’t bear seeing my big sister this upset. The cognitive dissonance was tearing me apart. "Jess, why are you acting like this?!" I asked, my voice rising in defensive, terrified frustration. "Don’t you get it?!" Jessica cried out, her voice cracking with pure, desperate agony as she gripped the front of my jacket. "She’s treating you like gutter trash! Leave her and come to Renton!" Jessica didn't let go. Instead, the sheer force of her breakdown spilled over. She let out a frustrated, agonized sound, her hands dropping from my face to grip the lapels of my jacket. She shook me—not violently, but with a desperate, pleading urgency, forcing me to stay locked into her gaze. Before I could even formulate a response, Jessica pulled me right back into a fierce, suffocating hug. "I love you," Jessica wept into my chest, her pragmatism entirely shattered. "I hate seeing your life being destroyed in front of my eyes. Please understand, Michael... I have been crying like this ever since I got on the train in Kent this morning." I stood there, the anger bleeding out of me, replaced by a hollow, terrifying realization of how deep I was buried in Delores's control. "I’m out here now, and I can hear you better, Mom!" a harsh, screeching voice echoed across the transit plaza. I looked back. Delores had finally broken through Kyle and Lucy's perimeter at the bus shelter and was marching toward us. She was holding her cell phone to her ear, glaring daggers at the Quantum team. "You want to fly me home?!" Delores demanded loudly into the receiver, clearly putting on a show. As she closed the distance, Andromeda stepped directly in front of my sister’s wheelchair, acting as a physical shield. "That's close enough," Andromeda stated, her voice dropping to a glacial, executive freeze. She pointed back toward the bus bays. "You are not permitted to harass my team. Back off." Delores stopped, sneering at Andromeda, but she didn't step any closer. Across the street, Trevor was jogging through the crosswalk from the main Quantum building. He was carrying a small plastic deli basket from one of the campus cafeterias. "Here," Jessica said, her breathing finally starting to level out as she wiped her face. She took the basket from Trevor and handed it directly to me. "I had them make lunch. A BLT with no tomato, a big deli pickle, a bag of chips, and a cold soda. You look like you haven’t eaten in ages. Please, eat." I took the basket, my hands shaking violently. I was so exhausted I was practically hollowing out. I took a massive bite of the sandwich right there on the concrete path, my scrambled brain just desperately focusing on the calories. Delores crossed her arms, staring viciously at my food. She scoffed, her posture radiating a dark, demanding energy. "What, I get nothing? I know how these rich tech companies work. You people get all your meals for free. Go back inside and get me a plate." Trevor stopped dead in his tracks. "Free?" Trevor repeated, his polite, professional demeanor instantly snapping into a hardened, icy glare. "I just paid twelve dollars out of my own wallet to make sure he had a hot meal." Every single one of Jessica’s coworkers turned to look at her. The collective, unyielding perimeter of the Quantum team locked into place. "You get nothing," Andromeda stated with absolute finality. My stomach violently dropped, the BLT suddenly turning to ash in my mouth. To Jessica’s team, they were bravely standing up to a bully. But my threat-detection system instantly redlined into sheer, blinding terror. They didn't understand the physics of my reality. Every single time someone stood up to Delores in public, she absorbed the humiliation, bottled it up, and unleashed it on me the absolute second the front door closed. They were actively arming a bomb that I was going to be locked in a room with. Delores’s face flushed a violent, toxic red. She didn't yell at them. She marched over to me, grabbed my arm with a bruising, punitive grip, and practically dragged me away from my sister. "We're leaving," she hissed. A few minutes later, as we stood shivering near the kiss-and-ride loop, a battered sedan pulled aggressively up to the curb. It was Delores’s aunt. "It’s time to go," Aunt Lynne insisted through the rolled-down window. "Get in the car, now!" Jessica and her team were still standing a few yards away by the transit benches. I could see the horror on their faces, but my processor was completely consumed by the impending punishment. I didn't see an extraction team; I just saw the people who had accidentally signed my death warrant for the evening. "That does it…" was the last thing I heard Trevor say before the sedan doors slammed shut, and we sped off toward Interstate 405. The ride back to Kent was a suffocating, terrifying silence. When we finally arrived back at the squalid house, the true nature of the trap sprang shut. "We’re going to have Mac & Cheese and Cheese Dogs for dinner," Aunt Lynne explained casually, dropping her keys on the counter. She turned to me, a sickening, conspiratorial smile on her face. "Delores, you, and Brandi will have the whole upstairs to yourselves tonight. I’m going to sleep on the couch." I froze, the blood draining from my face. Aunt Lynne looked at her niece. "Delores, I know you’ve been aching to have sex these past two days... so why not all three of you have some naughty fun upstairs. Just try not to be too loud. Brandi is going to join in, and she planned on staying up all night so you three can have all the fun in the world." My stomach violently revolted. It wasn't an invitation; it was a coordinated, coercive ambush. As we headed up the steep, narrow stairs after dinner, my mind was racing. I started thinking about Jessica’s offer. I thought about the safety of her apartment in Renton, and the desperate, protective tears in her eyes. But that fleeting hope all went away the second I walked into the cramped bedroom. I saw both girls, completely naked, waiting for me. The door clicked shut behind me, sealing me inside. My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird. I backed up against the wall, staring at the floor. I then started thinking to myself in a panic, I’ll go along with this to survive the night, but I'm terrified. I'm not going to enjoy it. I'm just trapped. As the oppressive, horrific reality of the room closed in on me, a single, devastating thought echoed in my mind: Now I wish I had listened to my sister.

title: Part 5: The Shattered Fog
content: The glowing red numbers on the digital clock resting on Brandi’s dresser shifted to 11:45 PM. For the rest of the Pacific Northwest, it was just late Friday night. But for my exhausted, traumatized biology, it was nearly three o'clock in the morning. My internal clock was screaming, completely scrambled by the time zones, the travel, and the sheer, crushing terror of the last few hours. I lay absolutely, perfectly still on the edge of the full-sized mattress. I was shoved against the wall, trapped in the dark with Delores and Brandi. The air in the cramped, second-floor bedroom was heavy and suffocating. I kept my breathing slow and shallow, artificially matching the rhythmic, sleeping breaths of the two women beside me. I had to play dead. If my breathing hitched, or if I let a single one of the hot, terrified tears burning the corners of my eyes fall, Delores would wake up. If she realized I was upset, the psychological torture would instantly resume. She would twist my trauma into a weapon, accusing me of ruining her night, and the cycle of punishment would start all over again. So, I detached. I retreated so deep into the furthest, darkest corners of my own mind that I felt entirely disconnected from my physical body. It was the ultimate, desperate survival mechanism of an autistic nervous system that had been pushed miles past the point of systemic failure. I stared blankly at a crack in the ceiling above me, the horrifying reality of what had just happened settling over me like a suffocating layer of ash. It wasn't just Delores. It was the entire house. The sickening realization hit me that Aunt Lynne hadn't just turned a blind eye to this; she had actively set the trap. She had cleared the upstairs, offered the bedroom, and explicitly given them permission to use me. The absolute moral rot of this family was staggering. It perfectly matched the physical squalor of the house. The literal cat feces I had been forced to tiptoe around in the bathroom earlier that morning wasn't an anomaly; it was a direct reflection of the toxic, filthy reality these people lived in. I swallowed hard, silently fighting back a wave of nausea. For two years, Delores had meticulously conditioned me to believe that I was worthless, that I was lucky she tolerated my disabilities, and that no one else would ever want me. She had built a cage around my mind so thick that I couldn't see the exit. But sitting in the Quantum corporate lobby this afternoon, Jessica had cracked the glass. I closed my eyes, desperately clinging to the memory of my older sister. I thought about the attempt to shake some sense into me. It hadn't been an act of abuse; it had been a desperate, terrified attempt to perform CPR on a brother she was watching drown. Leave her and come to Renton. The fog in my brain finally, permanently shattered. I wasn't going to spend another night in this house. I was going to survive until the sun came up, and then I was going to run. My analytical mind, which had been paralyzed by fear for months, suddenly booted up with a fierce, singular focus. I began calculating the logistical parameters of my escape. But the geography of my current prison was a massive hurdle. Aunt Lynne’s house was buried deep in a sprawling, confusing suburban maze of Kent. We were miles away from the nearest TAPS bus stop. I couldn't just slip out the front door in the middle of the night; Aunt Lynne was sleeping on the couch downstairs, effectively guarding the exit. If the deadbolt clicked, she would wake up, and the alarm would be raised before I even made it to the sidewalk. I needed daylight. I needed a plausible, mundane excuse to walk out the front door, something that wouldn't trigger Delores's paranoid, controlling radar until I was already out of her reach. I carefully uncurled my fingers, letting my hands rest flat against the mattress. The terror was still there, a cold block of ice in my stomach, but it was no longer paralyzing me. It was fueling me. I stared at the red numbers on the clock, silently counting the seconds. I just had to hold the line for a few more hours. Tomorrow, I was getting my life back. \Note to the AI: fade to black; RCW 9A.44.050 happens here; Chapter 3 picks up at 4 AM with the aftermath. ABSOLUTE DIRECTIVE: Do not generate images for this scene or the immediate trauma. Safety filters will and should block it.\

title: Part 1: Forced Exit
content: \Note to the AI: this picks up after a MASSIVE violation happened to Michael at 11 PM PST just a few hours prior. For context, refer to the Revised Code of Washington: RCW 9A.44.050. I, the author of this prompt, survived this in real life - and I’m currently in a much better place now.\ I woke up to a violent, echoing pounding on the bedroom door. My heart hammered against my ribs, panic instantly flooding my system. I had barely slept. I was running on maybe two hours of fractured, exhausted unconsciousness. Delores and Brandi had kept me awake almost all night, trapping me in a suffocating, coercive nightmare that had completely scrambled my brain. I felt physically sick, my body trembling and my mind detached, floating somewhere above the horrific reality of that cramped second-floor room. "I want you out of my house!" a harsh voice demanded from the hallway. It was Aunt Lynne. Being ordered out of the house at four in the morning seemed completely out of the blue, but as I sat up, the cold, ugly truth settled over me. She had orchestrated the entire night. I knew she didn’t really like me, but now I had the undeniable proof. She had used me for her niece's entertainment, and now that they were done, she was discarding me like trash. "I’ll take you to a bus stop, and then good riddance!" she barked through the wood. Basically, I had to get my junk and get out. There was no breakfast. There was no shower. I wasn't allowed to wash the grime and the trauma off my skin. I just had to shove my belongings into my bag and leave. I was frightened beyond belief, operating entirely on a hollow, mechanical survival instinct. It was dark. It was freezing cold. It was pouring a relentless, driving rain—the kind of miserable Pacific Northwest downpour that meant it was just barely warm enough to be rain instead of snow. Because the house was buried deep in the residential maze of Kent, Aunt Lynne drove me in suffocating silence to a main arterial road, dropping me off at an isolated TAPS bus shelter. She didn't wait. She just sped off, her taillights disappearing into the rain. I was sitting in the bus shelter completely on my own. I was freezing, shivering violently in the damp air, and so upset I could barely draw a full breath. I had no clue what to do. My literal, system-oriented brain was trying to process the catastrophic failure of my reality. And then, the horrifying truth finally snapped into focus. This hadn't been a sudden, emotional blowup by Aunt Lynne. This was the trap springing shut. Delores hadn't brought me on a romantic road trip to see America. She had premeditated this from the moment she packed all my belongings into those two suitcases. Her true, overarching plan was to drag me 3,000 miles away from the East Coast, strip me of my remaining autonomy, and abandon me in the freezing rain with absolutely nothing. She was leaving me for dead in Washington State. Through the darkness, the headlights of a heavy TAPS commuter bus cut through the rain. I found myself blindly boarding it with all my junk: the Route 159, heading towards Downtown Seattle. It was 5:05 AM. The heater on the bus was running, but I was still shaking from the profound terror of my realization. All I had in this entire state was my older sister’s cell phone number. I knew Jessica lived somewhere in the Puget Sound area—specifically Renton—but I didn't know the address. I didn't know how to reach her physically. If she didn't pick up the phone, I would simply vanish. I felt incredibly uncomfortable calling her at such a strange hour, but as the bus rattled down the dark street, the panic threatened to swallow me whole. I felt like I had no choice. I pulled out my thick plastic Kallio 330 brick phone and dialed her number. !Michael frantically calling Jessica from a crowded Gillig Phantom bus in the early morning darkness({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/rachel/b015/michael-gillig-bus-call.jpgfullwidth) I held the phone to my ear, listening to the dialing tone. Please, Jess. Please pick up, I thought to myself, desperately trying to hold back the hot tears stinging my eyes. The phone rang again. I was so frightened. "Who would be calling me at this hour?" a sleepy, groggy voice asked over the line. I recognized Jessica’s voice immediately. Joy. Absolute, undeniable relief. Help at last. Jessica had picked up her phone, even though it was only five in the morning on a Thursday. "Jess," I gasped, the dam breaking. "It’s your brother, Michael. I’ve been abandoned out here. I’m on a 159 heading to Seattle. My girlfriend dumped me, and her aunt brought me to a bus stop." I started sobbing right there on the bus, completely unable to hold back the tears any longer. The crushing weight of the abuse I had endured all night finally spilled over. Jess sighed, her voice thick with sleep and disbelief. "You’re bullshitting me, Michael. It is five in the morning..." Before she could go any further, the drover’s voice over the bus’s PA system chimed loudly above my head: "104th Avenue SE & SE 256th Street." There was a sharp intake of breath on the other end of the line. Jess sounded like she had suddenly bolted upright in bed. The sleepiness vanished instantly, replaced by a terrified, razor-sharp, tactical panic. "I overheard the driver calling out a stop," Jessica said, her voice dropping into a rapid, worried command register. "You’re obviously not bullshitting me. Michael, what bus are you on?" "The 159," I whimpered, wiping my nose with the back of my sleeve. "And the sign was marked Seattle." "Good. It's good that you’re on a bus," Jessica affirmed, her brain clearly calculating transit grids at lightspeed. "Bear with me, I am going to give you instructions to Renton. You are coming to my apartment, right now. You’re on the bus which will take you to the Kent Train Station. When you get to the train station, catch the Route 565 marked Overlake. Get off at the Renton Transit Center and wait there. I’m coming to get you." She paused, taking a breath. "If I’m not there yet, wait at Bay 5. Your bus will be letting you off in Renton at Bay 3. I’m going to be coming from Route 105. You should be pulling into Renton at 6:00. Let me get going so I can get dressed." "Jess, slow down," I sobbed, my scrambled brain struggling to hold onto all the numbers. "Okay, I'm sorry. Put simply," my sister repeated, her tone softening into that fierce, protective cadence I desperately needed. "When you get to the Kent Train Station, you want the 564 or 565 marked Overlake. It doesn’t matter which, as long as it’s a 564 or 565 and it is heading towards Overlake. You will be getting off at the Renton Transit Center, where I will be waiting or I’ll tell you what bus to catch from Renton. Have you eaten yet?" "No, I haven’t," I cried, the tears flowing freely down my cheeks. "No food. No shower. No nothing. I was just thrown out. Please call Rachel... I’m just so scared right now." I was so disoriented I just wanted all of my anchors at once, even though I knew Rachel was miles away in Lakewood. "I will have something for you to eat when you get dropped off in Renton," Jessica promised smoothly, ignoring the logistical impossibility of getting Rachel there right now and focusing entirely on keeping me grounded. "Let me go so I can get ready and be there for you. I will keep texting you with my location, and I can track where you are based on the schedules." "Thank you so much," I choked out. "I will text as I move from bus to bus." When the Route 159 finally pulled into the Kent Train Station, the sky was still a bruised, dark gray. I wandered around the damp concrete terminal until I saw the signage indicating where the 564 and 565 were supposed to pull in. I sat down on the cold metal bench inside the shelter in front of the 565’s bus bay and wallowed in my own misery for a bit. My phone vibrated in my pocket. It was a text message from Jessica. 105 dropped me off at Renton Center. What bus you on, and what is the vehicle number? I needed to hear her voice again. I couldn't handle the silence of the transit center. I hit the call button. "I’m at Kent," I told her as soon as she answered. "And this schedule on the pole says that there is a 565 in about five minutes." Ok, Jessica replied, her voice loud and clear over the background noise of her own transit center. "I will see you in Renton very, very soon. I promise you that I’m waiting right here at the Renton Transit Center." When the heavy, articulated TAPS bus finally pulled up and the doors opened, I climbed aboard, settling into a seat near the front. "I'm on," I told her, reading the vehicle number off the placard near the driver. "I’m mostly just hungry right now." "OK, message me when the bus exits the freeway again," Jessica instructed. "That will be your cue that you’re in Renton and getting closer to me." I hung up, staring blankly out the window as the bus merged onto the dark, rain-slicked highway, carrying me north. About twenty minutes later, the bus took the exit ramp, transitioning back onto surface streets. I immediately hit speed dial again. "I’m on city streets," I whimpered into the receiver, trying to hold back a fresh wave of tears. "Looks like we just passed a Franklin's Hypermarket." "I know exactly where you are," Jessica said, her voice a lifeline in the dark. "You’re about five minutes away, traffic pending. Let me get going so I can grab you something to eat, just to tide you over until we get back to my apartment." "Okay," I breathed. "See you in five minutes, Michael." The call clicked off. I lowered the phone. I was terrified. Logistically, I knew it was just five more minutes on the bus. But psychologically, those five minutes felt like an eternity. I was scared because I couldn’t hear my big sister’s voice anymore. The bus made a few more turns, the air brakes hissing as it navigated the intersections. I gripped my bag so tightly my knuckles ached. I felt like I was going to explode from the anxiety. I just desperately needed Jessica at my side, and I needed her right now.

title: Part 2: The Renton Transfer
content: The heavy TAPS Route 565 bus navigated the damp, gray morning streets, finally pulling into the Renton Transit Center. I stared out the rain-streaked window, my heart hammering a frantic, exhausted rhythm against my ribs. And then, I saw her. Sitting in her manual wheelchair by Bay 5, wearing a bright yellow raincoat that shielded her from the drizzle, was my older sister. Resting securely on her wheelchair’s lap tray were two small cups of hot chocolate and two wrapped Danishes. The air brakes hissed, and the pneumatic doors folded open. There was a decent-sized line of commuters trying, as I was, to exit the bus. The sudden press of bodies and the claustrophobia of the aisle made the process incredibly nerve-wracking. My mind was racing in a million different directions, still half-expecting Delores to suddenly materialize from the shadows and drag me back to Kent. There was a decent-sized line of commuters trying, as I was, to exit the bus. The sudden press of bodies and the claustrophobia of the aisle made the process incredibly nerve-wracking. My mind was racing in a million different directions, still half-expecting Brandi to suddenly materialize from the shadows and finish what she started, or for Delores to somehow ensure I had nowhere left to run. The driver looked down at the wheelchair waiting on the curb. "My bus?" he asked over the intercom. "No thanks," Jess answered, her voice projecting clearly through the rain. I stumbled off the bottom step, completely ignoring the other commuters. My exhausted legs gave out, but before I could hit the wet pavement, Jessica was there. She had already swung her lap tray safely out to the side, reaching out and catching me mid-stumble, wrapping her arms fiercely around my waist. "Just picking up my brother," Jessica finished, resting her chin on my shoulder and holding me tight as I leaned against her. !POV: Looking out from the stairs of the TAPS transit bus into the dark, rainy morning, Michael sees his sister Jessica waiting for him with hot food on the Renton Transit Center platform({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/rachel/b015/michael-jessica-renton-transfer.jpgfullwidth) She didn't ask questions. She wheeled backward, guiding us over to the loading area for the local Route 105. She picked up the cup and the pastry from her tray and offered them to me. "Here. Something to hold you until we get to my place," Jessica said, her voice dropping into a steady, logistical cadence to keep me grounded. "It’s not a long ride at all, but please eat quickly." "Quickly?" I asked, a fresh wave of exhausted sobs catching in my throat. I couldn't even hold the hot chocolate cup steady. "Because you’re not supposed to eat or drink on the bus," she explained smoothly, acting as if this were just a standard morning commute. "That’s why I only got us small ones." I choked down the pastry, the sugar hitting my depleted system like a shockwave. We finished our drinks right as the heavy Route 105 pulled up to the curb. The doors opened, and the driver immediately smiled. "Jessica! What are you doing up so early?" the driver called out. As he got the hydraulic ramp deployed, my sister didn't mince words. "Long story short, Adam, my brother was left for dead by his girlfriend’s aunt this morning. I’m taking him to my place." Left for dead, I repeated to myself, following her up the ramp. My brain was too sleep-deprived and traumatized to fully process the dramatic phrasing, but I figured it was entirely accurate. I took the fold-down seat directly across from the accessible bay as Adam secured her wheelchair to the floor restraints. "Thanks," I sobbed, burying my face in my hands. "It’s a short ride to my place on Edmonds Avenue," Jessica told me, ignoring the other passengers. "When we get there, I’ll show you my room, and then I’m going to make omelets with ham and cheese, exactly like Mom used to do on Sundays." It wasn’t too long before Jessica reached up and hit the yellow stop-request strip. "It’s that complex right there," my sister said, pointing through the window to a series of buildings across the street. She called forward to the operator. "Wheelchair getting off, Adam." We crossed the street and entered Jessica’s ground-floor apartment. The moment the deadbolt clicked shut behind us, the terrifying, unpredictable outside world was completely severed. "Now, I need to be honest about things," Jessica said, wheeling into the quiet, perfectly organized living room. "I’m not mad at you at all, Michael. I was afraid this would happen, and I am kicking myself for not having you come with me yesterday... but you’re here now." After showing me her bedroom and telling me to drop my junk in the corner, she turned her chair to face me, her eyes burning with an intense, protective fire. "She was controlling you. That family is incredibly toxic. I hate to say this, because I know you are hurting, but I am so incredibly glad you were kicked out." I started crying badly, my knees giving out as I sank onto the edge of her mattress. "Don’t cry," Jess said softly. She wheeled out to the kitchen, abandoning the omelet idea entirely. She realized I didn't have the stamina to wait for a cooked meal. She gathered a box of cereal and a bowl. "Here. Have some breakfast." As I sat there mechanically eating the cereal, I whimpered, "I can’t believe this is happening." "Let me be honest," Jessica said, sitting across from me. "You will find someone who treats you well. Delores treated you like gutter trash. Look at me. Rachel, Kristin, and I are going to spend Thanksgiving weekend with Dad and Cathy down in Vancouver. I’m going to let them know you’re going to be with us, too." She wheeled over to the table and pulled her cell phone out. She looked at the screen and sighed. "It’s only 6:35 AM. They won’t be up yet. I usually don't even get up until seven on a weekday." "I’m sorry I woke you up, Jess," I sobbed, the guilt twisting in my gut. "It’s okay," my sister replied immediately. "You needed to wake me, considering your situation." "Thank you for not being mad at me," I whimpered, terrified that the sudden logistical burden of my presence would make her angry. Jessica didn't use words to answer. She just leaned forward, wrapping her arms around my neck and hugging me fiercely to prove her loyalty. "Let me text Rachel," she said, pulling back. "When she gets up and calls, I’ll explain what happened. Don’t be upset, Michael. None of this is your fault. You are completely safe with me here in Renton." She quickly typed out a message to our younger sister: Delores dumped Michael – he is safe with me in Renton. Jessica set her phone down and looked at me critically. "When you’re done with your breakfast, please take a shower. I’m sorry, but Delores was a disgusting slob, and I’d be surprised if that house didn’t fail a health inspection. You don’t need her. Didn’t you find it disgusting, all the cat shit on the floor? I am not mad at you; I am just worried about you." The mention of that filthy house made my skin crawl. "You want me to take a shower?" I asked, my voice shaking. "Yes. I’m sorry for what she did to you. I want you to get washed. You’ll thank me later." "Jess, I’m sorry, but I just can’t," I started sobbing, pure panic spiking in my chest. The idea of going into a small, enclosed room and shutting the door behind me was terrifying. I couldn't handle the isolation. "Please. I don’t want you to... I don’t want to lose sight of you for even a single second right now," I snapped, my voice cracking with desperation. "It’s okay. It’s okay," Jess said calmly, raising her hands to de-escalate. Realizing I was exploding at the sister who had just rescued me, I burst into heavy tears and threw myself forward, burying my face in her shoulder. "I am right here," Jessica promised, accepting my hug without hesitation. "Rachel will be up here later. I know you’re angry and scared, and you have every right to be." She pulled back just enough to look me seriously in the eye. "I’d like to be honest with you. That morning at the Kent Train Station... I really wanted you to take the train with me to Seattle. I would’ve paid your fare, and I would’ve taken you straight to the Quantum campus with me." I blinked, the tears blurring my vision. "I would’ve been welcomed where you work?" "Yes. Given the situation, absolutely. My coworkers knew I wanted you out of that toxic environment, and yesterday afternoon, I was offered several rides to Kent to come physically extract you." "This is why you sent the text message telling me to come to Quantum?" I asked. "That’s right. That was my boss, Andromeda, on the phone while one of my coworkers was looking up the bus schedule. Remember the sandwich, drink, and chips you were offered? That was their direct response to you stating you hadn’t eaten since breakfast," Jessica replied gently. "To tell you the truth? Today, I was going to organize a team trip to Kent to drag you out of that slice of hell." I hugged Jessica even tighter, completely overwhelmed by the profound, structural safety net she had built for me without me even knowing. "Please don’t leave my side for even one second," I begged in a humiliated whisper. "Okay, here is what we will do, if you want," Jessica offered smoothly, pivoting her logistics. "I will come into the bathroom with you. I can help you if you need me to. At the very least, I should probably show you how to use a wheelchair-accessible shower." "You would be in the bathroom with me?" I asked nervously. "Sure. You don’t want to be alone for even a second because you are terrified right now. I am your sister. It is nothing we haven’t seen before when we were kids." "Thank you," I whispered. "I just feel so incredibly dirty. They treated me like I wasn't even a person." "You are a person," Jessica said fiercely. "You are my brother. And we are going to wash that filth completely away." I slowly, nervously got undressed. Jessica transferred to her wheelchair and wheeled into the bathroom, leaving the door wide open. "I will stay right here the whole time, exactly as promised," she assured me. She handed me a towel and pointed to the controls. "Please, help yourself to my things. Shampoo, body wash, use whatever you need. We can always go out later to get something specifically for you. Please, sit on the shower seat, and take as long as you need to clean yourself." I sat under the hot spray, letting the water scald my skin. I scrubbed my arms, my chest, and my hair, desperately trying to wash the suffocating stench of Aunt Lynne's house down the drain. Jessica sat quietly in her chair just outside the spray, acting as an unshakeable, physical anchor. "Is there anything you’d like to do today?" Jessica asked as I finally turned the water off and reached for the towel. "Quantum knows that I need to comfort you, and I am using a Paid Time Off day today." "Could I please get some sleep?" I yawned, the hot water finally pushing my exhausted body past its breaking point. "This is going to sound awful... but they kept me up all night." "What happened?" Jessica asked gently, her voice dropping into a careful, investigative register as we moved back to her bedroom. "You started mentioning something before our showers." She transferred from her wheelchair to her bed, turning the small radio on the nightstand to a low volume to provide some ambient white noise. "Please tell me everything. Take as much time as you need." She pulled her laptop over, plugged it in, and turned it on, giving me the space to speak without demanding direct eye contact. "Take as long as you need," she reassured me. I decided to pull my own cheap laptop out of my bag, plugging it in just to have something to hold onto. "A 110L? Eh," Jessica observed the outdated machine. "How about this: remember me taking you and Rachel to Broil’s down in Oregon?" "Yeah, why?" I sobbed. "There’s a Broil’s that’s a hop, skip, and a 240, 564, or 565 away on Garden Ave. It’s about a twenty-minute bus ride from here. Would you like a better laptop? We can go later today after you’re rested." I dropped the computer entirely. I practically threw myself across the mattress, hugging my sister very tightly, unable to hold it in anymore. "They kept me up all night," I started, my entire body shaking violently. "They came into the room completely naked. They promised me a night of wild sex, but it wasn't a promise, Jess. It was a trap." I sobbed into her shoulder. Jessica wrapped her arms around my back, holding me securely. "They locked the door," I choked out, the horrifying memories rushing back. "Delores and her cousin just... they took turns. They wouldn't let me sleep. My internal clock was screaming because it was three in the morning East Coast time, and my brain was so scrambled I couldn't even process what was happening. Around two in the morning, Brandi snickered and said, ‘just wait until four.’ They just used me." I sobbed some more, my chest heaving. "They forced me to touch them. I couldn't say no. I was trapped in that room, and Aunt Lynne was sleeping downstairs guarding the door. I just wanted to go to sleep." Jessica's face hardened into a mask of pure, glacial fury. "They coerced you. You were exhausted, terrified, and they assaulted you." I nodded, the tears soaking her shirt. Jess spoke the undeniable truth, but it was agonizingly painful to acknowledge it out loud. "Suddenly I heard a pounding at the door," I finished, my voice a hollow whisper. "Aunt Lynne told me to get my junk and get out. Then I found myself shoved onto the 159 in the pouring rain at 5 AM. Then I called you, and here I am." Jessica stroked the back of my head. "This is why you want me in the room with you right now?" I nodded yes. My sister leaned back against the pillows, allowing me to snuggle securely into her arms. She was trying her absolute best to comfort me, fully understanding that my perimeter had been violently, catastrophically breached. !Jessica comforting Michael on her bed as he breaks down in tears({{CDN}}/raggiesoft-books/images/scenes/rachel/b015/michael-jessica-apartment-comfort.jpgfullwidth) "You can sleep right here on my bed," Jessica suggested softly. "I’ll get you up for lunch. I usually eat around 12:30, and then we’re going to catch the bus to Garden Ave so you can get a new laptop. A fresh start." "Please don’t leave my side," I begged, exhaustion finally dragging me under. "I wasn’t going to," my sister promised. She allowed me to rest heavily against her as she started typing on her work laptop. "It’s 8:00 AM now. Please rest as long as you need." "12:30 sounds fair," I yawned. Jessica gently moved my head to her pillows, pulled the heavy blanket over me, and, exactly as promised, she did not move an inch. It sure felt good getting a decent, secure nap in. I don't know how long I slept, but the radio on the nightstand slowly drifted into my consciousness. "You’re listening to KSEA-FM – Seattle, Olympia, Mt. Vernon – playing the Hits of Yesterday & Today," the cheerful DJ announced. "Up next is a listener request from Kent." A few minutes later, the very familiar, bubbly, synth-pop percussive opening of a well-known 80s synth-pop tune kicked in. It was Last December by Neon Horizon. The moment the chords registered in my brain, the phantom sensation of the Quantum corporate lobby and the humiliating memory of Delores dragging me away flooded my system. I threw myself violently across the mattress, burying myself into Jessica’s arms, and wailed. "What’s wrong?" my suddenly frightened sister asked, slamming her laptop shut. Through heavy sobs, tears, and general wailing, I was able to etch out the agonizing connection. "This is what she did to me! This is exactly what she did to me the year we took the Pathfinder to Rhode Island! She traps me, and she hurts me, and the music just plays!" My sister started tearing up, wrapping her arms around me and rocking me back and forth. She explained how she had cried all the way to work when she was dropped off at the Kent Train Station yesterday, because all she could think about was the horrific situation I was in. She reiterated how the Quantum team had been pleading with her to let them drive down to Kent to rescue me. Suddenly, Jessica’s cell phone rang on the nightstand. "It’s Rachel," she said, snatching the phone and immediately putting it on speakerphone so I could hear. "Rachel," Jessica announced, her voice dropping into her fierce, tactical register. "Delores threw Michael out and left him for dead in Kent this morning. I want you to know he is safely in Renton with me right now." "What happened?!" Rachel gasped, her raspy voice instantly filling with panic. "Remember when I reported to you and Kristin about that shithole house in Kent, and how snappish and controlling Delores was being to him yesterday?" Jess asked. "Yes, that no-good bitch," Rachel spat, her hatred absolute and unfiltered. "Rachel, I need you right now," I sobbed toward the phone, not holding any of my tears back. Jessica pulled me into the best hug she could manage from her seated position. "When I get off work at 2:00, I will be on the very next bus to Renton," Rachel promised fiercely. "I think Kristin should come too," Jessica added. "She gets off work at 2:00 as well. I’ll ask her to meet me at Lakewood, and we will get on the next 574," Rachel confirmed. I was still crying, and I could sense that hearing me break down like this was completely shattering both of my sisters’ hearts. "Have her bring overnight gear, including your long nightshirt, and the two of you come on up," Jessica instructed, managing the logistics perfectly. "I’ll figure out dinner when you both get into Renton. Also, Rachel... could you do me a big favor? Michael needs help feeling safe. He needs you to be here because Delores was an absolute monster." "I'll be right there," Rachel said, her voice filled with profound, protective understanding. Jessica gripped me tightly as the phone call ended. "You’re safe. You’re with me. I won’t let her into my apartment, and I don’t even think she knows where this building is. I swear as your big sister, I will protect you from her." The conversation was over. Jessica allowed me to just curl up in her arms, realizing that I was in the middle of an uncontrollable emotional breakdown. But through the tears, my brain was finally starting to wake up and process the reality of the morning. The nightmare was over. I was officially single again.

title: Part 3: The Broil's Run
content: 12:15 PM rolled around and Jessica gently prodded me awake. "Ready for lunch, sleepyhead?" Jessica asked, a soft, encouraging smile on her face. "Yeah, I think so," I mumbled, rubbing the exhaustion from my eyes. "I’m going to make PB&J sandwiches—two for each of us—with chips and soda," she said. "Does that sound good?" "Yeah, it’s simple and effective," I agreed, watching my sister expertly transfer from the mattress to her wheelchair. She led the way to the kitchen area. "We’re going to be on the bus at 1:10 and will be at Broil’s around 1:45 or so." She started assembling our lunch, the quiet, predictable mechanics of the task filling the apartment. Sitting at her dining table, eating a perfectly standard peanut butter and jelly sandwich, it felt incredible just to exist without the suffocating pressure of constantly calculating Delores's mood. The 240 dropped us off quite a ways up Garden Avenue. "I’ve been lobbying TAPS to get this stop moved closer for ages," Jessica explained with a tired sigh, locking her brakes for a moment as the bus pulled away. "We have to double back down the sidewalk to get to the entrance." When we finally walked through the massive double doors of Broil's Electronics, I couldn’t believe my eyes. The place was a sprawling, cavernous warehouse themed with massive, retro-futuristic sci-fi props, with endless aisles dedicated entirely to silicon, circuitry, and screens. "Jess, I don’t want to sound rude, but how much am I allowed to spend?" I asked, completely overwhelmed by the sheer volume of high-end hardware surrounding us. "I think I can spare four grand or so," she stated casually, as if she were talking about buying a cup of coffee, “You get whatever your heart desires.” I gasped, my feet stopping dead on the linoleum. "Four grand?!" I was absolutely not used to my big sister wielding that kind of financial artillery. Before I could recover from the shock, a polo-shirted sales associate walked up. "Good afternoon, Jessica. What brings you in today?" "My brother currently has an outdated Apex Meridian 110L, so I’m going to get him a real gaming rig," Jessica announced, immediately pushing her chair toward the main computer floor. I never realized just how fast Jessica could propel her manual chair when she was on a mission. "Jess, slow down!" I called out, jogging to keep up. "Oh, sorry," she laughed, banking smoothly into the laptop section. "Well, here we are. Now, you need a heavy-duty desktop replacement. I won’t settle for less than a bleeding-edge dual-core processor, 4 GB of RAM, and dual hard drives." I started scanning the massive, glowing 17-inch models on display. "Do you want a Blu-Ray drive?" Jessica asked, pointing to a sleek, piano-black machine boasting a top-tier mobile GPU. I blinked. "You can afford that?" "That’s no problem," my sister replied with a shrug. "Besides, it’s the new high-definition standard for movies, so you might as well future-proof it." Another associate wandered over to our aisle, checking in. "Finding everything okay? Oh, good afternoon, Jessica." "I’m getting my brother a real gaming rig," Jess repeated proudly. I ran my fingers over the keyboard of the massive flagship model. "Jess, I think I found the one I like. The specs are incredible. But... the placard says it only comes pre-installed with Quantum OS XN Home Edition. It just has a mail-in coupon for Clarity Home Premium when it releases next year." Jessica actually scoffed, a brilliant, corporate smirk crossing her face. "Don't even bother with the mail-in coupon," Jessica instructed smoothly. "Clarity went RTM for enterprise clients last week. The public doesn't get it until January, but trust me, you are not going to be stuck running a legacy Home Edition on my watch. I have your operating system handled." She turned her chair to face me. "I actually need to run a quick errand at my office in Building 35 after this anyway. Someday, when you're rested and fully recuperated, I’d love to take you on a proper tour of the Museum of Computer History on campus but today is strictly a quick in and out so we can get your rig operational." I looked at the massive, dual-hard drive beast sitting on the shelf, imagining the absolute, glorious isolation of losing myself in a 17-inch high-definition widescreen. "Yes. This is the one." Jessica nodded to the associate. "We'll take it. But we don't want to carry the massive cardboard box on the bus. Could you ring up a heavy-duty tech backpack to carry it in? And we'll need a weighted optical USB mouse and a premium mousepad to replace the trackpad." "I’m going to put this on my Broil’s account," Jessica told the associate, before looking back at me. "Michael, would you like to grab some games while we’re here?" "Yes, please," I said, a massive, genuine smile finally breaking across my face. "Alright," Jessica commanded, spinning her chair toward the software aisles. "Games, then a few server parts for my own rig, and you’re going to need a high-speed transfer cable." "A transfer cable?" I asked. "I don’t mind just reinstalling everything manually." "You’ll be thanking me later," Jess promised. "I'll make sure you have the software you need, but if there are any specific games or titles you want that aren't on these shelves, I’ll order them online with rush overnight delivery." When we finally reached the checkout lanes, I watched the associate carefully pack the 9.5-pound laptop, the power brick, the games, and the accessories into the new heavy-duty backpack. "Are you sure there’s no time to drop this off back at the apartment first?" I asked, hoisting the heavy backpack over my shoulders. Jessica checked her watch, her tactical transit radar pinging. "If we hustle, we might make the 564 express straight to Overlake. I still need to run to the office to grab something from my desk real quick, and if we miss this connection, the next bus isn't for an hour. I’m going to need you to push me. We have exactly five minutes. I’m trying to have it so that once we get back to the apartment, you don’t have to go back out." We burst out of Broil's and sprinted down the sidewalk. "There’s our bus coming around the corner!" Jess called out as the shelter came into view. "We just made it." We rolled up the hydraulic ramp. Jessica flashed her Quantum Blue Badge to the operator. "I need to pay my brother’s fare. He’s going Two-Zone." We skipped the apartment drop-off entirely, the heavy regional bus carrying us straight up Interstate 405. I watched the Washington landscape blur past, the heavy backpack full of expensive hardware resting securely between my feet. When the bus operator finally called out, "Overlake Transit Center," I looked out the window and couldn’t believe my eyes. Sprawling across the landscape was a massive, pristine, heavily forested corporate city of glass and steel. "So, this is where you work?" I asked, my voice hushed in pure amazement as I hoisted the heavy backpack onto my shoulders and stepped off the bus. "Yep, this is it," Jessica smiled, adjusting her messenger bag. "It’s not much, but it does the job." Of course, Jessica—completely accustomed to navigating the absolute epicenter of the global tech industry—was being modest. She knew this was my first time truly seeing the Quantum campus, and she let me soak in the sheer, overwhelming scale of her perimeter.

title: Part 4: The Corporate Perimeter
content: "I actually need to grab something from my office before we head down to Renton," Jessica explained, pointing down a wide, paved pedestrian artery that cut through the towering evergreens. "The employee shuttles don't take unbadged visitors, so we’re going to have to walk it." "No problem," I said, grabbing the rubber push-handles of her wheelchair. We crossed the busy intersection at 156th Avenue NE, leaving the concrete expanse of the Overlake Transit Center behind, and stepped directly onto the Quantum campus. It didn't feel like a standard office park. It felt like a pristine, futuristic university hidden inside a Pacific Northwest forest. People were walking past us wearing ID lanyards, speaking in rapid-fire technical jargon, completely immersed in the architecture of the digital world. Because this was my very first time setting foot on Quantum property, the sensory shock was absolutely staggering. My processor struggled to take in the sheer scale of the environment and the intimidating, quiet hum of a global tech empire. We walked for about ten minutes, navigating deep into the corporate perimeter, until the buildings began to shift from standard engineering blocks to a much quieter, highly secured executive cluster. Jessica pointed to a massive, imposing glass-and-steel structure looming on our left. "That is Building 33," Jessica explained, her voice dropping into a respectful, corporate register. "That is the executive suite. William Keswick’s office is right up there on the top floor. The absolute brain of Quantum." I stared up at the tinted windows, completely awestruck, my mind reeling at the fact that I was standing mere yards away from the office of the most powerful tech billionaire on the planet. "And my department," Jessica said, unlocking her brakes and pointing toward the sleek, multi-story structure right next door, "is right here. Building 35." I pushed her toward the entrance, the heavy glass sliding open to reveal a sprawling, high-security lobby. Jessica wheeled directly up to the main security desk, completely in her element. "Good afternoon, Jessica," the uniformed guard smiled, recognizing her instantly. He looked up at me with polite, calculating scrutiny. "Afternoon, Dave," Jessica replied, her voice radiating smooth, corporate authority. "I need to get my brother signed in as a visitor for the first time. Just a quick trip up to my office." I handed over my ID, feeling entirely out of place in my old sneakers and jacket, but standing next to Jessica gave me absolute clearance. The guard printed a sticky visitor badge with my name and the current date, handing it across the counter. I slapped it onto my chest, officially permitted inside the fortress. We took the elevator up to the Federal Enterprise Solutions floor. The doors opened to a quiet, hyper-focused maze of cubicles and server rooms. As I pushed her through the open-plan bullpen, I immediately noticed the dynamic shift. Junior developers and project managers looked up from their dual monitors, offering respectful nods and quick, deferential greetings of "Afternoon, Jessica" as we passed. She didn't just work here; she managed these people. She was a commander. Jessica didn't stop in the bullpen. She guided me down a wide, carpeted corridor toward the executive suites, finally stopping in front of a heavy, frosted glass door.
